💡 Key Takeaways
  • We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 2 Arsenal 2 in the Premier League.
  • Out of the 1,000+ games I have watched in person, the 4-4 draw with Arsenal 15 years ago is the match that most deserves the ‘game of two halves’ label.
  • A blind man could have seen the gulf in class between the two sides in the first half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 2 Arsenal 2 in the Premier League.

Out of the 1,000+ games I have watched in person, the 4-4 draw with Arsenal 15 years ago is the match that most deserves the ‘game of two halves’ label. This one – against the same opponents – wasn’t far off.

A blind man could have seen the gulf in class between the two sides in the first half. Arsenal outclassed Newcastle without trying. Newcastle looked petrified, and it looked like no one wanted the ball. Having said that, Arsenal only scored a single goal, and didn’t really come that close again. Our centre halves were good.

According to recent reports, the second half could not have been more different. Newcastle tore into Arsenal from the get-go, and the Gunners looked shell-shocked. By the time Arsenal had recovered their composure, Newcastle were 2-1 up. In my opinion, we were playing as well as we had all season.

Arsenal were bound to come back into it, and they did. They scored an equaliser, but that’s not to say Newcastle were overwhelmed. We were giving as good as we got, and continued to do so.

Having conceded, most Geordies were fearing the traditional last-minute winner for our opponents, and when the officials came up with nine minutes of injury time, it seemed nailed on.

Sources indicate that but Newcastle held firm, and got a deserved point against the reigning champions, and this season’s most likely winners. It was a triumph of belief, effort, teamwork and quality, and it had a galvanising effect on the black and white faithful. St James’ Park was rocking to a degree I haven’t witnessed since our opener against Liverpool.

It’s hard to give the players a sensible mark. Everyone was poor in the first half. Everyone was excellent in the second.

Lukáš Horníček 5 Not at fault for Arsenal’s first, may have done better for their second, but he always looked nervy and unsure with the ball at his feet. His distribution was poor and he never looked confident.

Sources indicate that amar Dedić 4 Good player, bad game. Stranded for Arsenal’s first and took a pointless yellow card way before half time. Subbed off at half time, a bold move by the manager, but the correct one.

Malick Thiaw 8 If it wasn’t for our centre halves, Arsenal could have been 3-0 up at half time. Their challenges, blocks and clearances kept Newcastle in the game. Just. The second half saw Thiaw liberated to pick his passes, get up the pitch and score Newcastle’s second from all of four inches.

Industry observers note that dan Burn 8 A captain’s innings. Kept the Gunners from tearing us apart in the first half and made a nuisance of himself in attack in the second. I thought he wouldn’t get much game time this campaign. Now he’s one of the first names on the team sheet.

Lewis Hall 6 People – me included – were calling him the best left back in the world this week. I still think he is…but he wasn’t anything like that in that first half. Was mugged for Arsenal’s first and made a few other errors. He typified Newcastle’s second half – a much improved performance. Got up the pitch and had Arsenal on the back foot. Went off with what looked like a strain. Let’s hope it’s nothing serious.

Sources indicate that sean Steur 5 The game passed him by in the first half and he didn’t appear for the second. I don’t think he was bad, just not particularly effective.

In a recent development, lewis Miley 6 A mate of mine thinks he was our best player. I just thought it was a decent game from Lewis. Not exactly dominant, but decent on the ball, and another wiho improved in the second half. Had a run at goal which nearly came off.

According to recent reports, jacob Murphy 5 I only remember Newcastle having one attempt in the first half and it was Murphy who had it. It was on target as well, except it hit his own team-mate. Other than that, Jacob offered little else and was hooked at half time.

In a recent development, joe Willock 6 He’d be on a 7 or 8 if he got his head up and passed the ball instead of taking on ridiculous long distance shots. I thought he had a decent game, to be fair, and was full of energy. It looked to me like he played deeper in the second half and it worked. I think he got a dodgy assist for Thiaw’s goal.

According to recent reports, harvey Barnes 8 Another who seemed like a bystander in the first half but who came to life in the second. Scored the goal that gave us belief and even went past his man a few times on the wing. Well played lad.

In a recent development, william Osula 6.5 There will be some who say Osula ‘did nowt’ in the first half but I think that was due to his team-mates being pinned back in their own half. He was isolated, although he indicated his usual willingness to run. Second half was a different game. His colleagues actually got up the pitch to support him and he looked much better. A good assist for our first goal and it became a more confident display.

Industry observers note that tino Livramento 7 I’d forgotten what an excellent footballer Tino can be. He came on for the second half and looked like the player we saw two seasons ago. Quick, intelligent and good on the ball. It’s fair to say the half-time substitutes improved the team; none more than Tino.

It has been revealed that anthony Elanga 5.5 To be truthful, he didn’t do a lot with the ball that I remember, but he did inject pace and energy, qualities that were non-existent first half. We looked a different team. We were a different team.

Jacob Ramsey 6 We looked more secure when Jacob entered the fray. Suddenly our midfield looked better than Arsenal’s. Played some good balls but skied a shot that could have won us the game.

In a recent development, yoane Wissa 4 On for a tiring Willock. Found it difficult to get into the game.

In a recent development, sven Botman 5 Came on at a time when most fans’ hearts were in their mouths – Arsenal were looking dangerous. But Sven held his own and looked the part. Relief all round.

West Ham 1-1 Preston: Scott Parker Still Struggling To Unlock Jarrod Bowen

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division.
  • Recent findings suggest that edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did.
  • Sources indicate that the statistics certainly make for interesting reading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division. Whilst we had our chances, it would be a long stretch to suggest we were significantly better than Preston, particularly during a first half in which the visitors created opportunities of their own.

Recent findings suggest that edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did. In essence, the Hammers lacked magic, and watching our best player pinned to the right flank was depressing.

Sources indicate that the statistics certainly make for interesting reading. West Ham registered 30 attempts on goal, but only four were on target. We also hit the woodwork three times, with Bowen and Joël Veltman striking opposite posts during the same passage of play before Edvin Austbø rattled the crossbar shortly after half-time.

Preston took the lead through Liam Lindsay after just 18 minutes, following a corner which Joël Piroe inadvertently flicked towards his own goal.

Konstantinos Mavropanos eventually equalised on the hour mark, heading home Arne Engels’ cross after Manor Solomon had helped create the opening.

Yet even after drawing level, West Ham couldn’t find a winner against a team who arrived at the London Stadium bottom of the Championship.

Sources indicate that there were chances, certainly. Tomáš Souček had a late header tipped over, while Mavropanos headed over in stoppage time. But for all the possession and pressure, there was precious little composure in front of goal.

And as far as I’m concerned, this was a match West Ham simply had to win.

What makes the situation particularly frustrating is that we’ve already seen what Bowen can do when he’s given more freedom.

Sources indicate that during the remarkable comeback against Cardiff City, our captain was allowed to drift into central positions, where he caused all sorts of problems. His movement, passing and ability to find space helped transform a game which had looked completely lost at half-time.

I was so impressed that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker needed to restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon.

Unfortunately, against Blackburn, Bowen was back operating as a conventional right winger. And against Preston, we saw much the same thing.

That’s not to suggest Bowen didn’t contribute. He was involved throughout and managed eight attempts on goal, including the effort which struck the post.

But there’s a difference between getting Bowen involved in the game and getting the best out of him.

West Ham have spent far too long relying on our captain to produce something special from wide positions, often with defenders able to anticipate where he’s going to receive the ball.

Against Cardiff, we briefly saw something different.

In a recent development, bowen was the inspiration behind that second-half recovery. He looked far more dangerous when he was able to move into the middle and influence the game rather than remaining tied to the touchline.

I genuinely thought Parker had stumbled upon something which could change West Ham’s season.

Instead, two matches later, we seem to have gone backwards.

Of course, the manager has plenty of other complications demanding his attention.

There were some positives against Preston. Álvarez made his first Championship appearance for West Ham since May 2025 and looked reasonably comfortable in midfield, while young goalkeeper Finlay Herrick produced an excellent double save to prevent the visitors doubling their lead.

Mavropanos also deserves credit for another vital goal, particularly given that he is a centre-back who continues to contribute at the other end of the pitch.

But the bigger picture remains deeply concerning.

West Ham simply had to start turning the London Stadium into somewhere opposition teams feared visiting.

Instead, the bottom club have come away with a point, and Parker has now overseen two draws and a defeat in his first three matches.

I appreciate he hasn’t been in the job long, and I’m not suggesting he’s solely responsible for problems which have been developing for some considerable time.

However, the international break gave him an opportunity to work with the players, and I had hoped to see considerably more improvement than we witnessed.

For me, the biggest concern remains our inability to get the best out of Bowen.

We have a player capable of providing the creativity, movement and unpredictability that this team so desperately needs. Yet we’re still asking him to spend most of his time playing in the same predictable areas of the pitch.

It has been revealed that west Ham don’t lack effort. Against Preston, they certainly didn’t lack possession or attempts on goal.

And until Scott Parker finds a way of giving Jarrod Bowen the freedom to provide it, I fear we’re going to see plenty more afternoons like this one.

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER and KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

Thomas Frank has been unveiled as Crystal Palace’s upcoming manager on a two-and-a-half-year deal.

Frank has been out of work since being sacked by Tottenham Hotspur in February and has taken a significant pay cut to take over at Palace, who languish at the bottom of the Premier League.

However, he will earn more than his predecessor, Pierre Sage, who was sacked last week after winning just two of his ten league matches in charge.

Recent findings suggest that fresh Palace boss Frank noted: ‘It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic Football Club. I'm really, really looking forward to it.

‘Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them.’.

Across his spells at Brentford and Tottenham, Frank has managed 178 Premier League matches with a 34 per cent win rate.

Palace are set to approach Chelsea about Bernardo Cueva, who worked with Frank at Brentford before being poached to become the Blues' set-piece specialist.

We are pleased to confirm the appointment of Thomas Frank as Manager 🤝ℹ️ https://t.co/2wUzZAGt4S pic.twitter.com/zv2vMPGPFz.

Palace are set to approach Chelsea about Cueva (right), who worked with Frank at Brentford.

Industry observers note that but Cueva may now be elevated back to the forefront of football if Palace can strike an agreement to bring him in to join Frank’s backroom staff. It is stated Chelsea paid Brentford around £1million in compensation to hire him in 2024 at a time when his stock was high.

Cueva arrived at Chelsea in 2024. However, Daily Mail Sport revealed in the last summer how the 39-year-old Mexican’s role was changing after two seasons of work as Xabi Alonso’s side hired Austin MacPhee from Aston Villa as their new lead on set-plays.

Cueva has not been seen since then, either in training at Cobham or at matches at Stamford Bridge, but continued to work for Chelsea in more of an analytical role behind the scenes.

Club sources stressed at the time that it should not be seen as a demotion, and he is still listed on the first-team staff section of the website under the title ‘technical analyst’.

Chelsea are due to play Palace in two weeks' time at the Bridge on Wednesday, December 2.

Chelsea previously identified Cueva as a prime candidate for a role which had been vacant since Anthony Barry exited for Bayern Munich. Cueva, who also holds a UEFA Pro Licence through the Football Association, was regarded as an impressive acquisition in 2024.

In a recent development, before joining Brentford in 2020 and helping them secure promotion to the Premier League, Cueva was at Chivas in his homeland of Mexico. He has also had a role with Norway men's national team.

Tech Report: And so it came to pass with Bruno Guimaraes… Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The reaction to the departure of Bruno Guimaraes seems to have overshadowed that of Alexander Isak.
  • Fans had assumed the Brazilian’s deep connection with the United faithful was mutual, so discovering it was a bit more one-sided than anyone believed, only heightened the sense of betrayal when he left for the Emirates.
  • Some writers on The Mag were asked for 50 words on Bruno Guimaraes ahead of this match; most accepting that he’s still a legend, but that the manner of his departure left a sour taste such that he shouldn’t have been immune to a tempestuous reception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The reaction to the departure of Bruno Guimaraes seems to have overshadowed that of Alexander Isak.

Fans had assumed the Brazilian’s deep connection with the United faithful was mutual, so discovering it was a bit more one-sided than anyone believed, only heightened the sense of betrayal when he left for the Emirates.

Some writers on The Mag were asked for 50 words on Bruno Guimaraes ahead of this match; most accepting that he’s still a legend, but that the manner of his departure left a sour taste such that he shouldn’t have been immune to a tempestuous reception.

And so it came to pass; Guimaraes was roundly booed and jeered, with both his greed and his parentage loudly called into question, which felt a touch ironic, given how the faithful had once adored his father, a man who used to sit in the away end and soak up the adulation.

As it happens, Bruno was largely anonymous and replaced by the more energetic Lewis-Skelly when his side was trailing, although he hadn’t been far from converting a Declan Rice cross in the 28th minute, something that would have amounted to a low blow for most of the 52,661 crowd had his effort found its way into the back of the net.

That chance came just before Arsenal’s dominance saw them ahead. Kai Havertz dispossessed Lewis Hall high up the pitch and slid a sublime pass to Eberechi Eze, who whipped the ball past Lukas Hornicek.

Newcastle were struggling and it was what I’d expected, pre-match bonhomie with old friends and the lad, fueled by some decent ale, had swiftly evaporated when the team was announced.

Right on half-time, Madueke, who had already hit the base of the post in the sixth minute, passed up a golden opportunity to double Arsenal’s lead, as some of the boos that had been reserved for Bruno were now being directed at those in the black and white.

Thank goodness Matthias Jaissle had both seen enough and managed to hold his nerve, a decisive triple substitution that introduced Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey, and Anthony Elanga into the fray proving transformational.

Just four minutes after the restart, Joe Willock pressed Martin Odegaard into a costly mistake on the Arsenal left. Will Osula scooped up the loose ball and teed up Harvey Barnes, who fired clinically past David Raya to register United’s first home strike in over two months.

Barnes will tear you apart echoed around the stadium, Dedic unable to join in with the bow and arrow celebrations, Livramento now doing a better job at right back, whilst Ramsey had shored up the midfield as Steur’s replacement and Elanga looked a whole lot better than the lethargic Murphy.

Energised by a crowd that was itself suitably invigorated, United turned the game on its head.

In the 62nd minute, Lewis Hall’s corner was nodded back across goal by an unmarked Dan Burn. This sparked a frenetic goalmouth scramble that ended with Malick Thiaw poking home from close range, a goal confirmed after an agonising VAR check that looked at supposed handball and offside offences, that feeling of dread never materialising as Chris Kavanagh finally signalled the goal would stand.

At this stage, United were very much on top but just couldn’t muster that elusive third, and when David Raya left the field following a collision with Osula in the 70th minute, rather than worsen the Gunners evening, the long break before Kepa Arrizabalaga replaced his compatriot allowed them to regroup and turn the tide.

I’d said to the lad that this was going to be a long twenty minutes, possibly half an hour, for us to negotiate and somewhat inevitably, Arsenal hit us on the counter in the 78th minute.

It has been revealed that released down the flank by Odegaard, Noni Madueke cut inside to drill a shot that squirmed through Hornicek’s grasp to level the scores. Could he have saved it? Maybe, all that good work at Craven Cottage a fortnight ago undone in an instant.

At this point, had anyone feared an Arsenal winner was coming, that might have been justified, they are a very good team and their substitutions demonstrated a squad that has strength in depth.

But the final stages, including nine minutes of added time, saw both sides pushing for a winner and it’s Newcastle that will feel more aggrieved, first Kepa denied Lewis Miley before Havertz nearly scored an own goal, the crossbar coming to his rescue as the spoils were shared.

Recent findings suggest that I wrote an article for The Mag recently highlighting that United had picked up five more points from their opening ten fixtures when making a comparison with the same fixtures from the previous campaign. You can make that six following yesterday’s gutsy performance, and you never know, Matty Jaissle might just be getting the hang of things in the St James’ hotseat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

That eight point gap between West Ham United in tenth and the Championship front runners is starting to look mighty huge with just sixteen games completed.

Of course the reality is that there are still thirty games remaining but West Ham will have to find a way of converting all the huffing and puffing into points or else we will find ourselves scratching around even trying to make the enlarged play off places come May next year.

“Wasteful West Ham”: Not my words but the description on the official club web site which sums up perfectly an afternoon of toil and frustration against the bottom side in the league.

Scott Parker pronounced himself happy with the effort, if ‘bitterly disappointed’ with the result. As were we all.

The team announcement produced a wave of optimism, and I’m not sure yet that we should ditch that: Tenth place is not where we expected to be at the end of November but there is still plenty of time to turn the West Ham supertanker back on course and away from the rocky peril of mid table, second division mediocrity.

But three years’ decline won’t be fixed in three games.

In a recent development, introducing Fin Herrick and Edson Alvarez were bold decisions which could have backfired totally, especially after the maddening concession in the first half. Now Scott Parker needs to keep his nerve and persevere with that set up, go again on Tuesday night away at Fratton Park and trust for better luck and better finishing.

Ninety points still up for grabs this season, Hammers.

At least the ownership saw fit to ditch Nuno in time to turn the ship around. In the bad old days of David Sullivan, we’d still be on about game 5 of 20 ‘must win’ games before Nuno had to walk the plank. (Not sure where all the nautical terms came from this morning).

In any case, there’s not another manager who’d do any better in Scott Parker’s place right now. Don’t panic. Yet. COYI!

Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki have both been left out of Manchester City’s starting lineup for this afternoon’s Premier League fixture against Fulham at the Etihad Stadium.

The Citizens are seeking to bounce back from a run of three successive top-flight defeats, most recently losing 3-1 away against Nottingham Forest before the international break.

Manager Enzo Maresca has made a total of three changes to the side that were beaten at the City Ground, with Fernandez, Cherki and Josko Gvardiol all dropping down to the substitutes’ bench.

While Cherki scored in the defeat to Forest, Gvardiol was at fault for a first-half goal conceded by City and Fernandez’s position in midfield has come under question in recent weeks.

Ayyoub Bouaddi will start just his third Premier League game at the expense of Fernandez, while Phil Foden and Nico O'Reilly have been brought in for Cherki and Gvardiol respectively.

While Matheus Nunes missed out through injury, Abdukodir Khusanov has shaken off a knock to start at right-back, joining O'Reilly, Marc Guehi and Ruben Dias in a four-man defence protecting goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Bouaddi will links arms with Elliot Anderson in centre-midfield, with Foden set to operate in the number 10 role between wingers Iliman Ndiaye and Jeremy Doku.

Leading the line is goal machine Erling Haaland, who has scored eight goals in as many games against Fulham and is looking to net his 10th Premier League goal of the campaign this afternoon.

As for Fulham, head coach Alvaro Arbeloa has also made a total of three changes to the team that rescued a 1-1 draw with Newcastle United a fortnight ago.

The headline alteration see Gonzalo Garcia begin as a substitute for the first time since joining the Cottagers in the summer following a run of nine straight starts without a goal.

Rodrigo Muniz, who scored a late equaliser off the bench against Newcastle, has been rewarded with his first league start of the campaign at Garcia’s expense.

It has been revealed that arbeloa has also opted to change his full-backs, with Kenny Tete and Ryan Sessegnon coming in for Timothy Castagne and Antonee Robinson. Calvin Bassey and David Affengruber retain their places at centre-back, though.

Man City academy graduates Shea Charles and Oscar Bobb both start against their former club, with the former to play alongside Sander Berge in midfield and the latter continuing on the right flank.

Manchester City starting lineup: Donnarumma, Khusanov, Dias, Guehi, O’Reilly; Bouaddi, Anderson; Ndiaye, Foden, Doku; Haaland.

According to recent reports, subs: Rulli, Kovacic, Cherki, Fernandez, Reis, Gvardiol, Allan, F. Samba, Lewis.

Fulham starting lineup: Leno; Tete, Affengruber, Bassey, Sessegnon; Berge, Charles; Bobb, King, Iwobi; Muniz.

Subs: Kaiser, Castagne, Cuenca, Robinson, Larsson, Cairney, Angel, Palacios, Garcia.

An increase to the St James’ Park capacity was officially confirmed by Newcastle United, this news came on the Friday (21 August 2026) afternoon ahead of the Liverpool match.

The Newcastle United owners announcing the St James’ Park increased capacity as part of a number of improvements (see below).

Sources indicate that the official announcement stating: ‘We’ve expanded our safe standing provision with the introduction of fresh safe standing areas on Level 7. Thanks to additional work carried out by our operations team, we’ve also increased stadium capacity by approximately 500 seats, taking St. James’ Park’s capacity to 52,719 – enabling more supporters to experience live football in person.’.

Industry observers note that obviously not the tens of thousands increase in stadium capacity that we are all waiting to hear about BUT every little helps. Up to another 500 Newcastle United fans extra able to get into each St James’ Park match.

For the Liverpool match it was a latest Premier League era home record attendance for Newcastle United, a crowd of 52,630.

That St James’ Park record in the Premier League era was then broken again when 52,643 was the official attendance for the Bournemouth game on 5 September.

Then on September 19 against Hull City, the PL era record at SJP broken yet again, with 52,647 inside St James’ Park.

Now on Saturday 21 November for the 2-2 draw with Arsenal, edging up to 52,661.

That 21 August 2026 announcement also included: ‘We’ve invested £10 million into our hospitality offering, delivering one of the most extensive upgrade programmes ever undertaken at St. James’ Park. Highlights include full refurbishments of the Chairman’s Suite, and transformation of The Magpie into a stunning new pitch view hospitality space, Tidings. Plus, we’ve reimagined Heroes into Icons, which is a tribute to Newcastle United legends and inspired by one of the club’s most iconic retro kits. Additional improvements have been made across the Barracks, Four Corners and Moncur Suites, alongside the transformation of 22 executive boxes.’.

The St James’ Park pitch also having money spent on it: ‘This summer has also seen a significant investment in the heart of the stadium, with £3.6 million invested in a brand-new pitch structure; the first complete replacement in 21 years. The project includes the installation of a state-of-the-art SubAir system, helping to maintain playing conditions throughout the season.’.

The club also detailing: ‘Over the summer, we’ve completed a stadium-wide PA system upgrade and invested £2 million in a new LED floodlighting system, complete with a backup generator to improve resilience.

Work has also continued on improving mobile connectivity through the rollout of full stadium 5G infrastructure, helping supporters stay connected on matchdays. We’ve also installed four new in‑bowl replay screens, enhancing visibility of replays and key moments during games for supporters across the stadium.’.

Industry observers note that just over one year ago, West Ham’s Finlay Herrick was stepping out on loan for Boreham Wood in the National League – the fifth tier of English football. A far cry from London Stadium yesterday as he replaced Mads Hermansen in goal and made his Championship debut, apparently hearing about his impending start just on the morning of the game.

And despite the first half concession from the corner, Herrick did a pretty fair job with excellent double saves later in the game and some assured glove work catching the ball – which had seemed like a lost art at times in the last couple of years.

Herrick after his unforgettable FA Cup penalty shootout debut last year.

This was a massive gamble by Scott Parker which could have backfired dreadfully. With no Areola, the temptation must have been to revert to Hermansen yet the Hammers’ head coach stuck with his instinct. After the first half goal concession, Parker must have wondered – briefly – whether he’d made a huge howler.

Has Herrick done enough to keep his place? It seems Parker is dead set on replacing Hermansen so until Alphonse Areola is ‘fit and ready’ then Herrick should be prepared for more pitch time. He certainly has the ambition:.

“I hope this is the start. I hope I’ve done myself justice and proved to the fans that I don’t just want to be third choice, I want to be playing, I want to get back to the Premier League and be part of that”. (whu/youtube).

Describing the competition amongst the trio of goal keepers, Herrick was quick to praise Hermansen for the encouragement and help he’s received recently, describing the three keepers as a team more than individuals fighting amongst themselves for the sole starting spot:.

“There’s one goal keeper shirt and there’s three of us – but we’re like a band of brothers and we always stick together, me Mads and Fonz- no matter what. “.

It has been revealed that difficult to believe Herrick is still only 20 – he seems to have been around West Ham’s fringes for ever- but he joined the academy at six years old and looks to have the talent to go all the way. From yesterday’s solid start, he didn’t let his manager or his team mates down and should feel rightly pretty proud of himself.

The question for Scott Parker is whether he continues between the sticks at Fratton Park on Tuesday night.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I left the London Stadium to a chorus of boos, I found myself desperately searching for positives from a frustrating 1-1 draw against the league’s bottom club.

The first was the performance of Alvarez. Largely cast into the shadows through the stubbornness of our former manager, he grabbed the game by the scruff of the neck. He took control, lifted the crowd, and, above all, displayed the leadership qualities this team has lacked for much of the season.

Sources indicate that the second positive was that the statistics backed up what I’d watched unfold on the pitch. West Ham dominated possession with 79%, registered 30 shots, and recorded an xG of 3.13. The problem? Only four of those efforts were shots on target.

We gifted Preston their opening goal. It came from a calamitous mix-up, with Piroe’s flicked header looping backwards onto the crossbar before dropping kindly for Liam Lindsay to tap home from close range. It could be argued that Herrick should have been more commanding from the corner, but he made amends later with an excellent double save.

There were concerns that we wouldn’t pull one back, we did on the 60th minute, Mavropanos heading home his sixth goal in 15 league appearances this season.

According to recent reports, “Ifs” and “buts” don’t win football matches, and as Parker noted afterwards: “The overall performance suggests we should win. The fine margins of football are, and the reality is, if Tomas Soucek scores that last-minute goal, it’s probably a different interview.”.

According to recent reports, for me, I’m not going to be negative. We needed a win and we didn’t get the three points, but what I want to see now is the team build on the domination, the chance creation and the shot volume by going to Fratton Park on Tuesday and getting the job done. If we concede first there and deliver an abject performance, then and only then will there be more serious questions to ask.

Having been promoted from Serie B last season, Frosinone have been the surprise package so far in Serie A barring perhaps the league-leaders Lazio, as they sit sixth in the table having won six of their opening 11 games so far.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

They were heavily tipped to be in a relegation battle by pundits and the bookmakers, and yet they have scored 24 goals and allowed just 15, making them not just an effective team but also an entertaining one too.

The summer arrival Schmid – who signed from Werder Bremen – has been a part of that. He spoke at a press conference two days before Frosinone’s trip north to face Milan at San Siro. The questions and his responses were relayed by TuttoFrosinone.

After Cagliari, what will the match against Milan be like?

“The match in Milan will be completely different from the one in Cagliari. Milan are obviously the favourites, their game is different from Cagliari’s, and we’ll need a more proactive Frosinone.”.

How are you finding Serie A as a league?

Recent findings suggest that “It’s different from the Bundesliga, I like it. You have to always be on top of things otherwise you lose the duels, especially in midfield.”.

Did the fact that they play with a 4-2-3-1 like with Austria influence your choice to come to Frosinone?

“It’s not the main reason. With the national team, we don’t play man-to-man like here against Frosinone. It’s a similar game because we definitely play deep, we attack high.”.

Why did you miss Austria’s last match?

“My son had a problem, it wasn’t serious but he wasn’t feeling very well and since we had already qualified I preferred to stay with the family”.

You are one of the most key signings in Frosinone’s history, and it’s no coincidence that you started playing immediately under Alvini. How do you feel?

In a recent development, “My past performances in the Bundesliga were crucial; that’s one of the reasons Froisnone chose me, given my previous performances. They’re similar to what I played under coach Alvini. I’m enjoying myself and I’m happy.”.

Where do you prefer to play, in the attacking midfield role or in the pivot?

“My favourite position is number 10, an attacking midfielder behind the centre-forward. I feel comfortable playing there, I’ve also tried playing further back, but my favourite position is still number 10.”.

“I haven’t played PlayStation for the last 4-5 years, since I became a father. Last night my wife downloaded the game and we played together.”.

According to recent reports, yesterday was a bizarre and surreal experience at the London Stadium as we watched West Ham’s half-hearted attempts to beat a stubborn Preston North End side. Sure, the Hammers had 30 shots and an impressive 79% slice of the possession pie. But scratch below the surface and there are still major problems with Scott Parker’s team, some of which I suspect will not be sorted out until the January transfer window.

Despite West Ham’s impressive array of shots, passes and corners, I never truly felt that the team had the magic or the cutting edge to win the game. And as crazy as it sounds, considering we’d hit the post twice and had 14 corners, I don’t actually think we threatened enough. The Hammers lacked sparkle and magic, for sure.

Alvarez- first game back in claret and blue for a year and a half.

Edson Álvarez was an excellent addition to the team, but he is a defensive midfielder, and realistically, the defence was improved. Herrick made a bit of a blooper in goal for the opener, but I felt he redeemed himself with an excellent double save. By and large, West Ham restricted Preston’s chances, and so we should have done. After all, they’re the worst team in the division.

According to recent reports, but our biggest problems came in attack. Edvin Austbø on the left wing flattered to deceive, cutting inside and shooting just off target at one point, but never really terrorising his marker, despite the fact that he had him on a yellow card. Joël Piroe did okay but fluffed his big chance when put through by Arne Engels.

As for the supply line, Divine Mukasa flitted in and out of the game and did not create anywhere near enough, given his deployment in the number 10 position. Jarrod Bowen was wide. I mean, very wide for so much of the game that he was probably on first-name terms with the linesman. But realistically, he was just out of the game for large parts of it. We’ll get into more detail on that later.

Overall, it was nowhere near enough quality. Sure, we had momentum. Sure, we had possession. But this did not look like a group of Premier League-standard players against the worst team in the division.

Funny ha-ha or funny peculiar? Yesterday had plenty of both

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s a question: did last night’s Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2 match at St James’ Park show we can be the equal of the reigning Premier League champions?
  • At 16 minutes past six, after a miserably one-sided first half, you would have been embarking on mission impossible to find anyone saying “yes” among the 52,000+plus in the stadium or the millions watching on TV.
  • By the final whistle, blown nearly 10 minutes after the 90 by Chris Kavanagh, few would have replied “no”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a question: did last night’s Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2 match at St James’ Park show we can be the equal of the reigning Premier League champions?

At 16 minutes past six, after a miserably one-sided first half, you would have been embarking on mission impossible to find anyone saying “yes” among the 52,000+plus in the stadium or the millions watching on TV.

By the final whistle, blown nearly 10 minutes after the 90 by Chris Kavanagh, few would have replied “no”. Such is football.

According to recent reports, let’s start at the beginning, or at least on the 12.30 Azuma train from King’s Cross to Newcastle. The LNER service was predictably packed with Gooners. Passengers in Carriage J were overwhelming confident of a one-nil or two-nil to the Arsenal, as they like to crow in north London.

According to recent reports, based on their team’s results this season, that was to be expected. They don’t score many and, apart from a blip near Brighton, they concede even fewer.

In a recent development, arsenal are, in a word, efficient. I find them boring. The descriptions are not mutually exclusive. No way as the train rumbled into the magnificent Central Station about 32 minutes late was I looking forward to a feast of entertaining football.

In dire need of a drink, I walked up Pink Lane with Big Nige, who had boarded the delayed train at York after it made an unscheduled stop south of the old Viking stronghold of Jorvik. Known as Eboracum in Roman times, btw.

Industry observers note that pink Lane was awash with happy Londoners. There are many, many reasons to be proud of Newcastle; one is the warm welcome the natives offer strangers (excluding Mackems, obviously. There have to be limits).

Recent findings suggest that which was why the mild hostility that greeted me in the Mosaic Tap was a substantial surprise. A young chap called Rob walked up to our table, where Paul and Gowa had already got in the drinks, and mentioned: “You can’t wear that scarf in here.”.

His mate had apparently clocked me as a Gooner, having mistaken my half-and-half for an Arsenal favour.

Industry observers note that A little bit of background. Said scarf was a souvenir from the Bayer Leverkusen v NUFC match. Not that I bought it on my visit to the BayArena shop a mere 11 months ago, when it would have cost £20. This one was acquired in October for a tenner in the NUFC pre-Christmas online sale, while present-buying for my daughter Jo and her family. The PIF need all the help they can get . . .

It has been revealed that for all those who detest a half-and-half, that’s your prerogative. I view it as a reminder of a great trip, more useful than a match programme and less likely to be lost.

Rob promptly realised his error, probably because I had slipped into my best am dram persona by screaming: “Look at the scarf! Look at it! You need to go to Specsavers, mate!”.

The faux outrage reduced poor Rob to a gibbering, hilariously apologetic wreck. “Sorry, sorry, I’m really sorry. It was my mate . . . What are you drinking, can I get you one, please?”.

According to recent reports, the free glass of malbec was much appreciated, thanks. Considering the prices at Mosaic, the scarf has probably paid for itself. Funny ha-ha, Rob.

It has been revealed that we played the “who would you select” game and all four of us agreed Gonzalez was not justifying his place. Starting Steur was a no-brainer, the back five picked themselves, based on the Fulham game, with Livramento available if needed to give us a second-half lift. The midfield and attack, apart from Steur and Barnes, were as clear as a peasouper.

The significant news at 4.15 was Bruno G starting for his newly introduced team. Who had expected that?

Sources indicate that there was just time for a quick one in Bar Loco, where I bumped into the legendary Tony Mallabar, before safely negotiating Turnstile 31 at the Leazes End. My seat in row MM was in line with the edge of the six-yard box, which gave a perfect view of the fourth goal, unfortunately.

According to recent reports, the Booing of Bruno had been a hot topic. My opinion is that every opposition player should be relentlessly jeered, booed, abused and barracked (isn’t SJP on Barrack Road for a reason?) That’s what I recall, perhaps falsely, from substantial games in the Seventies . . .

Anyway, the Brazilian midfielder was booed from the warm-up until his replacement by Lewis-Skelly when we were leading 2-1. The effort of singling out our former captain probably backfired, because it distracted the more vocal supporters from doing the job of cheering their favourites.

In a recent development, not that the players or the play gave reasons to be buoyant in the first half. Arsenal did what Arsenal do, using their 11 players against our outfield 10. Whenever Osula or Willock or Murphy or Barnes or Steur attempted to put pressure on Raya, he found the spare man whom our would-be presser had just left unmarked. Boring and efficient by Arsenal. Half-cocked and aimless by the Mags.

In my opinion, Arsenal are no great shakes, whatever the title claims. A great team have a top, top striker. They don’t. As they proved by managing only one effort on target before the interval. Hornicek didn’t have a prayer once Hall chested down a long ball and instantly lost possession near the edge of his box.

Our left-back is a wonderful footballer but, having rarely played as a defender in his youth at Chelsea, he is still learning some of the skills essential to be a watertight obstacle.

Murphy tried to catch Raya off his line with a speculative long-range effort and one other shot flew narrowly wide of Raya’s left post via a deflection off Barnes. There was almost nothing else of note in the first half as the champions biffed nearly every shot high, wide and ugly.

It has been revealed that burn and Thiaw stood reasonably firm, Dedic and Murphy seemed on different wavelengths, Steur harried Bruno G and Barnes highlighted some unlikely aggression. Miley plugged away and Osula ran gamely but United lacked any sort of perceptible gameplan. We rarely managed to find a player in space. Worrying times.

Where was our next goal coming from, wondered my mate Dave at the interval. It had been a while at SJP.

The answer came within four minutes of the restart, soon after the first of three stoppages caused by apparent injuries to Raya. More importantly, after Matthias Jaissle made a triple substitution.

Harvey Barnes smashed a shot low to the keeper’s right, ending a quick attack. Willock had pressured Odegaard into presenting the ball to Osula. An assist on the headless chicken’s credits, fitting reward for another tireless display.

It has been revealed that this was when the match became funny peculiar. Miley man-marked Bruno, Arsenal misplaced passes, United won 50:50s, we found space to run with purpose. The gulf in monetary and player resources vanished as the Mags reverted to our best version of Howe-ball.

Only Hornicek of the summer 2026 signings was still on the pitch, Steur having been subbed.

Arsenal looked distinctly second-best. Raya went down again. A corner on our right from Hall was aimed beyond the far post, where the unstoppable Man from Blyth powered a header goalwards. In a frantic kerfuffle, a couple of blocks merely delayed the inevitable. Thiaw smashed it home and we were ahead.

Funny ha-ha and funny peculiar.

In a recent development, around me in row MM, the earlier, almost incessant moans and grounds became voices of encouragement. Supporters who had failed to back their team in a dire first half were suddenly full of the joys of November . . .

Recent findings suggest that ramsey, Livramento and Elanga all caused Arsenal problems. For a few minutes, we battered them.

Then Raya collapsed for a third time. The long delay gave the champions a break they desperately needed.

In a recent development, whatever anyone else says, Jaissle and his men were right to keep pressing for a third. Arsenal were always going to fashion at least one good chance in the time remaining after we went ahead. To sit back with 28 minutes left, plus a lot of stoppage time, would have been professional suicide.

Recent findings suggest that my suspicion is that those who now bemoan our aggressive play would have whinged even more if the team had sat back. The match became attack and counter-attack. Arsenal, through Madueke doing a decent impression of the absent Saka, kept cutting onto his left foot. Hall, sometimes having to mark two opponents, let the right winger swerve inside and slam a low shot through two defenders and past Hornicek.

The keeper got two hands to the ball but could only push it into the Leazes End net.

Industry observers note that havertz nearly produced what would have been a truly wonderful moment when his head diverted a late Hall corner beyond Kepa and against the crossbar. So near, yet so far.

Then Barnes capped what I reckon was his best game since Wembley 2025 by outstripping Rice on the left touchline and playing the ball perfectly to Ramsey on the edge of the 18-yard box.

In the words of John Ando Anderson, just hit the bloody thing, man. Ramsey did. Sadly, though, instead of putting his laces through it, he tried to bend the ball into the postage stamp and it flew high and wide.

Sources indicate that what a feather in Jaissle’s cap a win would have been. One point was good, three would have been great.

Recent findings suggest that the late introduction of Wissa, who replaced Willock, was a failure. He contributed almost nothing, which has been the story all too often since his expensive arrival.

I would have thrown on Fernandez-Pardo as the game opened up. No team enjoy speedy opponents running hard at them and the Belgium international could have been the joker in Jaissle’s pack.

On the balance of play a draw was reasonable but this, like the Liverpool result, felt like two points dropped.

Industry observers note that what is inarguable is the team’s willingness to battle for their mates, their manager and the Toon. Long may that continue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 21 Nov 2026 11:25.

Chelsea winger Mykhaylo Mudryk has continued his war of words with UAF president Andriy Shevchenko over the circumstances surrounding his failed drugs test.

Mudryk, currently on loan at Tottenham Hotspur, was given the green light to return to football in July 2026 after serving a ban of more than 18 months for testing positive for meldonium.

However, the winger did an interview earlier this week that reopened the saga, with the 25-year-old claiming that the drug could have only entered his system while on international duty with Ukraine.

Shevchenko, a former Chelsea striker and Ukraine legend, hit back at those suggestions, alleging that Mudryk wanted a UAF employee to take responsibility for his ban.

Recent findings suggest that he went as far as calling for Mudryk to retract his claims against the UAF and the Ukraine national team. Instead, Mudryk has since doubled-downed on his initial comments.

As quoted by BBC Sport, a statement read: "Neither I nor my representatives made any such request.

"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible.

"In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly highlights that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information.

"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case.

"For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong.".

Despite his previous status as Ukraine's best player, it feels unlikely that Mudryk will represent his country anytime soon.

There have been two opportunities for either Mudryk or Shevchenko to back down, but it is clear that both parties remain firm over their stance.

Mudryk is at the moment pushing to return from injury to feature for Spurs, his solitary appearance for the North Londoners having come in September.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses1,2. Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum, with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering fresh avenues for barley improvement.

Industry observers note that the genus Hordeum comprises approximately 33 species and is widely distributed across the temperate regions of Eurasia and the Americas1,2,3. Hordeum is classified into two subgenera based on cytogenetic evidence: one containing the H and Xu genomes and the other containing the I and Xa genomes4. The basic chromosome number is seven, and, although most species are diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid taxa have also been described. Cultivated barley (Hordeum vulgare) is the best known and most extensively studied species, as it represents one of the earliest domesticated cereal crops. Today, barley is the world’s fourth most important grain, valued for its use in food, animal feed and brewing5. Cultivated barley and its wild progenitor (H. vulgare subsp. spontaneum) constitute a single inter-fertile gene pool, allowing for frequent gene flow between wild and cultivated forms6. This primary gene pool has long been exploited by breeders to introduce desirable traits6. Hordeum bulbosum has contributed valuable disease resistance genes through introgression7,8,9,10 due to its ability to hybridize directly with cultivated barley. The other Hordeum species are not domesticated but have important ecological and agricultural roles in ecosystem stability, environmental adaptation and forage use11,12,13,14,15. Together, Hordeum is both an agronomically important genus and a powerful model for studying crop evolution, environmental adaptation and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. Factors such as incomplete lineage sorting, recurrent hybridization and gene flow partly obscure species boundaries, leaving major evolutionary questions unresolved1,2,4,16,17. Recent barley pangenomes have substantially advanced our understanding of genomic variation within cultivated barley and its closest relatives10,18,19. However, these studies were largely confined to two species (H. vulgare and H. bulbosum) and therefore could not resolve genome-wide evolutionary processes operating across the genus, including the origin of large-scale structural variation, ancient hybridization, polyploid genome evolution and the diversification of regulatory loci. Extending comparative genomic analyses to encompass the entire genus is therefore essential to capture the full breadth of diversity within the Hordeum gene pool and to facilitate both evolutionary studies and the effective utilization of wild germplasm for barley improvement. Pangenomics now offers comprehensive resources to address such complexity. In crops such as tomato, potato, maize, grapevine, citrus and cotton, genus-level pangenomes have uncovered extensive structural variations, gene presence–absence and evolutionary dynamics20,21,22,23,24. Investigating structural variations helps to explain evolutionary processes and can inform crop breeding strategies25. However, the full extent of structural variation within Hordeum remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we generated chromosome-scale genome assemblies representing all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. This comparative genomic framework provides a view of structural and regulatory genome evolution across the genus, yielding fresh insights into genome evolution and establishing a foundation for the utilization of wild diversity in barley improvement.

To maximize phylogenetic representation across the genus, we selected 27 accessions representing 24 Hordeum species, encompassing all recognized diploid genome groups1 together with representative tetraploid and hexaploid lineages (Extended Data Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–25). The dataset comprises 22 diploid accessions, 4 tetraploid accessions and 1 hexaploid accession. Twenty-four genome sequences were assembled using PacBio HiFi accurate long reads and Hi-C data (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Figs. 26–28), using the TRITEX pipeline26,27. The sequence assemblies of H. vulgare and H. bulbosum were sourced from our previous work10,28. The previously published chromosome-level assembly of Hordeum marinum H559 (ref. 29) was updated using the TRITEX pipeline, and previously published transcriptome data, Bionano optical maps and Hi-C data of Hordeum erectifolium NGB6816 were used30. The average contig N50 of the assemblies is 39.24 Mb. Assembly sizes range from 2.90 Gb to 4.48 Gb (mean, 3.92 Gb) in diploid species and from 7.49 Gb to 8.56 Gb (mean, 8.16 Gb) in tetraploid species, whereas the single hexaploid genome has an assembly size of 10.90 Gb. Chloroplast genome assemblies range from 136,335 bp to 137,079 bp (mean, 136,840 bp) (Supplementary Table 1). High assembly quality is supported by an average long terminal repeat (LTR) assembly index (LAI) of 14.79, a consensus quality value (QV) of 67.30 and k-mer completeness of 97.22% (Supplementary Table 4). For the heterozygous diploid species H. bulbosum, the two phased haplotypes were designated as Hap1 and Hap2. For polyploid species, independently assembled chromosome sets derived from different ancestral genomes were defined as subgenomes and denoted as Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 according to their phylogenetic relationships with diploid progenitor lineages (Fig. 1a). To assess the gene content in the Hordeum pangenome, we annotated all genomes using transcriptome data (Methods and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). A gene consolidation method was applied to ensure high comparability of gene predictions, including those for Hordeum parodii (6x) and Hordeum gussoneanum (4x). The number of high-confidence gene models identified ranges from 35,573 for diploid Hordeum murinum to 94,943 for hexaploid H. parodii (Supplementary Table 7). We assessed the quality of the Hordeum gene annotations using BUSCO (v5.8.0) with the poales_odb12 dataset, comprising 6,282 near-universal single-copy orthologues from Poales. On average, 97.35% of BUSCO genes were identified as complete, 0.69% as fragmented and 1.84% as missing (Supplementary Table 7). Independent benchmarking with OMArk and PSAURON further confirmed the high completeness and overall quality of the gene annotations (Supplementary Table 7). Transposable element (TE) annotation using the panEDTA pipeline31 revealed that transposons constituted on average 86.12% of the genome, ranging from 83.27% to 90.35% (Supplementary Table 8).

Based on the annotated gene sets of all species, we constructed a gene-based Hordeum pangenome. Overall, 42.4% of genes were classified as core genes, 56.5% as shell genes and 1.1% as cloud genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). Gene ontology enrichment analysis demonstrated that phosphorylation- and kinase-related functions were enriched among core genes, ATP and RNA binding were enriched among shell genes, and defence response and oxidative stress response were enriched among cloud genes (Supplementary Fig. 29). Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) genes are key components of the plant immune system and have essential roles in resistance to fungal and other pathogens32,33. A map of their diversity is critical for advancing our understanding of disease resistance mechanisms in crops. Analysis of NLR genes revealed that I genome species contain significantly more NLR genes than the other Hordeum genome groups (Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6) (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). To further characterize this diversity, we constructed an NLR pangenome across Hordeum haploid genome equivalents (haplomes), comprising 800 orthogroups, of which 13.75% were classified as core, 27.75% as shell and 58.50% as cloud gene families (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In addition, NLR gene clusters were significantly less abundant on chromosomes 4H and 5H than on the remaining chromosomes (Wilcoxon test, P < 2.2 × 10−16) (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Similarly, genome-wide analyses of pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins and mitochondrial transcription termination factors (mTERFs) revealed significant expansions of restorer-of-fertility-like (RFL) subgroups in the I and Xa genome groups relative to the H and Xu genome groups. Because RFL proteins are involved in fertility restoration in plants carrying cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)34, these expansions suggest that the smaller RFL repertoires of the H and Xu genome groups are derived rather than ancestral (Supplementary Fig. 30a–e and Supplementary Table 9). Expansion of RFL-PPRs was most pronounced in the I genome group, whereas RFL-mTERFs were significantly expanded in both the I and Xa genome groups. Notably, RFL-mTERF genes clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6H exhibited extensive copy-number variation between Xa–I and H–Xu genome groups (t-test, P = 5.2 × 10−6) (Supplementary Fig. 30f). This region includes the Rfm3 locus, which partially restores fertility in plants carrying the msm1 cytoplasm used in hybrid barley breeding35 (Supplementary Fig. 30g).

To assess the feasibility of graph-based pangenome analyses across highly diverged Hordeum genomes, we constructed a pangenome graph using Progressive Cactus and hal2vg, comprising 2.53 billion nodes and 3.46 billion edges (68.7 Gb). Approximately 68% of nodes represented single-base variants, illustrating the extensive sequence divergence captured by the graph. Although computationally intensive tasks such as indexing remained infeasible (Methods), we successfully performed global analyses of core, shell and cloud sequence content, graph saturation, sequence conservation and variant diversity (Supplementary Figs. 31–34). These results demonstrate both the potential of graph-based approaches for genus-wide comparative genomics and the need for more scalable methods for graph exploration and interpretation.

Industry observers note that previous studies have inferred the evolutionary relationships among Hordeum species from plastome and partial gene sequences1,17. However, the relationships among some species remained weakly supported. In this study, we reconstructed a maximum-likelihood tree using a genome-wide single-copy gene set. Unlike previous phylogenies1,17, our species tree resolved all major evolutionary relationships with maximum bootstrap support, particularly among the recently diverged I-genome species (Supplementary Fig. 35). To further evaluate the robustness of these relationships, we reconstructed an independent coalescent-based species tree using ASTRAL-Pro3 (Supplementary Fig. 36), which integrates individual maximum-likelihood gene trees, and a genome-wide phylogeny inferred by CASTER from whole-genome multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) (Supplementary Figs. 37 and 38). We also estimated the divergence times of these species using fourfold degenerate third-codon transversion (4DTV) sites, excluding genomic regions identified as putatively derived from ancient hybridization (Supplementary Table 13). We estimated the divergence time between H and Xu at 10.3 million years ago (Ma), whereas I and Xa diverged around 9 Ma. The crown-group age of Hordeum dates back approximately 12.27 Ma (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 10). The chromosomes of Triticeae species exhibit high collinearity at their distal chromosome regions36, which is also the case in Hordeum (Fig. 1b). However, when aligned, the proximal regions show substantial loss of collinearity and highly fragmented alignments. Whole-genome comparisons across Hordeum species revealed that chromosomal rearrangements accumulated progressively with evolutionary divergence, contributing to the loss of collinearity and increasingly fragmented alignments in proximal chromosomal regions (Fig.1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 39–44 and Supplementary Table 11). Quantification of reverse-orientation alignments across all Hordeum haplomes further demonstrated that putative inversions accumulated significantly more rapidly in proximal than in distal chromosome regions during Hordeum evolution (Supplementary Fig. 45). Among the seven chromosomes, chromosome 4H exhibited the most extensive loss of proximal collinearity (Supplementary Table 12). Recently diverged species retained strong chromosome-scale collinearity despite the presence of numerous structural variants, whereas comparisons between the deeply diverged H–Xu and Xa–I genome groups (more than 9 Ma) showed almost complete fragmentation of proximal collinearity (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 39–44). To estimate the size of non-collinear regions, we applied normalized coverage to identify these regions in species that diverged more than 9 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d, Supplementary Figs. 46–50 and Methods). In total, we determined the genome-wide distribution of non-collinear regions across chromosomes in Hordeum, with a cumulative size of 855 Mb identified in the H. vulgare genome (Supplementary Table 12). Given the central role of TEs in genome evolution, we compared TE composition between proximal and distal chromosome regions. Proximal regions contained a significantly higher proportion of TEs than distal regions (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10), primarily due to an increased abundance of LTR/Gypsy retrotransposons (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10) (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Fig. 51). Together with the accumulation of large chromosomal rearrangements, these observations motivated a ‘stretch and twist’ model describing two complementary processes underlying the progressive loss of collinearity. The stretch component represents alignment displacement caused by TE amplification, whereas the twist component represents large-scale chromosomal rearrangements driven by structural variation (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

Recent findings suggest that in contrast to the dynamic structural variations found in proximal regions, the distal regions displayed more conserved, shared structural variations. This highlights that the extensive loss of collinearity in proximal regions precludes reliable identification of structural variants across more distantly related Hordeum species. Notably, large structural variations in the distal regions were predominantly inversions. On chromosomes 3H and 7H, we identified two large inversions spanning nearly the entire chromosome and present in multiple species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In total, 1,407 inversions larger than 2 Mb were identified across Hordeum species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). The construction of a comprehensive inversion map revealed six inversions on chromosome 1H that were unexpectedly shared across divergent phylogenetic lineages (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5). We hypothesized that these large-scale structural variations might have originated from introgression events involving extensive chromosomal segments. We constructed a phylogenetic tree using the single-copy gene set from these regions to test this hypothesis. The resulting tree, resolved with maximum bootstrap support, confirmed that these structural variations are shared between one clade of the I genome group and the H–Xu genome groups (Fig. 2b). Moreover, 10 extant diploid Hordeum species diversified within 1.68 million years following the inferred hybridization event, whereas no comparable radiation occurred in other phylogenetic lineages during the same period (Figs. 1a and 2b and Extended Data Fig. 5). Notably, the alternative phylogenetic topology extends across contiguous chromosomal regions of approximately 200 Mb rather than isolated loci, indicating the inheritance of chromosome-scale haplotypes that are more consistent with ancient introgression than with stochastic gene tree discordance or incomplete lineage sorting.

Recent findings suggest that to identify additional signatures of ancient hybridization across the genus, we developed a genome-wide scanning approach based on local phylogenetic discordance among single-copy genes. The single-copy gene set was partitioned into sliding windows, and normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distance was calculated between local phylogenetic trees and the genome-wide species tree (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Peaks in nRF values indicate genomic regions with phylogenetic histories that deviate from the species tree and therefore represent candidate introgression events. Here, we define hybridization footprints as large chromosomal segments shared among multiple descendant species that consistently exhibit an alternative phylogenetic relationship relative to the genome-wide species tree. Using an empirical threshold of 0.21 derived from the genome-wide nRF distribution to distinguish discordance peaks from background variation (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 52), we recovered the chromosome 1H hybridization signal, validating the genome-wide scanning approach. Additionally, we detected more than ten consecutive windows with strong phylogenetic discordance signals at multiple regions (Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 52). To further explore the underlying causes of these inconsistencies, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the single-copy gene sets from these regions (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f, Supplementary Figs. 53–58 and Supplementary Table 13). Regions in which local phylogenies consistently supported a specific alternative relationship across a large chromosomal segment were interpreted as evidence of ancient hybridization. By comparing the regions that exhibited phylogenetic discordance with the whole-genome tree, we identified two large-scale segmental exchanges occurring within Hordeum jubatum, with maximum bootstrap support (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f and Supplementary Table 13). Surprisingly, this large-scale segmental exchange explains the major duplication and deletion pattern previously identified on chromosome 5H relative to the H. vulgare reference genome (Supplementary Figs. 12, 56, 59 and 60). The exchanged regions in the two H. jubatum subgenomes are each more closely related to different ancestral genomes, indicating that the apparent duplication and deletion resulted from ancestral segmental exchange rather than independent copy-number changes. (Extended Data Fig. 6d). In the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum, extensive segmental exchanges were detected between the two subgenomes on chromosomes 2, 5 and 7 (Extended Data Fig. 6e, Supplementary Figs. 53, 55 and 57 and Supplementary Table 13). In the allohexaploid H. parodii, subgenome 1 carried a large chromosomal segment on chromosome 7 derived from Hordeum stenostachys, whereas subgenomes 2 and 3 exhibited an additional segmental exchange on chromosome 4 (Extended Data Fig. 6f, Supplementary Figs. 54, 55 and 58 and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these megabase-scale structural variants preserve signatures of ancient interspecific hybridization and large-scale chromosomal exchange that are not evident from genome-wide phylogenies alone, providing latest insights into the complex evolutionary history of Hordeum.

Genetic variation is essential for species evolution. Beyond sexual reproduction, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) serves as an evolutionary shortcut for acquiring novel genes. Traditionally considered rare in vascular plants, genomic advances have revealed widespread occurrences of HGT, challenging prior assumptions37,38. Our previous research demonstrated extensive HGT in Hordeum. Notably, species within section stenostachys (I genome; 16 out of 22 diploid species) possess ribosomal DNA (rDNA) acquired from grasses in the subfamily Panicoideae (for example, Panicum, Paspalum and Setaria)39,40. The oldest transfers (from Panicum), estimated to have occurred between 5 and 1.7 Ma, resulted in large genomic insertions on chromosome 5H, some spanning over 400 kb and containing TEs and protein-coding genes41. Here, we identified Panicoideae-derived nuclear genes across 20 diploid Hordeum species, with H. vulgare serving as a negative control39,41. Our analysis revealed 611 foreign genes that corresponded to 126 orthogroups, predominantly matching Paspalum (63%) and Panicum (22%) (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 14 and 15). The extent of HGT varied, with Hordeum flexuosum carrying the highest number of foreign genes (68 genes corresponding to 43 orthogroups) (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These findings align with studies indicating that grasses frequently exchange genetic material42,43. HGT frequency correlates with Hordeum phylogeny, with Mediterranean and West Asian species exhibiting fewer transferred genes than their South American counterparts. This supports the hypothesis that HGT has a cumulative impact on eukaryotic evolution44. The presence of a single panicoid gene in H. bulbosum and H. murinum can be explained by the introgression of chromosomal segment 1H from I genome species, rather than by an early HGT event predating the diversification of Hordeum (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6c). Chromosomal mapping indicates that horizontally transferred genes are distributed across all seven Hordeum chromosomes, with chromosome 5H carrying the largest number (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These genes are significantly enriched in the distal regions of chromosome arms. Although distal regions generally contain higher local gene densities, negative binomial regression analysis demonstrated that gene density explains only a small fraction of the observed variation in HGT abundance (pseudo-R2 = 0.034; Supplementary Fig. 61), indicating that higher gene density alone cannot account for the distal enrichment of HGT genes. Although co-transfer of genes remains uncertain, previous research suggests that large fragments of foreign DNA may be transferred together41,43. A substantial fraction (82 out of 126) of Panicoideae-derived orthogroups lack native Hordeum homologues, indicating novel gene acquisition. Functional annotation suggests that these genes may have roles in key physiological processes such as auxin transport, light response and transcription regulation. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis detected at least one expressed HGT gene in 73 out of 126 orthogroups (Extended Data Fig. 7c and Supplementary Table 16). The potential adaptive significance of these genes warrants further investigation. Our genus-wide analysis establishes Hordeum as a model system for studying the evolutionary impact of HGT.

Recent findings suggest that the genome assembly sizes of Hordeum species range from 2.90 Gb to 10.9 Gb and are highly correlated with previous flow-cytometric estimates45 (Fig. 3a). After accounting for the direct effects of polyploidization, the haplomes exhibit pseudomolecule sizes ranging from 2.85 Gb to 4.68 Gb. Apart from a 19 Mb duplication detected in the subgenome of H. jubatum, no large duplication events were identified (Supplementary Figs. 59–60). A strong correlation was observed between total TE content and haplome size (Fig. 3b), confirming that TE accumulation has significantly contributed to genome size variation in Hordeum. LTR retrotransposons were identified as the primary drivers of these changes, although DNA transposons also had a role (Fig. 3c). Correlation analyses of individual transposon superfamilies demonstrated that multiple TE families contributed to genome size variation, although overall TE abundance remained the strongest predictor of haplome size (Supplementary Fig. 62a). We selected transposons annotated in the TREP database with an average content above 20 Mb and examined their variation across different Hordeum haplomes. These TE families clearly differentiated the major evolutionary lineages of Hordeum (Supplementary Fig. 62b). To investigate lineage-specific TE dynamics in greater detail, we focused on three LTR retrotransposon families (BARE1, Sabrina and BAGY2) and used TEpop46 to reconstruct their diversification histories. TE subfamilies correspond closely to the major Hordeum clades (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), demonstrating lineage-specific amplification histories that contributed to genome size evolution.
