To investigate TE evolution following polyploidization, we compared the TE landscapes of three independently formed tetraploid genomes with those of their diploid progenitors. The three polyploid species exhibited distinct evolutionary trajectories. In H. murinum, TE expansion was minimal (Extended Data Fig. 8c and Supplementary Table 17). In H. jubatum, both subgenomes were smaller than their diploid progenitors (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Table 17). By contrast, Hordeum secalinum experienced extensive TE proliferation, resulting in substantial genome expansion (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Table 17). Notably, LTR/Gypsy elements indicated the greatest expansion relative to the diploid progenitors and therefore contributed most to genome expansion in H. secalinum (Supplementary Table 17). Additionally, the Vagabond TE family showed renewed activity following tetraploidization, with significantly higher activity in the tetraploid genome than in either its diploid progenitors or the alternative subgenome (Extended Data Fig. 8e and Supplementary Figs. 63 and 64). To avoid bias introduced by large segmental exchanges between subgenomes, we excluded genomic regions inferred to originate from ancient hybridization before estimating TE insertion ages (Supplementary Table 13 and Supplementary Fig. 65). Although subgenome differentiation alone does not permit precise dating of tetraploid formation, post-polyploid TE dynamics can be reconstructed from TE insertions. Specifically, we inferred the timing of subgenome fusion from the insertion ages of full-length TEs shared exclusively between subgenomes but absent from their respective diploid progenitors (Fig. 3f, Extended Data Fig. 8f,g and Supplementary Figs. 65 and 66). These shared insertions must have occurred after polyploid formation, thereby providing temporal information on the origin of the polyploid genomes and subsequent TE activity. Our findings underscore that TE content is the primary determinant of genome size variation in Hordeum. Tetraploidization does not always lead to genome expansion relative to diploid ancestors; we also observed genome contraction. Nevertheless, post-polyploid LTR insertions provided an independent estimate of the timing of polyploid formation and newly introduced insights into the evolutionary history of tetraploid and hexaploid Hordeum genomes.

Industry observers note that whole-genome MSAs provide a framework for investigating sequence conservation and divergence across species. We therefore generated a whole-genome MSA of Hordeum haplomes using Progressive Cactus47. In total, we identified 170.4 Mb of shared aligned sequences across the Hordeum genomes (Extended Data Fig. 9a). As expected, rapidly evolving pericentromeric regions highlighted fewer alignments, whereas chromosome distal ends exhibited higher alignment densities (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The rapid contraction of these alignments is probably due to substantial reshaping of Hordeum genomes by TE activity over the past 12 million years. To further investigate sequence conservation across different functional genomic regions, we analysed open chromatin regions identified by assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq) together with annotated genomic features in eight Hordeum haplomes (Supplementary Table 18). Untranslated region sequences were the most highly conserved non-coding regions and were lost at a slower rate before the divergence of barley and wheat. By contrast, open chromatin regions exhibited a loss pattern similar to introns, whereas promoter regions underwent more rapid turnover (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Additionally, we used phastCons to identify 74.7 Mb of conserved elements across Hordeum genomes (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Among all conserved bases, 69.0% overlapped annotated genes and 6.0% overlapped open chromatin regions. Conversely, 44.7% of annotated gene bases and 31.9% of open chromatin bases overlapped conserved elements. Conserved elements were significantly enriched in both annotated genes (odds ratio = 138.0) and open chromatin regions (odds ratio = 27.4), with substantially stronger enrichment in genes, indicating stronger evolutionary constraint on coding sequences than on regulatory regions (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

According to recent reports, overall, our findings indicate that regulatory elements undergo substantially faster evolutionary turnover than coding sequences, generating extensive regulatory variation that may provide a valuable source of alleles for barley improvement. By contrast, the high conservation of coding genes provides opportunities for comparative functional analyses and cross-species transfer of biological knowledge.

In a recent development, in cultivated barley, spring and winter growth habits are largely determined by the vernalization genes VERNALIZATION 1 (VRN1), a MADS-box transcription factor, and VERNALIZATION 2 (VRN2), which is encoded by a cluster of zinc-finger/CCT (ZCCT) genes. In winter barley, prolonged cold induces VRN1 expression, which represses VRN2 and thereby permits flowering48,49. Flowering of winter varieties requires repression of VRN2 by cold-induced VRN1 (ref. 49). By contrast, spring barleys often carry deletions in the first intron of VRN1 and lack VRN2, eliminating their vernalization requirement50,51,52. Intermediate facultative types combine the vernalization-sensitive VRN1 with a non-functional VRN2 locus. It remains largely unexplored how wild Hordeum species regulate flowering across diverse climates.

It has been revealed that examining VRN1 in Hordeum genomes revealed extensive variation in the promoter and the regulatory first intron (5.7 kb to 19.5 kb) caused by TEs (Supplementary Table 19). To assess the functional effect of this variation, we recorded flowering time of 14 wild Hordeum species and 4 barley controls under non-vernalizing conditions with a 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 11a). Notably, Hordeum cordobense and Hordeum muticum flowered rapidly (approximately 61 days), surpassing spring barley cultivars (Fig. 4a). Both species share a unique 79-bp deletion in VRN1 intron 1 critical region51, suggesting a role in reducing the vernalization requirement (Extended Data Fig. 11b). All species contained the VRN2 locus with one to seven ZCCT copies (Supplementary Table 19). A key finding was an inverted repeat of two ZCCT genes in H. cordobense, Hordeum californicum, H. muticum and H. jubatum (Supplementary Fig. 67). Because inverted repeats may trigger RNA interference (RNAi)53, we expected silencing of VRN2 and a spring-type phenotype. Surprisingly, only H. cordobense and H. muticum flowered early (Fig. 4a,c and Extended Data Fig. 11a). Detailed analysis of H. cordobense revealed a non-functional ZCCT-1 owing to a premature stop codon, and the absence of a polyadenylation signal in the ZCCT-2/ZCCT-3 inverted repeat linker, enabling read-through transcription (detected as an aberrant mRNA transcript), hairpin RNA formation and small RNA production (Fig. 4b,d, Extended Data Fig. 11c and Supplementary Fig. 68). Winter-type H. californicum carried additional functional ZCCT copies and a polyadenylation signal in the inverted repeat linker that probably prevented RNAi, thus maintaining the VRN2 repressive function (Fig. 4b,e). This aligns with the expression of VRN1, VRN2 and their target FLOWERING LOCUS T1 (FT1) in the analysed species (Fig. 4f). These findings highlight that genetic diversity shapes vernalization in Hordeum. The studied spring-like accessions carry the 79-bp VRN1 deletion alongside disrupted or silenced VRN2, whereas winter-like genotypes retain functional ZCCT copies. Together, our results indicate that adaptation to spring growth habit in wild Hordeum species has targeted the same genes and variant types as in cultivated barley, pointing to conserved mechanisms of flowering-time adaptation.

Read mapping at the H. cordobense ZCCT-3 locus suggests the presence of improperly spliced, probably aberrant transcripts. f, Transcripts per million (TPM) values at 14 and 28 DAG in H. cordobense and H. californicum.

The glume is a distinctive floral organ in the grass family, which lacks a direct counterpart in dicotyledonous plants54. It appears as one or multiple pairs of bract-like structures subtending single or multiple fertile florets. Glume size and shape vary widely, from large lemma-like structures in Triticum species to rudimentary axillary buds in Oryza. In wild grasses, glume morphology influences seed dispersal, reproductive success and defence against biotic stress55. In cultivated cereals, domestication has favoured reduced glume size and roughness, facilitating easier threshing. In Hordeum, each floret possesses a pair of glumes positioned on the periaxial side, with considerable variation in length, width and awn extension across species (Fig. 5a). Transcriptomic profiling of five diploid species carrying the I genome (H. erectifolium, Hordeum pusillum, Hordeum intercedens H. stenostachys and Hordeum euclaston) identified spike-specific genes expressed in young spikes at early (Waddington stages 3–6 (W3–6)) and late (W9–10) developmental stages56 (Supplementary Table 21). Genes were classified as spike-specific if their transcript abundance in the remaining 11 out of 13 analysed tissues was less than 5% of their combined expression in the 2 spike samples. Five genes were consistently expressed across species, suggesting conserved regulatory mechanisms (Extended Data Fig. 12a and Supplementary Table 21). These genes encode a C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor, an auxin response factor, a TCP transcription factor, a subtilisin protease (SBT) and a MADS-box transcription factor. Three were predominantly expressed during early spike development, one at later stages and one at both stages (Extended Data Fig. 12b). In rice, loss-of-function mutations in NONSTOP GLUMES1 (NSG1), the orthologue of the C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor, result in uncontrolled glume growth57. Amino acid variations in this gene across Hordeum species along with glume variations suggested a relevance in regulating glume development (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 69). Mutations in its cultivated barley orthologue (EOG1) lead to the elongated outer glume (eog1) phenotype (Fig. 5b). These mutants develop enlarged glumes on the central fertile spikelet, with glume awns extending to lemma-awn length, giving the spike a brushy appearance (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed developmental divergence between wild-type and eog1 mutants as early as W3.5 (Fig. 5c). By integrating comparative genomics across Hordeum with tissue-specific expression data and cultivated barley mutant resources, we identify EOG1 as a conserved regulator of glume development.

a, Central spikelet from representative Hordeum species exhibiting glume morphology diversity. gl, glume. Scale bars, 500 μm. b, Allelic variations of a C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor gene (HORVU.MOREX.r3.2HG0170820.1) in cultivated barley (H. vulgare) lead to glume elongation. The rectangle denotes the exon or full-length coding sequence, with the red rectangle indicating the C2H2-type zinc-finger domain. The asterisk marks a premature stop codon. HTX (Hatiexie) represents the wild type, which exhibits suppressed glume development, whereas the mutants exhibit elongation in glume growth. The mutant allele lep-e.1 (ref. 59) carries a deletion allele of the EOG1 gene. Scale bars, 1 cm. c, Differentiation on the spikelet morphogenesis along Waddington stage between the wild-type HTX and the induced mutant M9630. W3, glume primordial present; W3.5, floret primordial present; W5, carpel extending. le, lemma. Scale bars, 100 μm.

Sources indicate that the chromosome-scale genome assemblies presented here provide a foundation for investigating the evolutionary history of the genus Hordeum. Chromosome-scale resolution enables us to investigate how structural variations have shaped genome evolution, particularly in disrupting chromosomal collinearity. Traditionally, grass genomes were thought to possess relatively stable chromosome structures58; however, our findings challenge this assumption. Extensive structural variations and chromosomal rearrangements have contributed substantially to genomic divergence, ultimately resulting in the near-complete loss of collinearity in proximal regions. These rearrangements not only mark evolutionary divergence but also provide insights into the processes underlying speciation within Hordeum. Structural variations accumulated at markedly different rates across chromosome regions. Whereas proximal regions exhibit high variability, distal regions evolve more slowly. This uneven evolutionary rate has preserved footprints of ancient hybridization events across the genus, offering a historical record of interspecific gene flow. These findings provide empirical evidence for ancient hybridization and genome fusion during Hordeum evolution and establish a framework for identifying compatible genomic segments in future interspecific breeding efforts.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, whether the large inversions identified in this study contribute to adaptive evolution, reproductive isolation or other phenotypic consequences remains unknown and warrants future functional investigation. Whole-genome MSAs enabled us to compare genome-wide conservation across Hordeum species. Compared with animal genomes, which often display strong interspecies conservation, plant genomes—especially within rapidly evolving genera such as Hordeum—undergo dynamic changes driven by short generation times and rapid transposon expansion. These processes fuel the ongoing remodelling of plant genomes, resulting in high variability even among closely related taxa. Despite this rapid evolution, many genes remain conserved, whereas regulatory elements exhibit considerable turnover. This contrast offers unique opportunities: lineage-specific regulatory innovation can be harnessed for crop improvement, while core gene functions are retained. For example, regulatory elements associated with vernalization responses were found to vary across Hordeum species, suggesting that novel regulatory variants could be introduced into cultivated barley to fine-tune flowering behaviour. Beyond expanding genomic resources for Hordeum, this work provides a framework for investigating structural genome evolution, reconstructing complex evolutionary histories and harnessing genetic and regulatory diversity for barley improvement.

Plant material was obtained from genebanks at Institut für Pflanzgenetik und Kulturpflanzenforschung (IPK) Gatersleben, the US Department of Agriculture and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center. Accession numbers are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Plants were grown under greenhouse conditions and high molecular weight (HMW) DNA was isolated from young leaf tissue according to published protocols10,60. Construction of HiFi libraries and Circular Consensus Sequencing using the PacBio Sequel IIe instrument (Pacific Biosciences) were essentially as described previously19. HiFi sequencing was done at IPK Gatersleben, Genomics and Transcriptomics Laboratory, Heinrich Heine University, Berry Genomics Co., Novogene and the University of Wisconsin Biotechnology Center DNA Sequencing Facility.

It has been revealed that in situ Hi-C libraries were prepared from young seedlings according to the previously published protocol, using DpnII for the digestion of crosslinked chromatin. Libraries were prepared as described61. Samples were quantified62 and sequenced with standard protocols from Illumina using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 devices (Illumina) at IPK Gatersleben and Novogene.

Industry observers note that A clone of the same H. erectifolium individual plant that was sequenced using PacBio HiFi was used for the construction of the optical genome map (OGM). A total of 2.5 million nuclei, purified from young leaves by flow cytometry, were embedded in agarose miniplugs and treated with proteinase K, following the protocol of Šimková et al.63. A total of 525 ng of HMW DNA was directly labelled at DLE-1 recognition sites using the standard Bionano Prep Direct Label and Stain protocol (Bionano) and analysed on the Bionano Saphyr platform. The resulting dataset, comprising 1.5 Tb of single-molecule data with an N50 of 247 kb, provided approximately 341× coverage of the H. erectifolium genome. This dataset was used to generate a de novo OGM assembly using Bionano Solve software (v3.6.1_11162020) with the standard configuration file optArguments_nonhaplotype_noES_noCut_DLE1_saphyr.xml.

To improve the contiguity of the PacBio HiFi assembly, the automatic hybrid scaffold pipeline integrated in Bionano Solve was run using the OGM assembly. The default DLE-1 Hybrid Scaffold configuration file was applied with the ‘resolve conflict’ option for conflict resolution. Conflicts between the sequence assembly and the OGM were manually curated and the pipeline was subsequently re-run using a modified conflict_cut_status.txt file.

According to recent reports, plants were grown under greenhouse conditions and total RNA was isolated from different tissues and developmental stages (Supplementary Table 5) using the RNAeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) or with Trizol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. RNA-seq was performed on replicated bulk sample representing a specific developmental stage or tissue type. RNA-seq of individual samples and PacBio IsoSeq of RNA pools was performed as described previously10. Library construction and sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 devices (Illumina RNA-seq) and PacBio Sequel IIe (instruments) was done at IPK Gatersleben, Biomarker Technologies (BMK), the Genomics and Transcriptomics Laboratory at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Kazusa DNA Research Institute or Berry Genomics. The PacBio IsoSeq sequencing data was processed with the isoseq3 (v3.8.2) pipeline (PacBio - IsoSeq3, 2018/2024). The ploy-A tails were trimmed and concatenated transcripts removed with refine -require-polya-min-polya-length 12 teloprime.fasta. To generate non-redundant transcripts, we mapped the full-length non-concatenated reads were mapped to the genome with pbmm2 (v1.10.0) align -preset ISOSEQ -sort -bam-index CSI and redundant transcripts collapsed with isoseq3 collapse -do-not-collapse-extra-5exons.

Recent findings suggest that pacBio HiFi reads were assembled using hifiasm (v0.13-r308 or v0.15.5-r350 or v0.16.1-r375)64. Pseudomolecules were constructed with the TRITEX pipeline26,27, and chimeric contigs or orientation errors were corrected based on manual inspection of Hi-C contact matrices. For allotetraploid species, subgenomes were phased using a previously developed haplotype-resolved genome assembly strategy10. The origin of the subgenomes and their potential ancestral contributors were previously investigated in detail by Brassac et al.1 To classify subgenomes in the polyploid genome, Mash (v2.3)65 was used to calculate pairwise chromosomal similarities between polyploid chromosomes and candidate ancestral genomes. The resulting distance matrix was used to infer subgenome origin and relationships. In species with high heterozygosity or outcrossing (H. brevisubulatum and H. murinum BBC2017), Hi-C data were incorporated during hifiasm (v0.15.5-r350)64 assembly to collapse haplotypes and assemble a representative haploid genome. Except for H. erectifolium, whose primary contigs were first hybrid-scaffolded using a Bionano optical map, followed by pseudomolecule construction with Hi-C data and the TRITEX pipeline30. Chloroplast genomes were assembled following previously published protocols10. HiFi reads were aligned to the barley cv. Morex chloroplast genome (GenBank accession EF115541) using minimap2 (v2.24-r1122)66 with the parameters -ax map-hifi–secondary=no–sam-hit-only. Alignments with mapping quality <30 were discarded. Aligned reads were converted to FASTQ format using SAMtools (v1.16.1)67 and assembled with Canu (v2.1.1)68 in PacBio HiFi mode with genome sizes from 120 to 400 kb in 10-kb increments. Circular sequences were identified and trimmed using BEDTools (v2.30.0)69 and annotated with GeSeq70. Fully annotated assemblies were aligned to the Morex chloroplast genome using MUMmer4 (v4.0.0beta2)71, and start positions and orientations of the SSC region were adjusted to match the reference using seqkit (v0.9.1)72. k-mer frequencies were calculated using Jellyfish(v2.2.6)73 and analysed with findGSE(v1.94)74 to estimate genome characteristics. Assembly quality, including QV and k-mer completeness, was evaluated using Merqury(v1.3)75.

We performed de novo structural gene prediction, confidence classification and functional annotation, following the protocol described in Mascher et al.28. As evidences we used RNA-seq and IsoSeq data as described under above and Poales-filtered protein sequences downloaded from UniProt76 (July 2023). An additional consolidation step was carried out using the liftoff77 tool. In brief, all predicted gene models from one species were lifted over to all other genomes. Using Mikado78, we selected the best mapped gene models and unified all gene predictions accordingly. We classified predicted proteins into high and low-confidence categories. High-confidence proteins had over 80% coverage and were complete, either with significant hits in UniMag or UniPoa but not PTREP (https://trep-db.uzh.ch). Low-confidence proteins were incomplete with hits in UniMag or UniPoa but not PTREP, or were complete without hits in any database.

We benchmarked the annotations with BUSCO (v5.8.0)79 (dataset: poales_odb12), OMARK (omamer verision 2.1.0/omark v0.3.1)80 and psauron (v1.0.6)81.

Orthogroups based on the primary protein sequences from 27 annotated Hordeum accessions were calculated using Orthofinder (v2.5.5)82. The scripts for the calculation of core, shell and cloud genes are deposited in the repository at https://github.com/PGSB-HMGU/BPGv2. Core genes contain at least 1 gene model from all 27 compared accessions. Shell genes contain gene models from at least 2 Hordeum accessions and at most 26. Genes clustered with genes only from the same genotype were defined as cloud genes. Annotations of H. vulgare Morex and H. bulbosum were not included during the consolidation step. Therefore, to counteract any potential over- or under-presentation of these two species in any of the core, shell or cloud categories, we aligned all cloud genes for H. vulgare cv. Morex and H. bulbosum back to all other genomes and corrected for any missing genes. Gene Ontology-term enrichments were conducted with goatools (v1.4.4)83. Gene-based collinearity plots were drawn with GENESPACE84.

The RGAugury (v2.2)85 pipeline was used to identify from our annotation and classify nucleotide-binding site (NB-ARC) domain-encoding genes into different subgroups, based on domain and motif structures: TNL contain TIR, NBS and LRR domains; CNL contain CC, NBS and LRR domains; RNL contain RPW8, NBS and LRR domains; RN contain RPW8 and NBS domains only; NL contain NBS and LRR domains but lack TIR, CC and RPW8; TN contain TIR and NBS domains only; CN contain CC and NBS domains only; and NBS-only genes contain only the NBS domain. TIR, NBS, LRR, CC and RPW8 refer to the Toll/Interleukin-1 Receptor-like, Nucleotide-Binding Site, Leucine-Rich Repeat, Coiled-Coil and Resistance to Powdery Mildew 8-like domains, respectively. An NLR gene cluster is defined based on the genomic proximity of NLR genes. Specifically, any two NLR genes located within 500 kb of each other are grouped into the same cluster by bedtools (v2.30.0)69. NLR genes were then grouped into clusters using bedtools (v2.30.0)69 merge with a maximum intergenic distance of 250 kb. Only clusters comprising no fewer than three NLR genes were retained. Pan-NLR analysis was performed based on orthogroups identified using OrthoFinder (v2.5.5)82 across all NLR genes. Core orthogroups are defined as orthogroups that contain at least one gene model from each of the compared Hordeum accessions. Shell orthogroups include gene models from at least two and at most 26Hordeum accessions. Gene models that were not assigned to any orthogroup (singletons) or were grouped only with genes from the same genotype were classified as cloud genes.

Recent findings suggest that open reading frames longer than 100 codons were searched for the presence of PPR and mTERF motifs using hmmsearch from the HMMER suite (http://hmmer.org) using hidden Markov models as defined in Cheng et al.86. for the PPR family and PF02536 from the Pfam 32.0 database (http://pfam.xfam.org)87 for the mTERF motif. Downstream processing of the hmmsearch results for the PPR proteins followed the pipeline described in Gutmann et al.88. The RfCTD domain recently identified as a unique feature of RFL-PPRs89 was included in the gene annotations. P-class and PLS-class genes with scores below 100 and 240, respectively, were excluded from the annotation as they are unlikely to represent functional PPR genes, as defined previously (IWGSC 2018)90.

The analyses described here used a number of tools from the toolkits vg (v1.61.0)91, odgi (v0.8.3-26-gbc7742ed)92, bcftools (v1.21)67 and seqkit (v2.9.0)72. All scripts used for graph construction and analysis are available at https://github.com/cropgeeks/panHordeum. Owing to computational limitations, we built an alignment of Hordeum whole genomes with Cactus47. We selected H. marinum BCC 2001 over H. marinum H559 on the basis of its higher assembly quality. Genome haplomes were soft-masked with bedtools69 using their respective repeat annotations. The guide tree required for the Cactus alignment was taken from the Orthofinder93 output generated as part of this study. Apart from setting appropriate resource parameters (that is, threads, memory and disk), we ran Cactus with default parameters. We transformed the resulting whole-genome alignment into a super-pangenome graph using hal2vg (https://github.com/ComparativeGenomicsToolkit/hal2vg), with the –noAncestors flag, and then further processed it with vg convert to get the final pangenome graph in GFA format (https://github.com/GFA-spec/GFA-spec). We computed basic graph statistics using odgi stats with the –summarize option, which included graph size, number of nodes, edges, paths and steps. To characterize the conservation of the different segments of the graph, we classified nodes as core, shell, or cloud. A node was considered ‘core’ if it was traversed by all samples’ paths, ‘cloud’ if it was traversed by a single sample’s path, and ‘shell’ otherwise. The same classification was done at the base level. Both computations were performed using the odgi toolkit (implementation details in class_stats.sh). To evaluate the agreement of haplotype sequences with their representation in the graph, we first extracted the linear sequences of all haplotypes as encoded in the graph using odgi paths with the –fasta option. These sequences were subsequently partitioned by source genome using seqkit grep, creating direct pairwise comparisons between input genomes and their graph-encoded counterparts. For each genome pair, we performed exact sequence matching, confirming whether each input sequence (or its reverse complement) was precisely preserved in the graph-encoded version (implementation details available in script fidelity.py). We computed pangenome graph growth curves based on the full graph using odgi heaps with 100 permutations of the input genomes. Results were plotted using script heaps_fit.R distributed with the odgi toolkit92. Whole-graph analysis turned out to be computationally prohibitive (job runtime limits and/or memory requirements) for several of the required tools from the vg and odgi toolkits, given a graph of this size and complexity. We therefore extracted subgraphs equating to individual chromosome paths for H. vulgare cv. Morex, which we used as the basis for all variant analyses. We used vg chunk for subgraph extraction. Variants were called from the chromosome-level subgraphs directly, using vg deconstruct. This generated VCF output containing the full range of variant sizes. To prepare structural variants from the graph for further analysis we broadly followed the variant decomposition approach used by the Human Pangenome Consortium94. This involved the removal of top-level variants of length >100,000 bp with vcfbub (https://github.com/pangenome/vcfbub), realigning alternate alleles against the reference for each variant using vcfwave (vcflib v1.0.2)95, and finally normalizing the resulting variants with bcftools norm67. We then added variant length information (SVLEN) to the VCF files with a custom script to allow extraction of structural variants based on the length difference between reference and alternate allele (>50 bp) and classified structural variations as deletions or insertions based on the directionality of the difference (insertion: string length REF  string length ALT). The resulting VCF files were converted to BED format with bcftools query. Variant density plots were computed with custom R scripts using ggplot2 (v3.5.1)96. To explore the possibility of using the graph for read mapping and genotyping, we attempted to index the graph using vg gbwt/vg index/vg minimizer. This turned out to be computationally prohibitive in terms of job runtime limits on two separate compute facilities used, and thus we were unable to use the graph for the valuation of read mapping. We conducted graph-based conservation analysis with Pansel97, a tool used for calculation of diversity/conservation metrics directly from pan-genome graphs. The default bin size of 1kbp was used, along with all other parameters on default settings. Results were plotted using ggplot2 (v3.5.1)96.

Sources indicate that single-copy genes were identified using BUSCO (v5.4.6)79 in B. distachyon (v3.0)98, O. sativa (IRGSP-1.0)99, S. bicolor (NCBIv3)99, T. monococcum100, H. vulgare FT11 (ref. 19) and the 29 Hordeum haplomes collected in this study. Protein sequences of BUSCO single-copy genes present in all 34 haplomes were concatenated and aligned using MAFFT (v7.490)101. Well-aligned regions were filtered using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with parameters -t=extractedp -b4 = 5 -b5=h. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was then constructed using RAxML (v8.2.12)103 with the PROTGAMMAWAG substitution model and the rapid bootstrap algorithm with 100 replicates. To facilitate genome-wide alignment, all 34 haplomes were masked using RepeatMasker (v4.1.1; http://www.repeatmasker.org) with a pan-genome TE library generated by panEDTA. The masked genomes and the inferred species tree were then used as input for Cactus (v2.6.5)47 to generate whole-genome MSAs. The loss rate of genomic elements was defined as the size of the reconstructed ancestral sequence at the corresponding genomic position in the multiple genome alignment.

It has been revealed that to precisely construct phylogenetic trees and estimate divergence times within the genus Hordeum, we included four additional outgroup genomes: B. distachyon (v3.0)98, O. sativa (IRGSP-1.0)99, S. bicolor (NCBIv3)104 (all downloaded from Ensembl Plants; https://plants.ensembl.org/index.html) and T. monococcum100 (https://wheat.pw.usda.gov/GG3/pangenome). We constructed phylogenetic trees using four approaches. The first two methods were based on whole-genome single-copy genes. Orthologous genes were identified from the genomes of our 34 Hordeum haplomes and four outgroup genomes using OrthoFinder (v2.5.5)82, yielding 2,198 single-copy genes. For the concatenation-based approach, the CDS sequences of these genes were concatenated and aligned with MAFFT (v7.490)101, and well-aligned regions were retained using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with the parameters -t=extractedp, -b4 = 5, -b5=h; phylogenetic inference was then performed in IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105. For the coalescence-based approach, the CDS sequences of each single-copy gene were aligned separately using MAFFT (v7.490)101, high-quality regions were selected with Gblocks (v0.91b)102 using the same parameters, individual gene trees were reconstructed with IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105, and a species tree was inferred from these gene trees using ASTRAL-Pro3 (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)106. The remaining two methods were based on whole-genome MSAs generated with Cactus. In the CASTER-pair (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)107 approach, the whole-genome MSA was used to infer a phylogenetic tree rooted with S. bicolor, while in the CASTER-site (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)107 approach, the whole-genome MSA was analysed similarly but using site-based inference, also rooted with S. bicolor.

Recent findings suggest that to estimate divergence times, genomic regions showing strong phylogenetic discordance (nRF > 0.21) were first excluded based on the genome-wide discordance analysis. 4DTV sites were extracted from MSAs of single-copy genes. Divergence times between barley and outgroup species were obtained from the TimeTree database (https://timetree.org/)108. Finally, species divergence times within the genus Hordeum were estimated using the MCMCtree program in PAML (v4.4)109.

Recent findings suggest that we excluded multiple haplomes from the same species and retained a final set of 32 Hordeum haplomes for comparative analysis. All haplomes pairs were aligned against each other using minimap2 (v2.24-r1122)66 with the parameters -2 -K 5 G -f 0.005 -x asm10, and the resulting alignments were stored in PAF format for visualization via dot plots. For each reference haplomes, we calculated the alignment coverage in non-overlapping 5 Mb windows, considering only alignments with a mapping quality greater than 20. Coverage values were normalized across the haplomes by the average coverage to produce normalized coverage profiles. In species that diverged more than 9 Ma, a bimodal distribution of normalized coverage was observed, allowing a threshold of 0.5 to distinguish distal and proximal regions (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Finally, genome-wide alignment and normalized coverage profiles were used to manually define the size and boundaries of proximal and distal regions across all species. Reverse-orientation alignments were extracted as indicators of putative inversion events. Two metrics were calculated for each pairwise comparison: (1) the number of reverse-orientation alignments per Mb and (2) the proportion of bases covered by reverse-orientation alignments. These metrics were separately calculated for proximal and distal chromosomal regions to compare the rates of inversion accumulation during species divergence. Linear regression models including divergence time, chromosomal region type (proximal or distal) and their interaction term were used to evaluate differences in the accumulation rates of reverse-orientation alignments between regions.

According to recent reports, all other Hordeum genomes were aligned to the MorexV3 (ref. 28) reference genome using wfmash (v0.9.1-3; https://github.com/waveygang/wfmash) with the parameters -p 90 -l 0. Inversions were then identified using SyRI (v1.5.5)110 with parameters -F P -f–nosnp. Only inversions larger than 2 Mb and located outside of the proximal regions were retained for further analysis.

Based on the 2,198 single-copy orthologues identified in the section ‘Phylogeny and divergence time estimation’ and using the genome-wide concatenated single-copy gene tree as a reference, we conducted sliding-window gene tree analyses (Extended Data Fig. 6a). All single-copy genes were grouped into non-overlapping windows of 25 genes with a step size of 2 genes. Within each window, protein sequences were aligned using MAFFT (v7.490)101, and well-aligned regions were retained using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with the parameters -t=extractedp -b4 = 5 -b5=h. Local window trees were built with FastTree (v2.1.11)111 (default GTR + CAT, 20 rate categories), starting from neighbour-joining trees and optimized with minimum-evolution and nearest-neighbour interchange moves; branch support was calculated using Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like values. Each resulting tree was rooted with S. bicolor as the outgroup using ETE3 (v3.1.2)112, and the nRF distance was calculated against the reference tree using the parameter –min_support_src 90. The nRF metric quantifies topological dissimilarity between trees, with values ranging from 0 (identical topology) to 1 (completely different topologies). Based on the nRF distribution, we identified 0.21 as a threshold to separate background from discordant signal peaks (Extended Data Fig. 6b). To evaluate the robustness of discordant region detection, we repeated the sliding-window analyses using alternative parameter settings (30 genes with step sizes of 1 and 5 genes). The major discordance peaks were consistently recovered across different window sizes and step lengths, indicating that peak detection was not sensitive to parameter selection (Supplementary Fig. 52). Genomic regions containing at least 10 overlap windows with nRF ≥ 0.21 were defined as candidate introgressed regions. For each candidate region, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the same procedure as for the genome-wide tree. The topological comparison of these local trees with the reference tree enabled the inference of introgression origins. The AU test113 implemented in IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105, was used to compare local reference trees and local phylogenetic trees. A P value (p-AU) lower than 0.05 indicated that the tree was significantly rejected.

Genomes of 20 diploid Hordeum species were searched for potential HGT genes from grasses of the subfamily Panicoideae. Regions of interest were identified in the genomes using BLAST (v2.12.0+)114 against four potential donor species: Panicum hallii (v3.2), Setaria italica (v2.2), Paspalum vaginatum (v3.1) and Paspalum notatum (GCA_036689595.1) (Supplementary Table 10). BLAST results were filtered to retain hits with a sequence identity of ≥95% and an alignment length of ≥150 bp. The same process was applied to H. vulgare cv. Morex (v3), which served as a negative control. H. vulgare is widely recognized as a species that lacks HGT genes from the Panicoideae subfamily39,41,42. Hits from potential donors that were found in both the Hordeum recipient genomes and H. vulgare were excluded from further analysis. This filtering was conducted using the intersect tool from BEDTools (v2.26.0)69, with an overlap threshold of 20%. Finally, the identified regions were compared with newly available annotations, and corresponding candidate genes were extracted. In this step, we identified 5,169 candidate genes.

Sources indicate that to verify the foreign (that is, Panicoideae) origin of the candidate HGT genes identified as described above, phylogenetic trees were constructed for each candidate. Homologues were retrieved from a set of representative Poaceae species and two outgroups (Ananas comosus and Musa acuminata) (Supplementary Table 10) using BLASTn (e-value cutoff of 10−10). The retrieved sequences were aligned with the Hordeum HGT gene candidates using MUSCLE (v3.8)115. The alignments were trimmed using trimAl (v1.2) with an automated trimming method116. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using PhyML (v3.1)117, with 1,000 bootstrap iterations and the GTR substitution model. The resulting trees were reviewed semi-automatically with the assistance of the Newick Utilities suite118. A candidate gene was considered a true HGT gene if the gene sequence was nested within the PACMAD clade. TE-related genes were filtered out and only high-confidence, protein-coding genes were retained for further analysis. Out of 5,169 candidate genes, 4,393 did not pass through the primary phylogenetic validation and 776 genes remained. Candidate genes that passed the first step of verification were cross-referenced with orthogroups previously created during pan-genome construction. For groups containing more than one candidate gene, a consensus sequence was generated using MAFFT (v7.520)102 for MSA, followed by the cons tool from EMBOSS (v6.5.7.0)119 to produce the consensus. These consensus sequences were subsequently used for BLASTn searches. Hits from at least five species, including minimally one from Panicoideae, were required for tree construction. Phylogenetic trees were then constructed as described above, using MAFFT as the aligner. Alignments and trees were reviewed manually: orthogroups supporting the HGT scenario were retained, and genes in these groups were classified as either foreign or native, based on their position on the tree. The neighbour of transferred genes was marked as presumed donor if the branch represented one genus or species, otherwise the donor was marked as unknown. The entire orthogroup was considered to have a native copy if it contained at least one gene marked ‘native’, regardless of which species that gene was present in.

According to recent reports, to determine the transfer times of genes during the evolutionary history of the lineage, an ancestral state reconstruction was conducted for each gene independently. The marginal ancestral state was inferred using the equal rate model120, applying the maximum-likelihood approach described by Pagel121 and implemented in the phytools package122. To ensure accuracy, the results were verified and adjusted for cases where genes were found in multiple tips but not in their common ancestor. In such instances, the presence of the gene was manually introduced at the ancestor node. For each node in the phylogenetic tree, both the originally reconstructed values and the manually adjusted values were visualized.

Genes from all orthogroups were annotated using eggNOG-mapper web server (v2.1.12)123,124. Gene Ontology terms were extracted for each group and enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package (v4.14.3), with a significance threshold of an adjusted P value of 0.05 (ref. 125).

It has been revealed that RNA-seq data for inflorescence, leaf and root tissues previously generated for 19 Hordeum species were used in this study (RNA-seq data for H. bulbosum were not available). Read trimming on quality (Q30) and removal of sequencing adapters were done using Trimmomatic (v0.32)126. Cleaned reads from each library were then mapped to the corresponding reference genome using the STAR aligner (v2.7.7a)127. Quantification of mapped reads was done using the subread package v1.5.2 with featureCounts (v2.0.1)128 followed by normalization using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method implemented in the edgeR package (v4.2.1)129. Genes were considered to be expressed if TMM ≥ 1 in at least one tissue.

Structurally intact and fragmented TEs were annotated for each genome using the panEDTA (v0.1) pipeline31. In addition to the curated TREP database (https://trep-db.uzh.ch/)130, TE classification followed the EDTA ontology (https://github.com/oushujun/EDTA/blob/master/bin/TE_Sequence_Ontology.txt), with manual curation of TE categories. High-confidence gene models from H. vulgare cv. MorexV3 was supplied via the -cds parameter to exclude genic sequences from TE annotation. For each genome, the length, classification, insertion time and divergence metrics of intact LTR retrotransposons were extracted from the intact.gff3 and pass.list output files. To investigate TE family expansion and intergenomic relationships, we used the TEpop framework (https://github.com/wicker314/TEpop) to treat each TE as an individual sample for population structure analysis46. PCA was then performed using FlashPCA2 (ref. 131) to explore the major patterns of TE variation across Hordeum species. To infer the formation time of tetraploid genomes from TE bursts, full-length LTR/Copia elements were extracted from tetraploid assemblies and clustered using CD-HIT (v4.8.1)132 with the parameters -n 5 -c 0.9 -d 0 -aL 0.9 -aS 0.9 -g 1 based on sequence similarity. To avoid potential bias caused by large-scale segmental exchanges between subgenomes, genomic regions identified as exchanged segments were excluded from this analysis (Supplementary Table 13). TEs that were shared between polyploid subgenomes but absent from their corresponding diploid progenitors were defined as post-allopolyploidization insertions. The insertion time distributions of these elements were used to reconstruct TE dynamics after subgenome fusion, and the onset of the insertion peak was used to estimate the timing of polyploid genome formation.

Recent findings suggest that to identify conserved elements across Hordeum genomes, outgroup species were removed from the HAL alignment file using halRemoveGenome in Cactus (v2.6.5). Genome-wide MSAs were then extracted in MAF format using cactus-hal2maf with the parameters “–chunkSize 1000000–noAncestors–onlyOrthologs–noDupes”, using MorexV3 as the reference genome. Alignment blocks containing fewer than 10 sequences were filtered out in MSAs. A neutral model of evolution was fitted to the Hordeum phylogeny using fourfold degenerate sites from chromosome 3H of barley, using phyloFit from the PHAST package (v1.4)133. Based on the genome-wide multiple alignments and the trained neutral model, conserved elements were identified using PhastCons with the “–most-conserved” flag. The conserved and non-conserved models were trained with a target genome coverage of 0.45, and the expected length of conserved elements was set to 8 bp.

ATAC–seq libraries were prepared from fresh leaf tissue at 3–5 leaf stage. Nuclei were isolated by fine chopping the tissue in isolation buffer (0.25 M sucrose, 10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 10 mM MgCl2, 1% Trion X-100, 5 mM β-Mercaptoethanol) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Following isolation, nuclei were quantified via flow cytometry and 75,000 nuclei were subjected to tagmentation using the Tagment DNA Enzyme (TDE1, Illumina) at 37 °C for 30 min. Transposed DNA was purified using the MinElute PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen), libraries were amplified with NEBNext High-Fidelity 2x PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs), and the final library purification was performed using VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (Vazyme) according to standard protocols from the manufacturers. Libraries were quantified as described previously62 and sequenced (paired-end, 2× 151 cycles, Illumina NovaSeq 6000, IPK Gatersleben) following protocols provided by the manufacturer (Illumina).

Industry observers note that adapter trimming and quality filtering were performed using Trim Galore (v0.6.4_dev; https://github.com/FelixKrueger/TrimGalore.git) with the following parameters: -q 25–phred33–stringency 3–length 60–paired -j 10. Only read pairs with both ends retained were used in subsequent analyses. Trimmed reads were aligned to the reference genome using BWA (v0.7.17)134. The resulting SAM files were converted to BAM format and sorted using SAMtools (v1.10)67. Only properly paired reads with mapping quality ≥ 30 were retained (-f 2 -F 1804 -q 30), and further sorted by read name to enable mate information correction using samtools fixmate. Duplicate reads were marked using Picard MarkDuplicates (v2.21.9, https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) with VALIDATION_STRINGENCY=LENIENT and REMOVE_DUPLICATES=false. After marking, only properly paired, non-duplicate reads were retained and re-sorted by coordinate to produce final cleaned BAM files for downstream analysis. BAM indices were generated using samtools index. Peaks were called using MACS2 (v2.2.9.1)135. The effective genome size (-g) was set to 4.2 Gb, approximating the size of the barley genome. Peaks were called with automatic threshold evaluation (–cutoff-analysis), and all duplicate reads were retained during the analysis to preserve biological signal.

According to recent reports, VRN1 and ZCCT genes were identified in all assembled wild barley genomes using blastn searches (blast-plus/2.12.0)114 with VRN1 MorexV3 (NC_058522.1:c528157887–528147799) and NCBI GenBank ZCCTa/b/c queries (AY485977, AY485978 and AY687931). Corresponding regions were extracted from genome assemblies by bedtools (v2.26.0)69 and manually annotated and analysed by Geneious Prime software (v2024.0.5; https://www.geneious.com). Sequence similarity visualization of the 2 kb region upstream of the transcription start site and the first intron of VRN1 genes was done by flexidot (v1.06)136. The 79-bp deletion in H. cordobense and H. muticum VRN1 gene was detected by MSA of the extracted VRN1 sequences from wild Hordeum species and winter cultivar Igri in Geneious Prime software (v2023.0.4; https://www.geneious.com) with MAFFT101. The critical region of cultivar Igri was identified in a previous study51.

Sources indicate that three biological replicates were analysed for each stage (14 DAG, 28 DAG) of H. cordobense and H. californicum grown under controlled non-vernalizing conditions (21 °C day:18 °C night, 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod). Total RNA was extracted from frozen leaf tissue using a Quick-RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research). RNA quality and concentration were evaluated with a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies) on RNA 6000 Nano chips (Agilent Technologies). H. cordobense 28 DAG RNA-seq libraries and small RNA-seq libraries were constructed according to Illumina instructions and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 platform at Novogene. Other sequencing libraries (H. cordobense 14 DAG and H. californicum 14 and 28 DAG; small RNA and RNA-seq) were constructed at the Institute of Experimental Botany (Olomouc) using NEBNext Multiplex Small RNA Library Prep Set for Illumina and NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina with poly-A selection and sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, 150 PE mode.

In a recent development, small RNA-seq read trimming and sequencing adaptor removal were done with cutadapt (v3.4)137. Only reads of length 21–24 nt were used for subsequent analyses. ShortStack (v4)138 was used to map small RNA reads to the corresponding genome with default parameters. Bigwig files were created from bam files in a combination of samtools (v1.11)67 and deepTools (v3.5.6)139 with parameters bigwigAverage, bamCoverage–binSize 10,–normalizeUsing BPM. Visualization of small RNA and mRNA bigwig files were done with pyGenomeTracks (v3.9)140.

RNA-seq read trimming on quality (Q30) and sequencing adaptor removal were done with Trimmomatic (v0.32)126. Resulting high-quality reads from each library were mapped onto the corresponding reference genome using STAR (v2.7.7a)127, with default parameters. Mapped reads quantification was done by rsem (v1.3.3)141.

Sources indicate that ten seeds per each of 14 selected Hordeum species accessions (BCC 2067 H. cordobense, BCC 2058 H. californicum, BCC 2014 H. muticum, BCC 2055 H. jubatum, BCC 2001 H. marinum, BCC 2009 H. murinum subsp. murinum, BCC 2017 H. murinum subsp. glaucum, BCC 2023 H. flexuosum, BCC 2026 H. erectifolium, BCC 2028 H. pubiflorum, BCC 2043 H. pusillum, BCC 2059 H. intercedens, BCC 2065 H. patagonicum and BCC 2069 H. roshevitzii) were used. Spring cultivated barley genotypes Morex and Golden Promise and winter genotypes Igri and Antonella were included as controls and were treated identically to wild species. Seeds were stratified at 4 °C for 4 days, germinated in Petri dishes on moist filter paper and then transferred to soil. Plants were grown under controlled non-vernalizing conditions (21 °C day:18 °C night, 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod) in a growth chamber and cultivated until senescence. Days to flowering were scored in three-day intervals, and the plants were considered flowering at the first emergence of the awn tips. Plants were imaged using a Nikon D5600 digital camera.

The elongated outer glume 1 (eog1) mutants from cultivated barley59, including eog1.a (GSHO 1891), eog1.c (GSHO 1892), eog1.e (GSHO 285) and macrolepis (lep-e.1; GSHO 960), were obtained from the Barley Genetic Stock Collection. Several mutants, namely M2342, M9630, M9815 and M11405, were identified from independent M2 lines of the previously established barley HTX mutagenesis population142. SEM observations were conducted using a Hitachi SEM SU8081 following a standard protocol143. Young inflorescences were sampled and examined. Allelism test was performed by crossing M9630 with GSHO 1891 and GSHO 1892, respectively. All F1 progeny exhibited elongated glumes on the central fertile spikelet (Extended Data Fig. 12d). Sequence-specific amplification of the C2H2-zinc-finger transcription factor gene was performed using primers T-70820-F (5′-TAGGACCGCATATTTCCAGG-3′) and T-70820-R (5′-GAACAGTTCCAAGGCGAAAG-3′). The resulting amplicons were sequenced using Sanger sequencing.

It has been revealed that clean reads (Supplementary Table 20) were obtained by removing the adapters, reads containing N bases and low-quality reads using fastp (v0.20.1) with default parameters144. Clean reads were mapped to their respective reference genomes via Hisat2 v2.1.0 with default parameters145. Read counts were determined from the mapping files via featureCounts (v2.0.1) using standard parameters128, and the TPM values of each gene were calculated. Spike-specific expressed genes were defined as having less than 5% TPM in other tissues146. The heatmap was generated using the pheatmap R package (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=pheatmap) based on the normalized TPM values. Venn diagrams were drawn using the eulerr package (v6.1.0; https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eulerr). A local BLAST search was performed using the deduced amino acids of HORVU.MOREX.r3.2HG0170820.1 (EOG1) as the query against the 24 Hordeum genome sequences to identify homologous proteins. Amino acid sequence alignment was carried out using MUSCLE (v3.8)115, and the resulting MSA was visualized with the Simple MSA Viewer function of TBtools II147.

Gene and TE annotations, MSAs and coordinates of conserved regions have been deposited at the Plant Genomics and Phenomics Research Data Repository148 (https://doi.org/10.5447/ipk/2026/11). The pangenome graph in GFA format has been deposited in the Plant Genomics and Phenomics Research Data Repository148 (https://doi.org/10.5447/ipk/2025/12).

The red line (nRF = 0.21) represents the empirical threshold separating the two peaks corresponding to background phylogenetic variation and regions with elevated phylogenetic discordance. (c) Distribution of normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distances between local gene trees and the species-wide reference tree across the genome. The local phylogeny revealed segmental exchanges between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum BCC2005 and between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. jubatum. (f) Local phylogenetic analysis of the segmental exchange region on chromosome 4H (495,575,039–607,499,705 bp), performed using the same approach as in (e). An AU test supported the local phylogenetic topology (p-AU = 1.0) and rejected the genome-wide reference topology (p-AU = 6.55 × 10−57).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fondazione Milan will be the Match Charity Partner for AC Milan vs. Frosinone on Sunday, and Matteo Gabbia has spoken as part of the initiative.

It has been revealed that since 2003, the Foundation has used sport as a tool for change, reaching more than 200,000 young people through 288 projects in Italy and 25 other countries. More than €13m has been invested over the years on various projects to help those that are less fortunate.

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Before kick-off on Sunday, the beneficiaries of the various schemes will take a photo with the starting lineup. They will also take part in pitch-side activities alongside Massimo Ambrosini, Daniele Massaro and Matteo Gabbia, who recently visited the Calcio Seduto project. Gabbia spoke at the event.

“It’s not easy to sum up in just a few minutes what Franco (Baresi) was like as a person and as a player. He was a key figure for the entire AC Milan club, for us kids who are trying to live up to him, and above all for all those people who always told me about his games.

“It’s always exciting for me to hear people talk about Franco and what he achieved with these colours, as a player and as a man.

According to recent reports, “I think Franco is a legend. Fondazione Milan embodies all the beauty and importance that Baresi had. I was moved when I met and got to know the kids from the sitting football team last week.

“I’m sure that if Franco had been there, he would have been proud of everything he organized and created for this foundation.”.

A post shared by Fondazione Milan (@fondazionemilan).

It has been revealed that “I’m feeling better. It was a strange start to the season, and I was a bit disappointed personally. Hopefully, from the moment I return, it can be a positive season for me too.”.

It has been revealed that the pregame will also honour the memory of Franco Baresi and his bond with Fondazione Milan. He was a dedicated supporter of its projects, including as a member of its Board of Directors. Club employees will take part in the tribute, along with his longtime teammate and friend Daniele Massaro.

At Sunday’s match, fans can continue to support the Foundation’s projects through donations and auctions of players’ shirts, helping create newly introduced opportunities for other young people.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nick Woltemade was left out of the Juventus starting eleven on Sunday.
  • After a woeful goalless opening half Juventus were booed off the pitch.
  • Nick Woltemade introduced for the start of the second half and the rest is history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Woltemade was left out of the Juventus starting eleven on Sunday.

A Serie A home match against Venezia.

After a woeful goalless opening half Juventus were booed off the pitch.

Nick Woltemade introduced for the start of the second half and the rest is history.

Within 14 minutes Juventus had the game won.

Nick Woltemade scoring the opening goal within eight minutes of entering the pitch.

It was then 2-0 within 14 minutes as the Newcastle United loan star got the assist for Teun Koopmeiners.

Juan Cabal a third goal, before then Nick Woltemade passed up the chance of scoring his second when he handed the ball to fellow striker Randal Kolo Muani to score from the penalty spot.

A goalless first half shocker transformed into a thumping second half 4-0 Juventus triumph.

Supersub Nick Woltemade handed the man of the match trophy after the final whistle.

Recent findings suggest that when Sports Dunia reported on the match. they waxed lyrical about the contribution of Nick Woltemade: ‘Came on and instantly changed the game. His close-range finish for the opener broke Venezia’s resistance and shifted all momentum. We noticed his intelligent movement between lines, dragging defenders out of shape. He also assisted Koopmeiners, showing composure in the box. From our perspective, a superb super-sub performance.’.

Nick Woltemade has still only started seven games in all competitions for Juventus but now has eight direct goal contributions, scoring five and getting three assists.

#129753. West Ham’s Answer Was There All Along – So Why Ignore It?

📖 Baca

West Ham’s Answer Was There All Along – So Why Ignore It?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Ham United’s lack of cutting edge against Preston North End was concerning, but perhaps the most frustrating aspect of Saturday’s 1-1 draw was that Scott Parker already appears to have the answer to the Hammers’ creative problems.
  • At the risk of sounding like a scratched record, West Ham have an emergency, break-glass solution to breaking teams down.
  • What’s particularly puzzling is that I genuinely believe the best we’ve seen Bowen play in the last couple of years came during the second half against Cardiff City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United’s lack of cutting edge against Preston North End was concerning, but perhaps the most frustrating aspect of Saturday’s 1-1 draw was that Scott Parker already appears to have the answer to the Hammers’ creative problems.

At the risk of sounding like a scratched record, West Ham have an emergency, break-glass solution to breaking teams down. It’s called Jarrod Bowen, and I’m not entirely sure I’ve ever seen our captain play wider than he did at the London Stadium yesterday.

What’s particularly puzzling is that I genuinely believe the best we’ve seen Bowen play in the last couple of years came during the second half against Cardiff City. On that occasion, Parker was effectively handed a blueprint for getting the best out of West Ham’s most key player, yet we’ve barely seen it since.

During that extraordinary second-half comeback against Cardiff, Bowen was given a certain amount of freedom, perhaps encouraged by Parker or maybe he just took it upon himself to drift into the middle of the pitch and cause havoc.

Whatever the reason, he had a hand in all three West Ham goals, and the difference was remarkable.

For the first, he drifted into what might be regarded as the number 10 position and chipped a lovely ball over the Cardiff back line for Divine Mukasa to finish.

Industry observers note that the second was similar, with Bowen again creating the opening from a central position. His pass found Joël Piroe, whose flick released Arne Engels to score.

The third goal saw Bowen back in his more familiar position on the right-hand side, where he supplied a wonderful inswinging cross for Max Kilman to equalise.

Jarrod Bowen was given license to roam against Cardiff.

But that only went to show quite how much freedom Bowen had. In essence, he was everywhere.

As a blueprint, Scott Parker couldn’t have been given a better gift on his first day in charge than discovering that West Ham’s best player could operate with devastating effect from a free role.

Indeed, I was so encouraged by what I saw that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker must restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon following the defeat at Blackburn.

Because for a brief period against Cardiff, it looked as though we’d stumbled upon something rather special.

Therefore, I was a little underwhelmed that we didn’t see it repeated against Blackburn and very worried when we probably saw our captain more straightjacketed than ever against Preston North End.

If I could offer Parker one piece of encouragement or advice, it would be to get the best out of Bowen.

I’m quite sure our latest head coach will improve the defence, and I think we saw signs of that yesterday, albeit against the league’s worst team.

But it can’t come at the expense of shackling our best player, who potentially could only be here for a few more months.

As I argued in my assessment of the Preston draw, West Ham had plenty of possession, shots and territory, but very little magic.

According to recent reports, and that’s the really bloody annoying part. We have a player who can provide exactly that, but we’re asking him to operate in a way which makes life considerably easier for the opposition.

I know one thing. If I was head coach of an opposition Championship team and I saw Jarrod Bowen shackled to the right wing, I’d breathe a huge sigh of relief.

Because West Ham get one shot at this.

If we don’t succeed in getting promotion, Bowen could leave for a pittance of £15m. That’s the release clause in the revised contract he agreed following relegation.

We do know that Bowen flew to Prague to meet Daniel Křetínský before pledging to remain at West Ham for another season, as he explained in his interview with Sky Sports.

And I’m now very fearful that we are going to waste what should really be something of a cheat code for the division.

Bowen is comfortably our best attacking player, and we’ve already seen how devastating he can be when allowed to roam. Yet rather than building upon that discovery, Parker appears to have returned him to a position where he’s easier to mark and less able to influence the game.

I wish it weren’t so, but I’ve now come to the conclusion that the second half against Cardiff was a pure accident rather than a window into what we could begin to see from Scott Parker as he got his teeth into the West Ham job.

But decisions like that could well make the difference between automatic promotion and a play-off place, if we’re lucky.

24 hours on from West Ham’s  tepid point against the bottom side in the league and whilst the justified criticism is flying around, there are definitely positives to pull out of a fixture in which West Ham dominated all the notable statistics save the most important one: The points tally at the final whistle.

It has been revealed that sadly, again the Hammers have lost ground on the leaders and now sit eight points adrift. And yet, from Scott Parker’s comments, there are definite signs that he’s learned from at least some of the mistakes made by his predecessor. Reversing Nuno’s decision to cast out Edson Alvarez from the senior team proved a massive success.. Who knew.

Yesterday’s re-integration of ‘El Machin’ into the starting line up was his first league appearance in a West Ham shirt since May 2025.

This was an Alvarez playing more like his first season as a Hammer.

As Scott Parker summed up, Alvarez did not let him down:.

“He brought every bit of what we needed. It’s a young team, and his experience today in terms of organising and his general presence on the pitch was very, very good for us for large aspects.

According to recent reports, “It was a significant ask and I knew that going into the game, he hasn’t played at all this year and probably hasn’t had a lot of training in and around the first team. But I just felt his experience and know-how around it was needed, and for sure he was a massive part today of why we performed the way we performed” (Justin Allen- YouTube).

The Mexican clearly cares: He was in tears before kick off, so tough has his time in the football wilderness been.

Having been such a critic of him during his card-strewn Lopetegui era, credit where it is due. Edson Alvarez was, indeed, excellent yesterday and it is a testimony to his professionalism that he played a full ninety after not playing competitive football since August.

If he can maintain that kind of focus and form, Parker may well have found the missing piece in West Ham’s defensive jigsaw puzzle, that proved beyond his predecessor who simply wouldn’t extend the olive branch to any of his ‘frozen out’ players.

Preston North End, the bottom side in the Championship, arrived in east London yesterday unaffected by the occasion and kept West Ham at bay for an hour until Dinos Mavropanos headed equaliser restored parity and saved Scott Parker’s blushes.

Two weeks’ work during the international break had accounted for very little as Preston withstood everything the Hammers and their almost 60,000 fans had to throw at their lowly opponents.

Sources indicate that and therein lies the problem. Having surrendered the small, intimidating, sometimes downright hostile atmosphere of Upton Park back in 2016, the distance from the pitch and the wide open spaces of the Olympic Stadium are about as intimidating as a day out at London Zoo for our opponents and their fans who continue to pour scorn on the venue.

Sources indicate that it just doesn’t strike fear into opponents as it should. Even when we score.

Isolated tiers in the stadium and poor pitch proximity do little to help the atmosphere at the London Stadium – as our opponents are finding out.

Preston fan Tm Mercer, writing in the Lancashire Evening Post, makes it abundantly clear that there was no noticeable crowd reaction to lift the home side, as there should have been once Mavropanos restored parity:.

“Aside from play-off finals, I’m pretty certain it is the first time I’ve been in a stadium for a league match with 60,000-plus through the gate.

Yet, when they equalised, it did not feel like the roar of that many people in such a cavernous ground. Give me somewhere like Gigg Lane, stood in their paddock pitch side, any day!”.

For the uninitiated, Gigg Lane is the home of Bury FC with a capacity of around…..12,000.

Nobody is suggesting the Hammers fans were silent. The cursèd accoustics from the soulless bowl and sheer distance from the pitch play right into opponents’ hands. And, ten years after moving in, it’s going to take a lot more than some safe standing and a couple of family zones to fix it.

  • When, at England's World Cup base in Kansas City, I then sat down with Trafford and he revealed that his partner had packed some Lego for him to build in camp, you wondered if sixth-form was a grade too high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 14:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:35 EST, 16 November 2026.

In a recent development, 'It was like meeting a kid at a sixth-form careers day'. That was the verdict, slightly unflattering but endearing all the same, of one Premier League chief after encountering James Trafford.

When, at England's World Cup base in Kansas City, I then sat down with Trafford and he revealed that his partner had packed some Lego for him to build in camp, you wondered if sixth-form was a grade too high.

Recent findings suggest that he is the son of a Cumbrian farmer and the Lego was of a tractor, which he would save for later in the tournament. 'You don't want to go too early,' he mentioned.

In a recent development, none of this is a criticism. Far from it. There was a boyish charm, an innocence, even, and Trafford was engaging company. Nonetheless, he did not sound ready for the likes of a World Cup semi-final against Argentina. Thomas Tuchel agreed.

In a recent development, but every boy will one day become a man. On a ferocious and febrile night in Madrid, no place for adolescents, we may just have witnessed James Trafford's graduation ceremony.

It has been revealed that without his double save in stoppage-time, England would have left Spain without a famous, and deserved, victory. One Spanish title labelled it 'la actuacion de su vida', the performance of his life. You wonder how much they saw of his loan spell at Accrington Stanley, but the sentiment stands.

James Trafford celebrates with Jarell Quansah, Dan Burn and Ezri Konsa during his starring performance in Spain.

Trafford pictured with his farmer father, David, in the cab of his tractor with their dogs (Source: James Trafford).

Madrid daily AS exclaimed: 'Magisterio de Trafford!' Translated, 'A Trafford Masterclass!'. They claim he was the reason Spain could not complete their comeback, and they would be right.

When Tuchel stood with us in a corridor of the Metropolitano Stadium on the eve of the game, he had no concern confirming that Trafford would start. His message, though, was clear - it was sink or swim for a goalkeeper who turned 24 last month.

Recent findings suggest that not only did Trafford keep his head above water, it was he who pulled the team ashore. It was he to whom his senior colleagues ran in celebration. Ezri Konsa nearly took the shirt off Trafford's back, such was the force of his gratitude. But maybe this was the occasion when Trafford took the No 1 jersey from the back of Jordan Pickford, the holder for nearly a decade.

Pickford has done nothing wrong. Were Trafford to still display that maturity deficit, Pickford would be a reliable custodian heading to Euro 2028. This is not Peter Shilton post Italia 90, an uncomfortable truth of a great in need of the retirement barn. The 32-year-old has plenty to give on the back of all he has already given.

This, admitted Tuchel after the 3-2 win, is a selection dilemma that allows a manager to sleep well at night.

'There is no headache at all!' he boomed. 'I'm so far away from a headache, I cannot imagine.

Trafford left Manchester City with the strategy to usurp Jordan Pickford as England No 1.

Jude Bellingham certainly seemed impressed with the performance of the goalkeeper.

Recent findings suggest that 'This is what we wanted. This is the best thing that can happen to all of us, also to Pickers. It is amazing how they push each other, and if then Traff has a performance like this, he has it because he knows he's well prepared. He gets the push from his colleagues and competitors.'.

According to recent reports, tuchel has seen enough of Trafford in training and around camp to believe he is ready for promotion. He has watched him for Leeds, where he rates as the best performing goalkeeper in the Premier League. His 'net goals prevented' (4.4) and 'save percentage' (81.4) are higher than any rival this season, including Pickford.

'You always have to deserve your place,' added Tuchel. 'You will never get a gift and just get a game (for the sake of it). So he deserved to play and we expected this kind of performance. It was not only the last save, but also the build-up play and not losing focus. He has proved it on this stage, so this gives him a lot of belief. Now, it's on him to keep going for it.'.

In a recent development, it, you presume, is the No 1 jersey. Trafford has made no secret of his desire to take it from Pickford, and he told us in the summer that such ambition was the motivation behind him wanting to leave Manchester City for a second time.

Sources indicate that that day, he flipped his room key with a magician's sleight of hand throughout the interview, a dexterity useful for Lego. Better still for fingertip saves such as the one to deny Aymeric Laporte in the 91st minute.

Also in the gift pack from his girlfriend were two face masks. 'Very thoughtful,' he quipped. But that is another observation, bordering on concern, that some prospective buyers have made in recent years - on the goalkeeping scale of uber professional to joker, he resides too close to the latter. We have seen, even this season, the odd concentration lapse that speaks to that thought.

Trafford has played a starring role in goal since moving to Leeds United in the summer.

But there was also a feeling that Trafford needed more exposure and responsibility before the penny dropped and his value was realised. Already, £95million has been spent on him in transfer fees.

At Leeds, and now with England, he has been given that stage, as Tuchel calls it. The head coach maintains that Pickford is his first choice, but it was Trafford he picked for both Nations League fixtures against Spain, the ones that really mattered, the ones that would strengthen or threaten his own employment.

As for Trafford's career prospects, to revisit our opening line, England's No 1 sounds like a fair vocation.

Thomas Tuchel wants England to use victory in the Nations League finals as a springboard to winning Euro 2028 at Wembley.

The head coach admits it has taken him a while to recover from the trauma of his side’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in July, for which he was heavily criticised.

But after beating world champions Spain 3-2 on Sunday night, topping their Nations League group ahead of March’s quarter-finals and next summer's finals, Tuchel is finally able to look forward with positivity and belief.

It has been revealed that ‘I saw the celebrations in Portugal when they won the Nations League,’ he remarked. ‘It’s just the best, the best preparation we can have for the Euros. We want to have these matches on the highest level to prove ourselves and to gain confidence, to see where we are and to adjust our game where we need to, that’s what this Nations League is perfect for. We want to win it.’.

According to recent reports, england have won five of their six matches since the World Cup, losing only to Spain at Wembley in September. In the build up to that game, Tuchel was involved in heated exchanges with observers who continued to question his tactics in the final half hour against Argentina.

’It took me a while to digest (the World Cup exit) and see the way forward, how we can help and adjust and improve, and how we can do this together,’ he mentioned.

‘We had reviews and so on, but clarity then came together with the players. Straight away we had the energy right to take the next steps. The ideas became more clear for me, even if it was not so easy the first week, to overcome and arrive with different emotions. Some were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not digested it. But it was important to have this kind of process together.

It has been revealed that ‘(Spain) was a complete performance that makes me very proud. It's a full package of belief, of courage, of commitment, of togetherness, of relying on each other and stepping up in this moment.’.

Tuchel, though, has rejected the idea that seeing out the win Madrid was proof that he has learned from his mistakes in Atlanta.

‘Not at all, I think we would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11,’ he said. ‘For me, it was Mexico reloaded (not Argentina). It's one man down, but what can you do? It is their strength to have ball possession, to overload and find the gaps. It just plays totally into their hands and it comes wave after wave. It felt like three hours and thirty minutes!’.
