These treatments were performed in parallel with S.Tm-infected epithelia, which served as infected controls, and were sustained until the end point of the experiment.

It has been revealed that to analyse the cytokines in the supernatant of the engineered intestines, 100 µl supernatant was collected from both basal reservoirs per engineered intestine and pooled afterwards. Supernatants were quickly centrifuged to remove cell debris and frozen at −20 °C, followed by a transfer to −80 °C until further processing.

In a recent development, assessment of the cytokines was performed using a custom-designed LEGENDplex panel (CXCL10, IL-8, sFas, BioLegend). Controls, standards and beads were prepared following the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were not diluted. In brief, 25 µl of the samples were mixed with 25 µl assay buffer and 25 µl mixed beads. The 25 µl diluted standard was mixed with 25 µl assay buffer and 25 µl mixed beads. Both samples and standard mixtures were dispensed in a V-bottom plate. Afterwards, samples were incubated for 2 h at room temperature on a shaker at 800 rpm. Samples were centrifuged at 500g for 2 min followed by removal of the supernatant. Samples were washed with 200 µl 1X wash buffer per well, followed by addition of 25 µl detection antibodies and incubation for 1 h at room temperature on a shaker at 800 rpm. Next, without washing, SA-PE was added and incubated for 30 min at room temperature on a shaker at 800 rpm. Samples were centrifuged at 500g for 2 min followed by removal of the supernatant to remove excess antibodies. Finally, 150 µl of 1X wash buffer was added before acquisition on Cytek Aurora with the 5 L configuration (Cytek) following the recommended experimental setup. To obtain absolute cytokine concentrations, the raw data were processed and analysed using the software provided by the manufacturer (LEGENDplex data analysis software, v2024-06-15, BioLegend).

Analyte concentrations were determined using a custom U-PLEX Immuno-Oncology Human Biomarker Group 1 Assay (Meso Scale Diagnostics (MSD)). The assay was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, U-PLEX plates were prepared by incubating linkers with their corresponding biotinylated capture antibodies for 30 min at room temperature, followed by overnight coating at 4 °C. Controls were reconstituted in assay diluent and standards were prepared via a sevenfold dilution; samples were diluted 1:5. Plates were washed, and either 25 µl of standard or 10 µl of sample (brought to a total volume of 50 µl with diluent) was added to each well. Plates were incubated for 2 h at room temperature with orbital shaking (500 rpm). Following a wash step, 50 µl of SULFO-TAG detection antibody solution was added per well and incubated for 2 h at room temperature (500 rpm). After a final wash, 150 µl of MSD GOLD read buffer was added, and the plates were immediately read using a MESO QuickPlex SQ 120 (or MESO Sector S 600) imager. Absolute cytokine concentrations were calculated using the MSD Discovery Workbench software (v4.0.13), accounting for the sample dilution. Samples under the limit of detection were set to 0.

Assessment of secreted cytokines from S.Tm WT and ΔinvG–ΔssaV strains was performed with the human cytokine 71-plex Discovery assay by the supplier. Samples below the limit of detection were not considered for analysis.

The following microscopes were used for confocal imaging of the stained and live engineered intestines: (1) Nikon Ti2 microscope with CSU-W1 spinning disk (Yokogawa) equipped with a sCOMS camera (ORCA-Fusion BT, Hamamatsu Photonics). Depending on the application, the following objectives were used: ×4 plan apo Lambda OFN25, ×10 plan apo Lambda OFN25 DIC N1, ×20 C S Plan Fluor LWD, ×25 apo LWD 1.1 W DIC N2, ×25 C Sil plan apo Lambda S (Nikon Instruments). The extended depth-of-focus feature of the NIS-Elements software (v5.42.05, Nikon) was used to create focused brightfield and fluorescent images of the engineered intestines. In certain cases, images were further processed and colour adjusted using ImageJ software (2.3.0/1.54f). (2) Leica STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope equipped with 3 power HyD detectors, white light laser (440–790 nm) using ×25 HC FLUOTAR L VISIR X25 objective (Leica Microsystems). Images were either visualized as maximum projection or 3D reconstructed using the Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) software (v4.6.1.27508).

Sources indicate that 3D reconstructions of the epithelial layer with integrated TRM cells from the engineered intestinal whole-mount stainings were generated with the Imaris surface function (v9.9.1). Surfaces were rendered based on fluorescence intensities of the iCas9 CDH1–mScarlet3 reporter and CD3, and CD8 antibody stainings.

Industry observers note that proliferative cells were labelled using the Click-iT Plus EdU Alexa Fluor 488 Imaging Kit (C10637, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Engineered intestinal tissues were cultured as described above for 10 days. On day 10, EdU was added to the standard culture medium at a final concentration of 10 µM, and chips were returned to the incubator. After 2 h, one chip was fixed immediately in 4% PFA. The remaining two chips were washed three times with chip medium (Supplementary Table 1), with 2 h of incubation between washes, and returned to the incubator. One chip was fixed 2 days later, and the final chip was fixed after 4 days post-EdU pulse. After fixation, samples were washed in PBS and processed for EdU staining according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Imaging was performed using a Leica STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope. Before immune cell seeding, TRM cells or T cells derived from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (isolation described above) were labelled with CellTrace Far Red (C34572, Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Afterwards, immuno-chips were prepared as described above. Timelapse imaging was performed 7–10 days (where indicated) post-co-culture setup with either a STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope with a ×25 HC FLUOTAR L VISIR X25 objective (Leica Microsystems) or with Nikon Ti2 microscope equipped with CSU-W1 spinning disk (Yokogawa) using with ×25 apo LWD 1.1 W DIC N2 objective (Nikon Instruments). Images on Leica STELLARIS 8 were obtained in bidirectional mode with 1,024 × 1,024 pixels at 600 Hz. Images were acquired with varying Z-stack depth (z-steps, 4 µm). Samples were imaged between 42 and 60 min (where indicated). During imaging, samples were maintained in a microscopy incubation chamber at 37 °C at 5% CO2 (The Box, Life Imaging Services). For live imaging along the crypt–villus axis, engineered intestines were collected from the glass slide and cut in two followed by placing the engineered intestines perpendicularly on top of a glass dish. The engineered intestines were then fixated with a thin glass coverslip to avoid buoyancy due to medium in the dish. After acquisition, maximum-intensity projections were generated for downstream analysis.

Recent findings suggest that timelapse movies were analysed using CellProfiler. In brief, cells were segmented at each frame with multiotsu, morphological parameters were extracted and segmented cells were tracked over time using LAP algorithm with the following parameters: number of standard deviations for search radius = 80, search radius limits = 3–80 pixels, gap closing cost = 2, split alternative cost = 1, merge alternative cost = 1, mitosis alternative = 1, maximum gap displacement = 100 pixel, maximum split score = 10, maximum merge score = 5, maximal temporal gap = 6 and maximum mitosis distance = 40. The output per cell was analysed using KNIME (v5.2). The means and standard deviation of morphological features per track over time were calculated. The standard deviation of morphological features over time is a measure of the dynamism of cells as they use amoeboid motility. In addition, track lifetime and track total distance were calculated. Tracks with less than five frames were discarded.

Timelapse imaging of S.Tm intracellular replication was performed at 37 °C at 5% CO2 conditions with a Nikon Ti2 microscope equipped with CSU-W1 spinning disk (Yokogawa) using ×25 apo LWD 1.1 W DIC N2 objective (Nikon Instruments). Images were processed using ImageJ software (2.3.0/1.54f) and NIS-Elements software (Nikon).

For fixed whole-mount staining and imaging, engineered intestines were washed once with 1X DPBS before fixation with 4% PFA in the chip slide. After 1 h of fixation at room temperature, the engineered intestines were washed three times with 1X DPBS. Engineered intestines were either stained in situ or collected using a biopsy puncher (3 mm in diameter) and transferred into a 24-well plate. Next, samples were permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich) in 1X DPBS for 2 h at room temperature on an orbital rocker at 50 rpm. Permeabilization was followed by a blocking step with blocking buffer (10% donkey serum (S30-M, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.01% Triton X-100 in DPBS 1X) for 4 h at room temperature on an orbital rocker or 16 h at 4 °C. Primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 1) were applied and incubated overnight at 4 °C on an orbital rocker. Afterwards, samples were washed three times for 1 h each at room temperature with 1X DBPS on an orbital rocker. Anti-species secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 1), DAPI (1 µg ml−1; 62249, Thermo Scientific) and phalloidin (Alexa Fluor 568 phalloidin A12380; Alexa Fluor 488 phalloidin A12379; Alexa Fluor 647 phalloidin A30107, Thermo Fisher Scientific) were incubated for 4 h at room temperature or 16 h at 4 °C on an orbital rocker, covering the sample with aluminum foil. Samples were washed three times for 1 h each with DPBS on an orbital rocker before imaging.

For engineered tissue, samples were washed once with 1X DPBS before fixation with 4% PFA in the chip slide. After 2 h of fixation at room temperature, the engineered intestines were washed three times before using a biopsy puncher (3 mm in diameter) to detach the ECM and tissue. In parallel, the engineered intestines histomold, specifically designed to facilitate co-planar embedding of up to 50 engineered intestines, was prepared as previously described8. In brief, liquid histogel was dispensed into the chip histomold and allowed to polymerize for 20 min at 4 °C. Following polymerization, the histoarray was demoulded. Engineered intestines were then transferred with a thin tweezer into the slits of the histoarray. After careful glueing of the engineered intestines in the wells of the histoarray (see Harter et al.8), the histoarray was completely filled and distributed into biopsy cassettes. Samples were dehydrated overnight using a vacuum filter processor (HistoCore PEARL, Leica). The following day, samples were embedded in liquid paraffin.

Sources indicate that for primary intestinal tissue, samples were washed three times in 1X DPBS and fixed in 4% PFA at room temperature. Fixation was performed for 24 h, although reduced to 3 h for smaller specimens to prevent over-fixation.

It has been revealed that the basal compartments of the engineered intestines were washed once with 1X DPBS before fixation with 4% PFA. The apical reservoir was neither washed nor fixed to preserve the integrity of the luminal content. After 2 h of fixation at room temperature, the engineered intestines were washed three more times only in the basal compartment. Next, the bottom glass of the chip slide was detached by applying mechanical pressure and the matrix was punched from the bottom of the hydrogel in upwards direction, keeping the epithelium and luminal content. The punched sample was then carefully covered with 8 µl of TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50 ml, Advanced Biomatrix) neutralized according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Finally, the sample was incubated for 15 min at 37 °C before the transfer to the slits of the histoarray, as described before.

Samples were dehydrated using a graded ethanol series as previously described8. In brief, tissues were held in 10% neutral buffered formalin for 5 min, followed by sequential dehydration steps: two washes in 70% ethanol (30 min each), one wash in 80% ethanol (1 h), and two washes in 96% ethanol (30 min each). Next, two steps of two 1-h incubations in 100% ethanol were performed, followed by two 45-min xylene baths. Finally, samples were held in paraffin until regular formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) setting.

FFPE blocks were, unless otherwise specified, sectioned at a thickness of 3.5 µm and transferred on Superfrost Ultra Plus Gold Adhesion Slides. Slides were incubated in a slide oven overnight at 37 °C.

Industry observers note that H&E staining was executed in a fully automated manner following the standard protocol on a Ventana HE600 stainer (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). AlcianBlue–PAS staining was performed fully automated using the AlcianBlue for PAS (860-003, Ventana) and PAS staining (860-014, Ventana) kits on the Ventana Benchmark (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). In brief, after three cycles of deparaffinization, slides were washed and 200 µl of PAS AlcianBlue incubated for 16 min at 37 °C. Wash was repeated, and 200 µl of PAS periodic acid was applied for 4 min, before another wash and 12 min of PAS Schiffs staining. Next, slides were washed again and 200 µl PAS neutralizer was added and incubated for 4 min. Finally, slides were washed with 100 µl before counterstaining the slide with 200 µl of PAS haematoxylin for 8 min. Afterwards, slides were coverslipped as indicated in the manufacturer’s instructions. H&E-stained, IHC and AlcianBlue–PAS-stained slides were imaged with a brightfield whole-slide scanner at ×40 (Hamamatsu, NanoZoomer, S360; pixel size of 0.23 µm per pixel) and viewed in NDP-view2 (v2.9.29).

According to recent reports, as previously described52, IHC staining of FFPE slides was performed using a Ventana Discovery Ultra automated tissue stainer (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). The slides were baked for 8 min at 60 °C, followed by a deparaffinization cycle for 8 min at 69 °C (deparaffinization cycle repeated three times). Heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed with Tris-EDTA buffer (pH 7.8, CC1, 950-227, Ventana) at 95 °C for a total of 40 min. Depending on the host species of secondary antibody, the slide was incubated with either Discovery goat Ig block (760-6008, Ventana) or 10% donkey serum for 32 min at 37 °C followed by application of Discovery inhibitor (760-4840, Ventana) for 8 min. Afterwards, primary antibodies were applied (diluted in Discovery antibody diluent, 760-108, Ventana; for specific concentrations and incubation times, see Supplementary Table 1). Primary antibodies were detected using anti-species secondary antibodies conjugated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP; OmniMap anti-rabbit HRP (prediluted), 760-4311, Ventana; OmniMap anti-mouse HRP (prediluted), 760-4310, Ventana; OmniMap anti-rat HRP (prediluted), 760-4310, Ventana; and OmniMap anti-goat HRP, 760-4647, Ventana) for 16 min and visualized by conversion of 3,3′-diaminobenizidine (DAB; Discovery ChromoMap DAB kit, 760-159, Ventana). Samples were counterstained with haematoxylin (Haematoxylin II, 790-2208, Ventana) and blueing reagent (760-2037, Ventana). After dehydration with a standard series of alcohol (75%, 95%, 100% and 100% v/v; CAS64-17-5, Roche) followed by 100% xylol baths (444240050, ACROS Organoids), slides were coverslipped in the RCM7000 coverslipper (MEDITE) using a standard histology glue (00811-EX, Pertex). Slides were dried for at least 2 h before imaging.

Industry observers note that as previously described52, opal mIF staining of FFPE slides was performed using a Ventana Discovery Ultra automated tissue stainer (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). The slides were baked for 8 min at 60 °C, followed by a deparaffinization cycle for 8 min at 69 °C (deparaffinization cycle repeated three times). Heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed with Tris-EDTA buffer (pH 7.8, CC1, 950-227, Ventana) at 95 °C for a total of 40 min. Depending on the host species of secondary antibody, the slide was incubated with either Discovery goat Ig block (760-6008, Ventana) or 10% donkey serum for 32 min at 37 °C followed by application of Discovery inhibitor (760-4840, Ventana) for 8 min. Afterwards, primary antibodies were dispensed onto the slide (diluted in Discovery antibody diluent, 760-108, Ventana; for specific concentrations and incubation times, see Supplementary Table 1). Primary antibodies were detected using anti-species secondary antibodies conjugated with HRP (see above for catalogue numbers) for 16 min. Next, the corresponding opal dye (opal 480 FP150001KT, opal 520 FP1487001KT, opal 570 FP1488001KT, opal 620 FP1495001KT, opal 690 FP1497001KT and opal 780 FP1501001KT, Akoya Biosciences) were applied, previously prepared following the manufacturer’s instructions. After each application of the primary antibody, followed by the corresponding secondary antibody and opal dye (with increasing fluorophore excitation wavelength), an antibody neutralization and denaturation step was applied to remove residual antibodies and HRP, before starting the staining cycle again with the Discovery inhibitor blocking step. Finally, samples were counterstained with DAPI (Roche). When used, fluorescein-labelled Jacalin (FL-1151-5, Vector Laboratories) was integrated into the mIF staining protocol by swapping it with the 520 opal dye and always applied last in the staining protocol.

As previously described52, opal mIF stainings were imaged and digitized using multispectral imaging of the Vectra Polaris (Perkin Elmer) using the MOTiF technology at ×20 magnification for all seven opal dyes (opal 480–780) and DAPI. Slides were imaged in a batch manner to ensure identical imaging settings and cross-comparability within each experiment for subsequent image analysis. Unmixing of channels and processing of images were performed with PhenoChart (v1.0.12) and inForm (v2.4). Images were processed as .qptiff tiles and fused in HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs). A pixel resolution of 0.5 µm per pixel was used.

It has been revealed that high-resolution opal mIF images were obtained using a STELLARIS 8 microscope (Leica) with a water-immersion objective (HC FLUOTAR L VISIR ×25/0.95 NA WATER). A white-light laser (440–790 nm) was used to image all opal dyes. Channel signals were acquired sequentially to reduce cross-bleeding. Images were obtained in bidirectional mode with 1,024 × 1,024 pixels (pixel size of 384.56 × 384.56 nm2) or 2,048 × 2,048 pixels (pixel size of 273.8 × 273.38 nm2). Images were either visualized as maximum projection or 3D reconstructed using the Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) software (v4.6.1.27508).

Sources indicate that image analysis of opal mIF images was performed with HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs) and HALO AI (v3.6.4134, Indica Labs). Sample annotation was either manually performed or by deploying the TMA module in HALO. For detection and annotation of the engineered intestines, a RandomForest (v2) classifier was used to distinguish organoids from background (for example, matrix; minimum object size more than 1,000 µm). Following validation, engineered intestines were handled as individual regions of interest (ROIs) and quantification was executed per ROI. The RandomForest (v2) classifier was integrated in the Area Quantification FL (v2.3.4) modules and used to quantify positive marker staining against either overall size of each individual object or normalized to the DAPI+ area of the object (as indicated in the figure legends) as well as for quantification of intensities. The HighPlex FL (v4.2.14) module was used to perform nuclear segmentation based on DAPI+ cells, assisted by HALO AI’s integrated ‘AI default nuclear segmentation type’) for phenotype analysis. The FISH-IF (v2.2.5) module was used to perform DAPI-based nuclear segmentation and identification of cells positive for single intracellular bacteria. Specific cell phenotypes were determined by colocalization of the respective markers of interest with the DAPI+ nuclei (including the cytoplasm radius (1.25 µm) and nuclear signals, depending on the marker of interest). By integrating the RandomForest (v2) or DenseNet (v2) classifier in the HighPlex analysis module, for example, localization of the T cells in the matrix or epithelium, was determined.

Assessment of the spatial patterning was performed by manually annotating the crypts and the top epithelial layer along the E-cadherin+ signal as separate ROIs. The basal side of the top epithelial layer served as the ROI border to the crypt underneath. Cell quantification was then performed within the separate annotations per engineered intestine using the Highplex FL module. Similarly, quantification of the thickness of mucus was performed by manually outlining two lines within the same annotation layer: one along the apical side of the E-cadherin+ epithelium of the top epithelial layer (excluding the crypt depth), and a second line along the lumen-facing top layer of the Jacalin+ mucus.

Recent findings suggest that positive controls on primary matched or non-matched primary intestinal tissue were included in every staining. In case of some experiments, negative controls were co-embedded within the same histoarray by experimental design, easing unbiased threshold adjustment and detection of potential unspecific antibody binding (for example, the epithelium-only control served as the negative control for immune markers; different intestinal regions within one FFPE block).

Sources indicate that quantification of the number of viable crypts per engineered intestine was performed with a RandomForest classifier (v2) in HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs). Dozens of viable intestinal crypts from different donors were manually annotated using brightfield images of the engineered intestines acquired with the ×2 objective of the Leica Dmi1 inverted microscope (11526227, Leica Microsystems). After brief verification, the algorithm was deployed to detect the number of viable crypts per engineered intestine. All brightfield images were acquired with the Leica Dmi1 inverted microscope with ×2, ×4 and ×10 objectives.

Recent findings suggest that statistical analysis was carried out with GraphPad Prism (v10.6.1; GraphPad software). The number of donors is indicated as ‘d = x’, whereas the number of independent engineered intestines within each donor is referred to as ‘n = x’ in the respective figure legend. The number of repeated independent experiments is indicated as ‘e = x’. Data normality was evaluated with Shapiro–Wilk normality test and Q–Q plots. When comparing two sets of data, paired or unpaired two-tailed t-tests were carried out, including Welch’s correction when the standard deviation determined not identical between the groups by a F-test. In case the data were not normally distributed, Mann–Whitney sum-rank tests were performed. For comparisons involving more than two datasets and multiple variables, we performed one-way and two-way ANOVA, including Tukey’s, Dunnett’s or Šídák’s multiple comparisons test comparisons when comparing to a control condition. Nested one-way ANOVA was performed when d < 3, comparing the data across the number of independent engineered intestines (n). A Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparison test was performed instead of one-way ANOVA when the data did not follow normal distribution. Data were visualized with their mean and standard deviation, with the exact P values highlighting the statistical significance in the respective figure legend.

Before dissociation, surfaces were cleaned with RNase AWAY Decontamination Reagent (10328011, Invitrogen) and all tubes were coated with a coating solution containing HBSS −Ca2+/−Mg2+ (14175095, Gibco) + 1% BSA (130-091-376, Miltenyi Biotec) at 4 °C for at least 15 min. Multiple engineered intestines were pooled for each scRNA-seq and scMultiome, as indicated in the figure legends. Intestinal monolayers were detached from the matrix, collected and transferred to DNA LoBind 1.5-ml tubes (22431021, Eppendorf) with 1 ml of coating solution using forceps. In the case of the scMultiome experiment, where the epithelium integrity was compromised, the epithelium and hydrogel matrix were apically punched using a 3-mm puncher and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube. The punched hydrogel was dissolved by incubating the mix with 1 ml of collagenase type I (100 U ml−1; 17100017, Gibco) in Advanced DMEM/F12 for 15 min at 37 °C, following three washing steps in coating solution to clean the presence of collagenase in the sample and remove the digested hydrogel. Pooled and cleaned monolayers were pipetted up and down 50 times to mechanically disrupt the monolayers into smaller fragments. The single-cell dissociation was performed using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (130-092-628, Miltenyi Biotec). In brief, the samples were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was removed and the samples were incubated with 1 ml of the enzymeP Mix 1 at 37 °C for a total of 15 min, homogenizing the sample every 5 min by pipetting up and down a total of 50 times with a P1000 tip. After the first incubation, 30 µl of enzyme A Mix2 was added to the sample and incubated for 10 min, with homogenization steps every 5 min and inspection of the suspension under a brightfield microscope. The single-cell suspension was filtered through a PluriStrainer Mini 40 µm (43-10040-40, Pluriselect), previously coated with coating solution, into latest 1.5-ml DNA LoBind tubes and centrifuged at 450g for 5 min at 4 °C.

In a recent development, for scRNA-seq or scMultiome experiments, the pellets were washed a total of three times with coating solution at 450g for 5 min at 4 °C. Next, the samples were counted using the Countless 3 FL (AMQAF2000, Invitrogen) and adjusted to the desired concentrations for multiplexing, nuclei isolation or loading on the Chromium X (10X Genomics).

In a recent development, for flow cytometry, FACS and Imagestream experiments, the pellets were washed 1× in DPBS before incubation with eBioscience Fixable Viability Dye eFluor 780 (1:2,000; 65-0865-14, Thermo Scientific) + TruStain FcX (1:200; 422301, BioLegend) in DPBS for 5 min at 4 °C in dark conditions. Next, the samples were spinned down, resuspended in FACS buffer (DPBS supplemented with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS), and incubated with PE-EpCAM (1:100; 324206, BioLegend) for 5 min at 4 °C in dark conditions. Single stained and unstained controls were prepared in parallel for compensation. After FACS, the sorted cells were centrifuged, resuspended in FACS buffer and counted before loading on the Chromium X.

Sources indicate that cell suspensions were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C before filtering through 70-µm strainers. For flow cytometric quantification of S.TmGFP-infected cells, fully stained, single stained and unstained samples were resuspended in 250 µl of FACS buffer and analysed using a five-laser Cytek Aurora spectral flow cytometer. Spectral unmixing with autofluorescence extraction was performed using Cytek Spectroflo CS software, and quantification of GFP+ cell fractions was performed in FlowJo (v10; BD Biosciences).

For FACS, fully stained, single stained and unstained samples were resuspended in 150 µl of FACS buffer. Bulk GFP+ and GFP− populations were isolated using a five-laser Cytek Aurora CS spectral cell sorter equipped with a 100-µm nozzle. Spectral unmixing with autofluorescence extraction was performed using Cytek Spectroflo CS software. Target cell populations were collected into low protein-binding 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes (Eppendorf). Next, the cells were centrifuged, resuspended in FACS buffer and counted for scRNA-seq on the Chromium X.

Recent findings suggest that for single-cell total RNA-seq (VASA-seq), single cells were index sorted using a five-laser BD FACSAria Fusion with a 100-µm nozzle into individual wells of a 384-well plate filled with lysis buffer (Single Cell Discoveries). Cells were grouped and sorted by GFP level (GFP−, GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi) to ensure equal representation in the final dataset of each group. Following sorting, plates were immediately stored at −80 °C until library preparation. Additional cells were also sorted into a lysis buffer containing 0.5% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich) for CFU counting within the same experiment.

Sorted GFP+ and GFP− cells were concentrated by centrifugation and resuspended in 25 µl of FACS buffer for analysis using a four-laser Cytek Amnis ImagestremX MKII dual CCD camera imaging flow cytometer. The 488-nm and 642-nm excitation lasers were set to a power of 10 mW and 150 mW, respectively, and data were acquired using the ×60 objective. Brightfield images were collected in channels 1 and 9, whereas fluorescence signals for GFP, EpCAM-PE and eFluor-780 were detected in channels 2, 3 and 12, respectively.

Industry observers note that imageStream data were analysed using IDEAS (v6.4.9.0). For each dataset, a compensation matrix was generated using the single-colour controls and the software compensation wizard, and applied to the relevant dataset. Events were gated to only keep contrasted, unclipped, EpCAM+GFP+ images of single host cells. The IDEAS internalization tool (GFP) was used to filter for host cells displaying intracellular GFP signal from the analysis and to quantify the prevalence of bacterial internalization. To perform spot counting in host cells, another filtering step to discard unfocused GFP signal was performed. With this filtering in place, we could start performing GFP spot counting using a series of machine learning classifiers. This was performed using IDEAS machine learning functionality. First, we manually selected two mutually exclusive populations of cells: 25 cells displaying a single GFP colony, 25 cells showing 2 or more than 2 colonies. A first machine learning classifier was trained on these two populations, and subsequently used to classify cells in two categories: ‘one colony’ and ‘more than one colony’. From the more-than-one-colony pool of events, the same strategy was used to train a second machine learning model on two mutually exclusive populations: 25 cells displaying 2 colonies, and 25 cells displaying more than 2 colonies. The model was run on the more than one colony data to classify cells in two newly introduced categories: two colonies versus more than two colonies. The obtained mutually exclusive populations were manually curated to fix misclassification of a few events. Cells belonging to the more-than-two-colonies population were manually classified into further populations: ‘three colonies’ and ‘more than three colonies’. Of note, the features weighting the most in our two machine learning classifiers were related to the area and ellipse-fitting parameters of the GFP signal displayed by the colonies.

It has been revealed that after collection of the epithelium using forceps, the remaining matrix and TRM cells were punched using a 3-mm puncher and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube containing warm RPMI supplemented with L-glutamine (1X), 5% FBS, HEPES (1X), DNAse I (40 U ml−1), collagenase D (2 mg ml−1) and trypsin inhibitor (1 mg ml−1). Samples were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min with mechanical dissociation via vigorous pipetting every 3 min. After incubation, the sample was centrifuged at 500g for 2 min at 4 °C and washed with 1 ml of HBSS (−Ca2+ or −Mg2+; 14175095, Gibco) + 1% BSA (130-091-376, Miltenyi Biotec). This step was repeated twice. Before final cell counting, the Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was used following the manufacturer’s instructions to remove apoptotic cells and then passed through a 40-µm Flowmi filter (BAH136800040, Millipore Sigma). Afterwards, the TRM cells were transferred to a 0.5-ml tube to facilitate visualization and accurate cell counting using the Countless 3 FL before loading into the Chromium X (10X Genomics).

Nuclei isolation was performed based on 10X Genomics demonstrated protocol CG000365 rev C. In brief, single cells were centrifuged for 4 min at 400g and 4 °C. The cell pellet was resuspended in cold lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1% BSA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Tween-20, 0.1% Nonidet P40 substitute, 0.01% digitonin and 1 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor). After 6 min on ice, cold wash buffer was added (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1% BSA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Tween-20 and 1 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor) and nuclei were spun for 5 min at 500g and 4 °C. The pellet was resuspended in cold wash buffer and nuclei were counted with propidium iodide (ViaStain AO/PI, CS2-0106-5ML, Nexcelom Bioscience) using the Countess 3 FL (AMQAF2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific). After spinning, nuclei were resuspended in diluted nuclei buffer (10X Genomics) at recommended concentrations for 10X Genomics scMultiome. The quality of isolated nuclei was evaluated by microscopy with DAPI and brightfield.

Single-cell RNA-seq libraries were generated using 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ (v3.1) reagents according to user manual CG000315 rev E. For multiplexed scRNA-seq, single-cell suspensions of nine biological samples were individually tagged with 10X Genomics 3′ CellPlex Set A reagents according to the demonstrated protocol CG000391 rev B protocol 1. Equal amounts of tagged cells were pooled together for each sample. Three lanes of Chromium Next GEM Chip G were loaded targeting 30,000 cells per lane. Cell encapsulation and library preparation were performed according to user guide Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits (v3.1) with Feature Barcode technology for cell multiplexing CG000388 rev C. Single-nucleus multiome was performed using 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression reagents and corresponding user guide CG000338 rev F. Two lanes were loaded per sample targeting 10,000 cells per lane. All single-cell libraries (scRNA, single-nucleus RNA, Multiplex and single-nucleus ATAC) were quantified with Qubit 1X dsDNA HS (Q33231, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA Kit (5067-4626, Agilent Technologies) and were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X Plus platforms.

It has been revealed that for total single-cell total RNA-seq (VASA-seq), libraries were generated by Single Cell Discoveries, with the inclusion of a depletion step targeting the S.Tm 5S, 16S and 23S rRNAs. Libraries were sequenced aiming for a target coverage of 300,000 raw reads per cell.

Recent findings suggest that we ran Cell Ranger (v8.0.0) multi-pipeline with 10X Genomics References 2024-A (hg38, GENCODE v44) as reference for read alignment, demultiplexing and gene quantification of multiplexed scRNA-seq data; Cell Ranger (v7.1.0) for scRNA-seq data of TRM cells; Cell Ranger (v9.0.1) for scRNA-seq data from FACS-sorted epithelium after infections with S.Tm WT and mutants (hereafter referred as ‘sorted infection dataset’); and Cell Ranger Arc (v2.0.1) with 10X Genomics References 2020-A (hg38, GENCODE v32) for scMultiome data. We then loaded the Cell Ranger and Cell Ranger Arc pipelines filtered count matrix to Seurat (v4.3.0.1)77 and Signac (v1.10.0)78 for further preprocessing.

In a recent development, for the multiplexed scRNA-seq data of engineered epithelium, cells with fewer than 500 or more than 6,000 genes expressed, or total unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts exceeding 30,000, or mitochondrial gene percentage above 25% were removed. For the TRM cell data, we only retained cells with more than 500 genes, UMI counts between 1,000 and e10 and mitochondrial percentage less than 15%. For the epithelial data with and without TRM cell co-culture, we only retained cells with more than 1,000 genes, UMI counts between 3,000 and 50,000 and mitochondrial percentage less than 25%. For the sorted infection dataset, we only retained cells with more than 1,000 genes, less than 30,000 UMI and mitochondrial percentage less than 50%.

Recent findings suggest that for all datasets, raw counts were normalized using the ‘NormalizeData’ function with a scale factor of 10,000. Three thousand highly variable genes (HVGs) were identified using the variance-stabilizing transformation (‘vst’) method. Data were scaled and principal component analysis was performed using these variable features. The first 20 principal components were used as input for ‘FindNeighbors’ and dimensional reduction with UMAP. The resulting graph was used for ‘FindClusters’ with the Louvain algorithm at resolution 1.0.

For the multiplexed data, after inspection of regional marker gene expression, we excluded the potential foregut sample (‘don55’) marked by SOX2 and a sample with mixed ileal and colonic identity (‘IF17ile’, FABP6+ and SATB2+). We then removed ribosomal genes, mitochondrial genes, genes located on sex chromosomes and genes without proper gene symbols to avoid influence of these confounding factors to the integration of this dataset derived from multiple donors and reran the pipelines from normalization to clustering.

Epithelial cell-type annotation was initialized on cluster level based on expression of canonical intestinal cell type and regional markers, including: stem cells (LGR5, OLFM4, SMOC2 and ASCL2), absorptive cells (APOA4, FABP6 and CEACAM7), goblet cells (MUC2 and FCGBP), enteroendocrine cells (CHGA), transit-amplifying cells (MKI67), BEST4+ cells (BEST4), epithelial regional identity markers (SATB2, GATA4, CDX2 and PDX1) and leukocytes (PTPRC). Clusters with similar expression patterns were merged and resulted in a coarse-grained annotation. Differential features between proximal, distal and colonic enterocytes and colonocytes were derived from the top 500 marker genes using the ‘wilcoxauc’ function of the ‘presto’ R package on normalized RNA expression values (Wilcoxon test, logFC > log(1.1), adjusted P < 0.05). Enrichment for ‘BP’ (biological process) and ‘MF’ (molecular function) Gene Ontology was performed with the function enrichGO from the clusterProfiler package. Detected genes were used as background and all terms in the org.Hs.eg.db database were used. The enrichment score for each term was calculated by subtracting the significant −log10-transformed hypergeometric test Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected P value of the region of interest and the average of those from the other two regions. Missing values or not undefined numeric results for one region were set to the minimum of the other two regions for visualization.

Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) subtype annotation was performed following subclustering. Subtype-specific signatures (‘EC’: TPH1; ‘MX’: GHRL and MLN; ‘K’: GIP; ‘L’: PYY and GCG; ‘D’: SST; ‘I’: CCK; and ‘Prog’: NEUROG3) were calculated using the AddModuleScore function in Seurat on normalized RNA expression values. Cells were assigned to the identity with the highest score, provided the score exceeded a minimum threshold (0.1). Cells that did not meet this criteria were categorized as ‘EEC unassigned’.

For the multiplexed data and the sorted infection dataset, which did not resolve a cluster representing distal small intestine stem cells, we extracted stem cells from the continuum to absorptive cells based on summarized expression levels of stem cell marker genes. For the multiplexed data, we selected the top ten genes with the highest correlation with summarized scaled expression of LGR5, SMOC2 and ASCL2 across stem cells and absorptive cells and calculated the stem cell score of each cell by summing the scaled expression of selected genes. We defined cells with stem cell scores higher than the 60th percentile of positive scores as stem cells and others as absorptive cells. To reduce the noise of classification solely based on scores of individual cells, we performed high-resolution clustering (resolution = 5), and defined cells belonging to the high-resolution clusters with more stem cells than absorptive cells were defined as stem cells, regardless of their individual scores. For the sorted infection dataset, we subsetted two initial clusters (resolution = 1 from the whole dataset) with LGR5+ cells. We selected the top five genes with the highest correlation with summarized scaled expression of LGR5 and SMOC2 across stem cells and colonocytes and calculated the stem cell score of each cell by summing the scaled expression of selected genes. We defined cells with stem cell scores higher than the 90th percentile of positive scores as stem cells and others as colonocytes. The distribution of the manually extracted stem cells fits the visual inspection on the LGR5 feature plot. For the colonocyte-subtype annotation in the sorted infection dataset, colonocyte clusters with more than 80% cells from the GFP+ samples were collectively defined as ‘enriched in GFP+’, the colonocyte cluster with less than 0.1% cells from the non-infected sample were defined as ‘depleted in non-infected’, and other colonocyte clusters were defined as ‘shared’.

To resolve the goblet cell heterogeneity in the multiplexed data, we subsetted goblet cells from the entire dataset based on their coarse-grained cell-type annotation. The subset was re-normalized, and variable features were recalculated and reclustered (resolution = 1). We excluded clusters with enriched expression of MKI67 to get non-proliferative goblet cells and performed subclustering. We identified cluster markers using the wilcoxauc function implemented by the presto package and defined significant cluster markers with Wilcoxon rank-sum test Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05, expressed cell percentage difference (pct_in) > 10%, expression logFC > 0.1.

In a recent development, TRM cell-type annotation was performed on the cluster level. We first annotated epithelial cells (EPCAM+), B cells (CD79B+) and proliferative CD4+ T cells (MKI67+), then annotated non-proliferative T cell subtypes based on mapping to a public adult human intestine tissue immune cell reference with two complementary approaches. We identified cell-type markers of the in vitro and tissue data separately using the wilcoxauc function with cut-off Wilcoxon rank-sum test Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05, expressed cell percentage difference > 10%, expression logFC > 0.1. We quantified the marker gene overlap significance between in vitro and tissue cell types using −log10-transformed Fisher’s two-sided exact test nominal P value. For each in vitro cell type, we got the top three tissue cell types with the strongest overlap, or the subset of top three if the significance difference between pairs of top three was larger than 10. In parallel, we calculated Spearman correlation between our in vitro and tissue cell types based on the markers defined in both systems. For each in vitro cell type, we got the top three tissue cell types showing the highest transcription program similarity, or the subset of top three if the significance difference between pairs of top three was larger than 0.1. We then annotated the in vitro T cells as the overlap of overlap-based and similarity-based matched tissue cell types. On the basis of further inspection of individual canonical marker gene expression, we manually renamed activated CD4 T, activated CD8 T and MAIT-like CD4 as CD4 TRM, CD8 TRM and CD4 TRMTH17, respectively.

To construct an adult human intestine tissue transcriptome reference, we collected the count matrix and cell-type annotation of epithelial cells from three public adult intestine multi-region scRNA-seq datasets79,80,81. All datasets were processed using Seurat (v4). After merging the datasets, we performed LogNormalize normalization with a scale factor of 10,000. We identified HVGs independently for each dataset using the vst method, selecting 3,000 HVGs per dataset. We then selected integration features across datasets using the SelectIntegrationFeatures function. We ran principal component analysis using the selected integration features and retrieved the top 50 principal components. We integrated the data with Cluster Similarity Spectrum (CSS)82 stratified by sample, and default setting for other parameters. We performed dimension reduction with UMAP, and Louvain clustering based on CSS embeddings using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions at a resolution of 1.0. We compared the data without batch effect correction, integration with Harmony or with CSS integration, and chose CSS-integrated results based on visual inspection of canonical cell-type marker gene expression.

To establish a consistent cell-type annotation scheme across datasets, we created a mapping between original annotations and standardized categories. We classified cells into major epithelial lineages: absorptive cells (enterocytes and colonocytes), goblet cells, BEST4+ cells, EECs, follicle-associated epithelium, stem cells, M cells, Paneth cells, secretory progenitors and tuft cells. We further refined these annotations by incorporating regional information. We defined the G2M-phased cells defined by the CellCycleScoring function in Seurat within the clusters with enriched expression of MKI67 as the transit-amplifying cells. Cell-type identities were validated using established marker genes. For rare cell populations (for example, Paneth cells and tuft cells), we calculated expression-based scores using canonical markers (DEFA5 and DEFA6 for Paneth cells; RGS13, AVIL and ALOX5 for tuft cells) and assigned cells based on these scores. To be more specific, we identified the top five positively correlated genes with summarized DEFA5 and DEFA6 scaled expression profiles across epithelium among the 3,000 HVGs as feature genes of Paneth cells. We summed up the scaled expression levels of the selected top five Paneth-associated genes for each cell as the Paneth cell feature score, and defined cells with scores exceeding 97.5th percentile of all positive scores as Paneth cells. We applied a similar procedure to identify tuft cells, with 10 tuft cell feature genes and using 95 percentile as the selection cut-off.

To establish a tissue reference for colonocyte subtype annotation in the Salmonella dataset, we subsetted to non-small intestine transit-amplifying cells, stem cells and colonocytes, integrated the data with CSS and performed subclustering based on the CSS embeddings at resolution = 0.4. We identified cluster markers using the wilcoxauc function in the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1. We selected the top 100 markers ranked by logFC from each cluster and unified them as features for comparison between in vitro and tissue colonic stem cells and colonocytes.

In a recent development, to further reconstruct the differentiation trajectory from stem cells to colonocytes in primary tissues (excluding transit-amplifying cells), we computed a diffusion map using the DiffusionMap function in the destiny package on the CSS space and we defined the rank of the first diffusion component (DC1) as the inferred differentiation pseudotime. We ordered the cells along the pseudotime, partitioned them into 25 bins and calculated the average gene expression of each bin. We calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients between the bin average expression levels and the bin order for each gene. The 50 genes with the strongest positive correlations were selected as pseudotime-positive correlating genes, which show higher expression levels in mature colonocytes, and the 50 genes with the strongest negative correlations as pseudotime-negative correlating genes, which show higher expression levels in stem cells and early colonocytes. We then applied these tissue-derived differentiation-related genes on the sorted infection dataset. We used the AddModuleScore function in Seurat based on normalized RNA expression values of the pseudotime positively and negatively correlating genes separately. A composite differentiation score of the cells in the chip was defined as the difference between the positive and negative module scores. We ordered the colonocytes according to the differentiation score from premature to mature, partitioned them into 25 bins and calculated the average gene expression of each bin. The obtained bin average gene expression profiles are defined as expression profiles along the reconstructed pre-mature-to-mature colonocyte differentiation trajectory.

To create a unified peak list across samples, we called open chromatin-accessible regions in each sample using MACS2 (v2.2.9.1) with the CallPeaks function and then quantified them with FeatureMatrix in Signac. We only kept regions located on standard chromosomes. We annotated peaks to most nearby genes using the annotatePeak function in ChIPseeker based on the Ensemble (v98) annotation. We only retained cells with ATAC UMI count between 200 and 50,000, RNA UMI count less than 20,000, RNA gene number between 500 and 5,000, mitochondrial percentage less than 50%, nucleosome signal (calculated by NucleosomeSignal) less than 1, transcription start site enrichment score (calculated by TSSEnrichment) less than 1 and hg38 genome blacklist ratio less than 0.5%. We ran the same pipeline of scRNA-seq data from read count normalization to dimension reduction and clustering as described in the previous section (‘Preprocessing and cell-type annotation of scRNA-seq data’). For the scATAC-seq data, we performed term frequency-inverse document frequency normalization on read counts using the RunTFIDF function. We defined the regions with over 1% detection rate as top features and RunSVD based on the top features. We projected cells into two-dimension UMAP embeddings and FindNeighbors based on top 2–50 latent semantic indexing.

Recent findings suggest that we performed major epithelial cell-type annotation on RNA cluster level based on canonical cell-type marker expression. We subsetted to colonic stem cell and colonocyte clusters, calculated the Spearman correlation coefficients between in vitro and tissue stem cell to colonocyte clusters using the in vitro-expressed colonic stem cell and colonocyte feature genes defined in the tissue reference. We performed hierarchical clustering on the in vitro clusters based on the similarity profiles and classified them into stem cells and four colonocyte subtypes indicating differential maturity accordingly. Colonocyte clusters with mostly exclusive presence in the Salmonella-infected sample were defined as infection-specific colonocyte clusters. We transferred RNA-level cell-type annotations to ATAC data, and merged subtypes that could not be clearly resolved by ATAC data as annotations on the ATAC level.

Industry observers note that we performed differential analysis for co-clustered S.Tm infection and control cells in each cluster of stem cells, colonocytes and goblet cells, which have sufficient cell numbers for robust estimation. For infection-specific clusters, which have less than 20 control cells in the clusters, we first identified matched control sample cells for each infected sample cell using get.knnx of the FNN package with k = 1 in the top 20 principal component space. We identified DEGs between matched control and infected cells using the wilcoxauc function by the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1. We applied the same procedure to identify DEGs in the epithelium induced by TRM cell co-culture except that we did not need to use the k-nearest neighbour search approach to get matched control cells as there was no condition-specific cluster.

It has been revealed that to identify DARs between Salmonella-infected and control conditions, we implemented a statistical framework based on linear regression modelling of binarized chromatin accessibility data, with sequencing depth (UMI counts) as covariate. Specifically, for each open chromatin region i, we fitted:.

Null model: glm(e ~ UMIcounts, family = binomial).

Full model: glm(e ~ UMIcounts + condition, family = binomial).

Industry observers note that where e represents the binarized accessibility state vector for region i across all cells. We applied a Chi-squared test comparing the two models using ANOVA. Regions were considered differentially accessible if they had Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 and indicated at least a 0.5% difference in the proportion of cells with the region accessible between Salmonella-infected and control conditions.

Industry observers note that we reconstructed the gene regulatory networks from the scMultiome data along the stem-cell-to-coloncyte trajectory and each of the stem cell, colonocyte and goblet cell types shared by both control and infection conditions using Pando83 separately. We used the infection-induced DEGs and 5,000 HVGs of each data as input HVGs for Pando. We constrained our candidate regulatory regions to be either conserved in mammals (defined in phastConsElements20Mammals.UCSC.hg38 provided by Pando) or overlapped with ENCODE regions (defined in SCREEN.ccRE.UCSC.hg38 provided by Pando), and showing significantly correlated profiles with HVGs as output by LinkPeaks in Signac at the default distance threshold of 500 kb. We ran find_motifs and used the Pando-provided transcription factor-binding site (TFBS) motif database compiled from JASPAR and CIS-BP as reference for Pando to identify TFBS in candidate regulatory regions. We ran the infer_grn function with a Gaussian generalized linear model (model = ‘glm’) to infer regulatory coefficients from log-normalized transcript counts and binarized peak counts summarized to SLM algorithm-defined ATAC clusters (resolution = 10). We identified transcription factor–target gene modules using the find_modules function with default settings. We combined the modules from different datasets as inferred transcription factor–target pairs.

For visualization, we selected the condition-dependent DEGs with the top 500 absolute value of expression log-transformed fold change between conditions and the union set of the top three-correlated Pando-predicted transcription factors of each selected DEGs. We calculated pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients of expression profiles across cell types and conditions between selected genes, reduced the dimension of obtained correlation matrix to 20 principal components using prcomp_irlba in the irlba package and further projected genes to two-dimension embeddings using umap in the uwot package with the obtained principal components as input.

We ran the AddMotifs function in Signac to add the TFBS motifs information on our detected open chromatin regions and obtained a motif occurrence matrix. To identify TFBS motifs over-represented in open chromatin regions with increased accessibility upon infection in each cell type, we ran FindMotifs in Signac on the top 200 upregulated accessible regions, with 30,000 open chromatin regions with matched overall GC content retrieved by the MatchRegionStats function as background.

We defined three comparisons to characterize the luminal effects: (1) ΔSPI-1/2 non-invaded (ΔSPI-1/2Out, GFP−) versus non-infected, (2) WT non-invaded (WTOut, GFP−) versus non-infected, and (3) WTOut versus ΔSPI-1/2Out; and three for intracellular effects: (1) WT invaded (WTIn, GFP+) versus WTOut, (2) ΔsteE invaded (ΔsteEIn, GFP+) versus WTIn, and (3) ΔSPI-2In versus WTIn. We subsetted to colonocytes. Genes detected in at least 50 colonocytes were retained, excluding features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ‘ENSG’. Pairwise comparisons were conducted between predefined experimental conditions within each colonocyte cluster. Comparisons were performed only when at least 20 cells were available in at least one condition. When one of the conditions contained fewer than 20 cells, we supplemented with cells from other clusters of the same condition that were defined as nearest neighbours of the other condition, using get.knnx of the FNN package with k = 1 based on Euclidean distance in the top 20 principal component space. Differential expression testing was performed using the wilcoxauc function of the presto R package on normalized RNA expression values. We identified DEGs between conditions per cluster using the wilcoxauc function by the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1.

According to recent reports, we then pooled genes defined as significant DEGs in at least one comparison in at least one cluster as the union set of condition DEGs. We then calculated the colonocyte average expression levels of each condition. We calculated the expression difference between WTOut and non-infected—namely, diff_WT_vs_NI, where positive values indicate upregulation in WTOut versus non-infected—and between WTIn and WTOut—namely, diff_WT_GFP_vs_WT, where positive values indicate upregulation in WTIn versus WTOut. We ranked the gene according to diff_WT_vs_NI, took the top 50 genes as feature genes and used the AddModuleScore function to calculate the luminal effect gene module score, and applied the same procedure for diff_WT_GFP_vs_WT values for intracellular effect gene module score.

We used CellChat (v2)84 to infer intracellular communications between co-cultured intestinal epithelial cells and TRM cells. Normalized expression data were extracted from the epithelium and TRM cell combined Seurat RNA assay, and cell-type labels were used to group cells for interaction analysis. We used the built-in human CellChatDB database as reference for ligand–receptor interactions. To reduce computational cost, we subsetted the expression data to include only signalling genes present in the database. Overexpressed genes and interactions were identified using the identifyOverExpressedGenes and identifyOverExpressedInteractions functions. Communication probabilities were computed using the computeCommunProb function with type = truncatedMean and trim = 0.05. We subsetted to interactions between proximal small intestinal enterocytes and immune cell types, excluding proliferating CD4+ T cells for visualization.

Recent findings suggest that read alignment, gene expression quantification and cell filtering of the VASA-seq data were performed by Single Cell Discoveries. In brief, raw sequencing data were processed using Cutadapt (v4.9) to remove adapter sequences and homopolymers, followed by Ribodetector (v0.3.1) to filter out ribosomal reads. Processed reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STARsolo (v2.7.11b), with the parameter–soloFeatures set to GeneFull_Ex50pAS. The human reference genome used was GRCh38, ENSEMBL release 103. The S.Tm reference genome was downloaded from EnsemblBacteria Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium str. 14028S str. LT2 14028S (GCA_000022165) release 62. The resulting single-cell-level gene count matrices were used as inputs for downstream analysis in R.

In a recent development, to improve the gene annotation for the S.Tm genome, we performed sequence alignment for the genes in the S.Tm strain 14028S annotation against the S.Tm strain 14028 annotation (GCF_028596185.1_ASM2859618v1). Out of the 1,542 genes with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 242 were mapped to annotated genes with common names in the S.Tm 14028 annotation by blastn85,86 with more than 90% of sequence similarity.

Industry observers note that cells without GFP signal, UMI count of less than 3,500 or External RNA Controls Consortium (ERCC) counts of less than 450 were excluded. Raw counts were normalized using the NormalizeData function in Seurat with a scale factor of 10,000.

According to FACS index sorting values, cells with GFP < 500 were defined as GFP−, 500 or more and less than 2,000 as GFPlo, 2,000 or more and 10,000 or less as GFPint, and more than 10,000 as GFPhi. For human genes, only genes detected in at least 10% of cells in at least one GFP signal group were included in the differentially expressed test. For each retained gene, expression was modelled using two nested linear models. The reduced model included log-transformed total UMI counts per cell and the percentage of mitochondrial reads as technical covariates, whereas the full model additionally included the GFP signal group as a factor. The contribution of the GFP signal group was assessed by ANOVA comparing the full and reduced models. Genes with Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. To assign directionality, we calculated the difference in average expression between the GFPhi and GFPlo groups and assigned the directionality accordingly.

In a recent development, for S.Tm, we applied the same differentially expressed test strategy, but only included GFP+ cells for comparison. Given the sparsity of the bacteria transcripts, we reduced the detection rate cut-off to 1%. After further excluding ERCC transcripts and features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 3,137 genes were left as input for the differentially expressed test. We used nominal P < 0.05 as the cut-off to get marginally significant bacterial DEG.

The raw flow cytometry data files used to generate the immune UMAP have been deposited in the Zenodo repository87 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21786694). Source data underlying all graphical representations used in the figures are provided as Supplementary Information. Public adult intestine multi-region scRNA-seq datasets were retrieved from an interactive website of the Space-Time Gut Cell Atlas (https://www.gutcellatlas.org/)79, ArrayExpress (E-MTAB-10187)81 and Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE185224)80.

Recent findings suggest that R.L.-S., M.F.H., Q.Y., M.N., N.G. and J.G.C. conceived the study. R.L.-S., M.F.H., Q.Y., N.G. and J.G.C. wrote the manuscript. M.N. designed and fabricated the fluidic device and crypt stamps, with support from J.A. and S.M. M.P.L. contributed to the development of the fluidic device holding the tissues. M.N. and R.L.-S. generated the artwork design. M.F.H. and R.L.-S. designed and performed most of the experiments in the article. R.L.-S., M.F.H., M.N., N.A. and J.B. optimized the epithelium growth conditions. M.F.H. isolated the organoid lines and TRM cells from primary tissue. R.L.-S., M.F.H., M.A.-B., L.G.-T. and S.S. performed scRNA-seq, scMultiome and VASA-seq experiments. M.A.-B. and L.G.-T. generated the sequencing libraries. Q.Y. performed the computational analysis of scRNA-seq and scMultiome data, with support and data interpretation from R.L.-S., S.S. and M.F.H. M.F.H., R.L.-S. and J.A. co-developed the histomold. I.C. and S.T. performed the FFPE processing, sectioning, H&E and AlcianBlue–PAS stainings, with support from M.F.H. M.F.H. performed the immunohistochemistry and mIF stainings, imaging and analysis with support from R.L.-S. and M.N. M.F.H., R.L.-S., M.N. and L.K. performed whole-mount stainings and imaging. M.F.H., K.K. and S.K. performed the flow cytometry experiments and analysis of immune cells. R.L.-S., D.C. and I.C.-A. performed the flow cytometry and image stream experiments and analysis of epithelial cells. L.K., A.M.F. and M.F.H. performed the cytokine measurements. N.A., S.R.V., Y.B. and J.B. generated the organoid reporter lines. J.F., A.A. and C.S. performed and processed the proteomic measurements. Live imaging was performed by M.F.H., R.L.-S. and M.N., and analysed by M.B. M.H. and D.B. generated and provided the S.Tm strains. T.R. and F.G. supported with data interpretation. All authors read and approved the manuscript.

a-c) Representative mIF cross-section of engineered duodenal, ileal and colonic epithelia in direct comparison to the donor-matched primary tissue (ileum not matched), highlighting the stem-niche specific SOX9+ (cyan) and transit-amplifying Ki67+ cells (pink), matching abundance of MUC2+ goblet cells (green) and high expression of the region-enriched absorptive lineage marker (orange) in the E-Cadherin+ epithelium (grey). The duodenal epithelium was marked by strong expression APOA4+ enterocytes, matching the parental tissue. Expression of distal FABP6+ enterocytes in the top-layer of the engineered epithelium matched ileal tissue. The colonic epithelium exhibited CA1+ colonocytes at comparable levels to the organ of origin, e = 4. Scale bars: 50 µm.

GdS: Cisse becomes a pillar as Amorim as experiments with four-man attack

  • Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alphadjo Cisse has definitely been the breakout player of the season so far and Ruben Amorim has no intention of dialling down his presence in attack.

Recent findings suggest that milan had a very clear blueprint when they headed into the current season: Goncalo Ramos would be the main man in attack. Instead, however, it’s the underdog Cisse who has been running the show, while the Portuguese striker has been at the bottom in terms of output.

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In a recent development, as highlighted by Gazzetta dello Sport this morning (see image below), that’s why there cannot be – and likely won’t be – a Milan without Cisse in attack. Ruben Amorim now wants to build the attack around him, as opposed to introducing him every now and then.

In a recent development, the most recent clash, the 2-1 win against Genoa, was a good example of this. Amorim went for a bold formation with Cisse, Ramos, Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira, Luka Modric and Adrien Rabiot together. A team with a lot of quality and an attacking-minded style.

According to recent reports, it was a shape that reminded us of 2009-10, when Milan were guided by another foreign coach: Leonardo. He chose a very attacking-minded side with four attackers and two midfielders, which is something that Amorim almost replicated.

Modric and Rabiot in front of the defence (Pirlo and Ambrosini then) and the fantasy project with Pulisic, Moreira, Cisse, and Ramos, comparable to the Ronaldinho, Pato, Seedorf, and Borriello of the old days.

Despite this, the goals were scored after two mistakes by Genoa (even if Milan’s pressing helped), so the goal is to repeat the experiment against Frosinone and to increase its effectiveness, the experiment should be repeated tomorrow.

Recent findings suggest that in that sense, Cisse will be notable as he’s the top scorer: three goals in Europa League and five in Serie A. He has scored with both feet and his head, demonstrating a combination of talent and an eye for goal: characteristics that are very important for a team like Milan.

Recent findings suggest that the average also speaks for itself: eight goals spread across 658 minutes means he scores a goal every 82 minutes. Best of all, his versatility means that he can play as an attacking midfielder, a left-winger, and even as a centre-forward.

At just 20 years and 17 days old, thanks to the fifth goal in his ninth Serie A appearance, Cisse became the second-youngest player to reach the milestone in the first ten games with Milan, at least since 1994-95. Only Pato did it younger, at 18 years and 181 days.

Furthermore, he’s one of only three players born after 2006 (top five leagues) to have scored eight or more goals in all competitions, along with Lamine Yamal (13) and Paris Brunner, who also scored eight.

As the pink newspaper concludes, Ramos has also produced eye-catching numbers, but in this case in a negative sense: 1,191 minutes on the pitch, three goals scored, meaning one goal scored every 398 minutes.

By Seye Omidiora | 21 Nov 2026 14:00.

Second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion travel to face newly promoted Hull City on Sunday in the first-ever Premier League meeting between the sides, with Fabian Hurzeler's men bidding for a third consecutive top-flight victory.

Meanwhile, Sergej Jakirovic's Tigers sit 13th and three points clear of the relegation zone, aiming to preserve their unbeaten home record while ending an eight-match winless run in the league.

Here, Sports Mole rounds up all of the latest team news for both clubs.

Out: Matt Targett (ankle), Hidemasa Morita (muscle), Eliot Matazo (knee), Ilyas Ansah (back).

Doubtful: Mohamed Belloumi (thigh), Nobel Mendy (knee), Charlie Hughes (groin).

Sports Mole's predicted XI: Tzolakis; Coyle, Ajayi, Egan, Mendy, Stroud; Belloumi, Gourna-Douath, Iroegbunam, Slater; McBurnie.

Out: Kaoru Mitoma (hamstring), Evan Ferguson (ankle), Stefanos Tzimas (knee), Zadok Yohanna (thigh).

Doubtful: Yankuba Minteh (thigh) and Femi Azeez (thigh).

Sports Mole's predicted XI: Verbruggen; Costinha, Vuskovic, Dunk, Boscagli; Chema, Gross; Gomez, Ayari, De Cuyper; Kostoulas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 18:36 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:37 EST, 16 November 2026.

Max Dowman broke another record as the 16-year-old became the youngest-ever goalscorer for England's Under-21 side on Monday night.

The Arsenal teenager has already broken a plethora of records at club level, and is now taking that to the international stage too, breaking a record set by senior team star Jude Bellingham, who scored aged 17 years and 67 days in 2020.

Dowman was called into the U21 squad for the first time this international break, and made his debut off the bench in the 1-0 defeat by Portugal on Friday.

On Monday, meanwhile, he was given a start by manager Lee Carsley, and rewarded his manager's faith with an 89th-minute winner to break the record and earn his side a 3-2 win.

It's a record he can add to his already-extensive collection, which includes being the youngest Champions League player, the youngest Premier League goalscorer, and the youngest Premier League winner.

Industry observers note that manager Lee Carsley said after the game: 'He played really well - he was one of four or five outstanding performances. Mikey Moore, Max, Ethan (Nwaneri), they were very good.

Max Dowman became England Under-21s' youngest-ever goal scorer when he scored against France on Monday.

'We see how good on the ball he is but he was outstanding off the ball. You have to keep reminding yourself about his age. There's a lot of expectation around him and he seems to handle that so well.

Recent findings suggest that 'It's vital we keep supporting him and he develops at his own pace. It's so important he enjoys his football.

'Obviously all the players in the squad are under pressure from their clubs and the expectation that surrounds them, so as much as we can we have to make that as easy as we can.'.

Despite bursting onto the scene last season, Dowman has just 19 minutes to his name in the top flight this campaign as Arsenal look to defend their title.

He has played a number of games for the Gunners' U21 side, while he was sent off against League Two side Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup.

It has been revealed that arteta scolded his player at the time, but mentioned: 'I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction. Whether that's positive or negative. You need to understand the context, the relationship I have with him and what we discussed before we went out.

'If you see the reaction from my mother and father with me sometimes, you'd say "you don't like that reaction", but for me it was the best reaction ever as it enabled me to be who I am.

The Arsenal teenager, 16, broke the record held by Jude Bellingham with his late winner.

Recent findings suggest that 'But you want to see the best and most beautiful reaction. You want to see the reaction of his team-mates when they have to play with 10 men.

It has been revealed that 'What do you expect? That's the level and that's the reaction. Whether it's right or wrong, that's the reaction. And the reaction when I don't win, I'm f****d off, substantial time.

'This is the environment and the reality. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League. We look after him so much but we are also demanding as he needs to earn the right to play otherwise what are the rest of the boys going to tell me?'.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 14:12, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:12.
  • Manchester United goalkeeper Altay Bayinidir is reportedly at risk of having his Celta Vigo loan stay terminated in the upcoming year.
  • Bayinidir was allowed to leave in the summer after Man United recruited Karl Darlow to be Senne Lammens' deputy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 14:12, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:12.

Manchester United goalkeeper Altay Bayinidir is reportedly at risk of having his Celta Vigo loan stay terminated in the upcoming year.

Bayinidir was allowed to leave in the summer after Man United recruited Karl Darlow to be Senne Lammens' deputy.

The Turkey international joined Celta on a season-long loan move with the objective of enjoying regular game time.

However, Bayindir has experienced a similar situation to the one he had at Man United, having been forced to play a backup role to Ionut Radu.

Having been overlooked in La Liga and the Europa League, Bayindir's only appearance for Celta came in the recent 5-0 victory over Salamanca in the Copa del Rey.

With Bayindir's playing situation unlikely to change, Faro de Vigo via Sports Witness are reporting that Celta have a significant decision to make over the goalkeeper's loan spell.

The Galician club are assessing the situations of their loan players who lack prominence and are not ruling out the prospect of cutting Bayindir's loan short.

From Man United's perspective, there is no indication they will look to terminate the goalkeeper's loan stint, but it could still end prematurely if Celta or the player express frustration with how the move is panning out.

Bayindir headed out to Galicia after being deemed surplus to requirements under former Man United head coach Michael Carrick.

While Mauricio Pochettino has since replaced Carrick in the Old Trafford dugout, the managerial change is unlikely to affect Bayindir's status at the club.

Even if his current loan switch is cut short, the 28-year-old will likely leave in January in another temporary deal or a permanent transfer.

In truth, it is only a matter of time until Bayindir leaves Old Trafford on a permanent basis, with his contract set to expire in the summer of 2028.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bruno Fernandes has ended up on AC Milan’s radar ahead of the summer, according to reports, with a free transfer potentially on the cards.

In a recent development, ever since the summer, when the BBC were the first to report on Milan’s interest, Fernandes has been brought up by various outlets as an option for the Rossoneri. Just a few days ago, Fabrizio Romano mentioned he is ‘more than a dream’ for them and that Ruben Amorim could be key.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Having just turned 32, Fernandes is still at a good age and he’s showing that with Manchester United so far this season. In 14 appearances, he has bagged six goals and three assists, so it’s no surprise that many clubs are monitoring his situation given the expiring contract.

Industry observers note that as reported by both Corriere dello Sport (via MilanNews) and Tuttosport (via MilanNews) this morning, Milan are seriously evaluating the idea of signing him. It’s still too early to talk about negotiations, but he’s definitely on their radar and will likely remain there.

Of course, if he does end up leaving on a free transfer, there will be no shortage of suitors so Milan would likely have to table a hefty contract offer. The club owner, Gerry Cardinale, seems more willing to do that now, though, than he did just a year ago.

It has been revealed that one potential problem is that Manchester United have confirmed that they are discussing a renewal with the player. The CEO Omar Berrada showered the Portuguese star with praise, as cited by Fabrizio Romano, so it seems a stay in Manchester cannot be ruled out either.

Man City 1-1 Fulham: Highlights, man of the match, stats as Anderson, Muniz score in stalemate
