💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Oliver Thomas | 21 Nov 2026 14:35, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 18:39.
  • Manchester City’s winless run in the Premier League has been extended to four games after they were held to a frustrating 1-1 draw by Fulham at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday afternoon.
  • Enzo Maresca’s “main target” was to secure all three points against the Cottagers following a dismal run of three consecutive losses to Aston Villa, Brighton, and Nottingham Forest prior to the international break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 21 Nov 2026 14:35, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 18:39.

Manchester City’s winless run in the Premier League has been extended to four games after they were held to a frustrating 1-1 draw by Fulham at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday afternoon.

Enzo Maresca’s “main target” was to secure all three points against the Cottagers following a dismal run of three consecutive losses to Aston Villa, Brighton, and Nottingham Forest prior to the international break.

However, the Citizens fell behind inside the opening 16 minutes when Fulham striker Rodrigo Muniz – starting his first PL game of the season at the expense of Gonzalo Garcia – curled a sweet strike into the top corner following a sweeping counter-attack.

Erling Haaland thought he had equaliser less than 10 minutes later, but he was controversially deemed to have fouled goalkeeper Bernd Leno before prodding the ball over the line.

Elliot Anderson did restore parity for the hosts, though, with a superbly-struck volley just before the hour mark, but in a second half that saw both teams create decent openings, the visitors admirably held on to claim a share of the spoils, ending an English record 20-game losing streak against the Sky Blues.

The draw represents Man City’s first in the top flight this season and leaves them sitting third in the Premier League table, five points behind leaders Arsenal – who face Newcastle United later tonight – and just behind second-placed Brighton on goal difference, with the Seagulls to take on Hull City on Sunday.

As for Fulham, a third successive draw has seen them extend their unbeaten run in the division to five matches, with Alvaro Arbeloa’s men sitting 14th in the top-flight standings and three points above the relegation zone.

Oliver Thomas live from the Etihad Stadium.

After winning his first seven Premier League games in charge of Man City, a feat no other manager has ever achieved in the division, Enzo Maresca has since seen his team stumble and hand Arsenal a significant title boost even before entering the month of December.

One of the biggest concerns for Maresca is how frail his defence has looked for the majority of this season, with 18 goals conceded across their last nine matches in all competitions, while City have failed to keep a single clean sheet in each of their last seven matches at the Etihad.

Maresca has acknowledged that finding the right balance is key for his new-look Citizens side and it’s ‘normal’ for teams in transition to have moments of struggle, but concerns over his defence, team structure and the performances of individuals are growing heading into a hectic fixture period.

Regardless of the outcome regarding their well-documented guilty verdict appeal, Man City would face an uphill battle to stay in the Premier League title race if they lose at Arsenal next weekend, with a fourth league defeat in five games leaving them trailing the Gunners by a daunting margin before the festive schedule even begins.

As for Fulham, Arbeloa has now steadied the ship following a challenging start to life in Premier League management, with nine of their 11 points accumulated across the last five gameweeks.

The Cottagers are by no means out of trouble just yet, but this positive run of form, extended by a hard-earned point at Man City, has given the club’s supporters genuine hope that a protracted relegation battle can be avoided.

Why Sandro Tonali is out for Tottenham against Ipswich as Roberto De Zerbi offers explanation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 14:40, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:53.
  • Tottenham Hotspur manager Roberto De Zerbi has confirmed that Sandro Tonali is missing from Saturday's Premier League clash with Ipswich Town due to illness.
  • The Italy international was a surprise absentee from the Lilywhites' squad against the Tractor Boys, as Conor Gallagher was instead given the nod in central midfield with Mateus Fernandes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 14:40, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 14:53.

Tottenham Hotspur manager Roberto De Zerbi has confirmed that Sandro Tonali is missing from Saturday's Premier League clash with Ipswich Town due to illness.

The Italy international was a surprise absentee from the Lilywhites' squad against the Tractor Boys, as Conor Gallagher was instead given the nod in central midfield with Mateus Fernandes.

Tonali was not name-checked in De Zerbi's pre-game press conference, and the expectation was that the former Newcastle United man would make his 11th Premier League start of the season.

However, Tonali's perfect starting streak in the top-flight campaign is now over, and De Zerbi explained the midfielder's absence when speaking to reporters ahead of kickoff.

"(The reasons for the changes are) a combination of physical condition (and defeat to Leeds). Many players, they came back (from international duty) not in the right condition. (Sandro) Tonali was sick for a couple of days. Rodrigo Bentancur arrived yesterday, just yesterday working with us," De Zerbi stated.

Recent findings suggest that "I am lucky because I have a great squad. Many players. All players are very close in level so now we start a very tough period of three games in a row. We are ready.".

De Zerbi made a total of six changes to his starting lineup from the XI that began the 1-0 loss to Ipswich Town before the international break, including a landmark start in attack for Luca Williams-Barnett.

The 18-year-old makes his full Premier League debut at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as part of a much-changed attack, which also sees Dominic Solanke and James Maddison replace Omar Marmoush and Archie Gray.

Further back, Destiny Udogie and Marcos Senesi have displaced Andy Robertson and Micky van de Ven, who are on the bench alongside Marmoush, Gray and the returning Savio and Lucas Bergvall.

Tonali has played over 500 more Premier League minutes than Gallagher so far this season, but the England international nevertheless leads his Italian colleague in several per 90 metrics.

As per the comparison chart, Gallagher ranks higher in terms of duels won, tackles and interceptions per 90, as well as winning more free kicks and committing more fouls.

The former Chelsea man also attempts more shots per game and boasts a higher ratio of shots on target, but Tonali triumphs in terms of successful passes, big chances created and dribble success rate.

However, with a fully-fit Maddison back in the starting lineup, Spurs should have little in the way of creativity concerns as De Zerbi's men bid to return to winning ways on home territory.

Florian Wirtz scores twice (including a stunner) as Germany thump Netherlands 5-0 in UEFA Nations League... as Liverpool misfit receives a hug from Jurgen Klopp after impressing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:56 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 19:19 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz scored a stunning brace for Germany as Jurgen Klopp's side thumped the Netherlands in the Nations League.
  • The 23-year-old has had a tough time of it at Anfield since his £116million move to the club last summer, but has never really struggled on the international stage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 17:56 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 19:19 EST, 16 November 2026.

Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz scored a stunning brace for Germany as Jurgen Klopp's side thumped the Netherlands in the Nations League.

The 23-year-old has had a tough time of it at Anfield since his £116million move to the club last summer, but has never really struggled on the international stage.

And he continued that trend on Monday evening with two goals for his side to help them top their Nations League group.

His first was the pick of the bunch. Wirtz moved along the forward line as a Dutch side without Virgil van Dijk struggled to contain him. He picked up the ball around 25 yards out, cut inside onto his weaker left foot, and curled a pearling effort into the far corner off the post.

That goal, which came on the hour mark, put his side 2-0 up after Freiburg's Derry Scherhant had scored the opener, and Wirtz wasn't done there.

Centre back Nico Schlotterbeck made it 3-0 before the Liverpool man picked up his second of the night after drifting into the penalty box unmarked and finishing high after good work from Brajan Gruda.

Cette version de Wirtz avec le maillot de la Mannschaft c’est celle qu’on aimerait voir chaque semaine en PL. Quel missile pour faire le break ! Meilleur buteur allemand sur cette édition de l’UNL. 🇩🇪🔥 pic.twitter.com/m0DqaOungS.

Florian Wirtz scored a brace for Germany as they thumped the Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League action.

Liverpool midfielder Wirtz received a big hug from a smiling Jurgen Klopp at full time.

Gruda himself, who is on loan at RB Leipzig from Brighton, wrapped up the five-star win on a night that arguably saw Klopp announce himself as Germany boss.

After full-time, the ex-Liverpool manager gave Wirtz a huge hug as the duo beamed with big smiles on their faces.

While it was a night to remember for Germany, a Netherlands team that included the likes of Micky van de Ven, Jurrien Timber and Wirtz's Liverpool team-mate Cody Gakpo were left exasperated.

Van Dijk had pulled out of the squad with a knock after playing with a knock in recent weeks.

His side will still, though, compete in the Nations League quarter-finals after finishing second in the group, finishing ahead of Greece on goal difference.

As for Wirtz, he will hope his performance will help continue what has been an uphill climb so far this season.

He also found the net for Germany in their first match of the international break – a 3-1 win over Serbia – and picked up a goal and assist in Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace before the international break.

In total, he has two goals and five assists in 15 games for Liverpool this season – though the Reds will hope those numbers increase as the season goes on.

His second goal came as he drifted into the penalty area and finished high into the net.

Last month, meanwhile, Reds manager Andoni Iraola insisted he has full faith in his midfielder.

'I think he has had a little bit of everything this season,' he noted. 'He has had good games, probably the other day was not his best game, especially offensively. We trust Florian.

Sources indicate that 'Florian is a very good player. He was coming from good performances in the international break, I think. I think it is a matter of everyone to find his moment.'.

Klopp hailed him 'exceptional', meanwhile, during the last international break.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, chelsea cruised to victory over Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Saturday. Goals from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to their second win on their Far East tour.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Moises Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

The west London side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

MOISÉS CAICEDO THAT IS INCREDIBLE 🤯 pic.twitter.com/C6CEcUG1sE.

Chelsea had further chances to extend their lead in a dominant second-half performance but were unable to add to their three goals.

Chelsea conclude their tour of the Far East with a game against Johor Darul Ta’zim on Sunday in Malaysia before returning home.

Their final pre-season game will be against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge before beginning their Premier League campaign at Fulham.

AC Milan take on Amorim’s former club Manchester United next Saturday before they kick off their Serie A campaign at Torino on August 23.

Chelsea managed to lure Austin MacPhee to take care of their set-pieces and today Chelsea scored two goals from corners. Here is a snippet of Mike McGrath’s piece on MacPhee’s arrival at Chelsea:.

According to recent reports, he is among the new breed of coaches who are rock stars in their own right, taking centre-stage since rules were changed so that only one person is allowed in the technical area at a time. For MacPhee to get closer to the players for a set-piece, it will mean Xabi Alonso taking a step back onto the bench.

It has been an incredible rise for MacPhee, 46, who was working on Michael O’Neill’s staff with Northern Ireland 10 years ago this summer, helping them reach the knockout stages of the European Championship.

Chelsea take on Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia tomorrow before returning to the UK. Their final pre-season game will be against Real Sociedad before taking on Fulham on the opening weekend of the new season.

AC Milan will play Manchester United next weekend and then kick off their Serie A campaign against Torino.

Possession: Chelsea 50%-50% AC MilanShots: 18-5Shots on target: 8-0Corners: 7-2.

The final whistle is blown in Jakarta and Chelsea have cruised to a 3-0 win over AC Milan. Goals from Caicedo and a double from Pedro either side of half-time have led Xabi Alonso’s side to the victory. They have one more game out in the Far East before returning home to the UK.

What a performance! 👏 pic.twitter.com/GcUZXwXbRj.

Ramos is picked out after making a run into the Chelsea box and is denied by Sanchez. However, the offside flag has gone up anyway against Ramos. AC Milan have barely threatened the Chelsea goal in this second half.

A late change for Chelsea as Sarr replaces Fofana.

There will be five added minutes.

Sources indicate that chelsea are seeking their fourth goal as Quenda strikes a shot powerfully from just outside the box but it goes narrowly wide. Xabi Alonso’s side have dominated this second half.

Estevao has the chance to score moments after coming on after good work from the Brazilian down Chelsea’s right but is denied by a good save from Torriani.

Chelsea make a triple changes as Estevao, Mudryk and Watson come on. Mudryk made his return after his doping ban against Juventus during the week.

In a recent development, chelsea hit the frame of the goal once more. Jackson gets the better of Vladimirov down Chelsea’s left and moves into the AC Milan penalty area. Jackson opens up his body as if he is going to curl his shot into the far corner but instead shoots towards the near corner, with his effort coming off the post.

Ricci goes for an audacious strike with the outside of his right foot from outside the box but his effort misses the target.

Palmer was deep in conversation with his boss Alonso during that water break.

Chelsea made a substitution during that break as Anselmino comes on for Hato. Thus far, Chelsea have made three changes in this game and Alonso did confirm before the game that some players should be able to go the full 90 this far into pre-season.

Sources indicate that the trophies won by Franco Baresi, who has died at the age of 66, are their own monument to the AC Milan and Italy defender’s greatness. Six times a Serie A champion, five as captain, three European Cup-winning campaigns, 10 other winners’ medals and the distinction of being a member of Italy squads that finished in first, second and third places at World Cup tournaments demonstrate that his career, in a significantly more meritocratic era, stand alongside the giants even if the bias towards attacking virtuosos denied him the Ballon d’Or his talent deserved.

According to recent reports, yet they do not tell us why the grief, so tangible in Milan and beyond today, transcends tribal rivalry. It would be unfair to say that he transformed the art of Italian defending. Gaetano Scirea, the elegant Juventus sweeper who kept the 21-year-old Baresi confined to the bench when Italy won their third World Cup in 1982, had a surplus of natural ability, composure and intelligence. He did not need the raw-elbowed brutality of Claudio Gentile, heir to generations of Italian defenders influenced by the post-war influx of players brought up in the traditions of Argentina and Uruguay.

Chelsea’s pre-season continues out in the Far East as they take on AC Milan in the Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta, Indonesia. Both clubs now have upcoming managers, with Xabi Alonso taking over at Chelsea and former Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim now at the helm at AC Milan. These sides met in pre-season last year, with Chelsea winning 4-1 at Stamford Bridge. At that time, now-Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca was in charge whilst Max Allegri, who is now at Napoli, was leading AC Milan. The last time they met competitively was during the 2022/23 Champions League season, with Chelsea winning both games.

Chelsea lost 1-0 to AC Milan’s Serie A rivals Juventus on Wednesday in Hong Kong, in which Danny Welbeck made his first Chelsea appearance after joining from Brighton in the last week.

“We want to have a great team spirit and that is built on a daily basis with a great culture in the building,” Alonso said in his pre-match press conference. “That helps in the moment you have to compete. You feel better having that togetherness, trust, and the bonds between the players are so important to ultimately building a winning mentality, and a team that can compete anywhere. So the football side is so important, but the mental side is as important. And the strength of the team is the most important. We have been able to train and prepare [during pre-season] and I am very happy with the attitude and personality, we know that it is a very important part of this tour.”.

It has been another busy week on the transfer front for Chelsea; not only has Welbeck arrived over the last week but so too have Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco. Alonso’s men have two more games after this against Johor Darul Ta’zim and Real Sociedad before getting their Premier League campaign under way with a derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage.

According to recent reports, AC Milan finished fifth in Serie A last season to earn a spot in the Europa League last season. Their massive-money acquisition this summer as been Portuguese striker Goncalo Ramos from PSG. They have played two pre-season friendlies so far, which have both ended in draws; 2-2 against Celtic and then 1-1 against city rivals Inter. They kick off their Serie A campaign at Torino on August 23.

AC Milan are thinking about bolstering their academy with the Malmö FF talent Leon Da Silva, according to a report.

In recent months, a lot of focus has been on how Milan will reinforce the first team in January and next summer. Understandably so, as Gerry Cardinale seemingly has substantial spending plans, keen on making it back to the Champions League next season.

Industry observers note that amidst all of the first-team rumours, however, Milan are also working on the academy. Jovan Kirovski is evaluating players for the Futuro side with his team, while Vincenzo Vergine (pictured) and his team are doing so for the Primavera and below.

It has been revealed that according to Gianluca Di Marzio, one of the players on Milan’s wish list is Leon Da Silva, who currently plays in the academy of Malmö FF. At the age of 16, he’s yet to make his debut with the first team, but he did feature in a friendly game last month.

In addition to Milan, the likes of Inter and Torino are also monitoring the Swede, though it seems Malmö are keen on keeping him for a few more years.

#129657. Latest Update: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands

Latest Update: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 73 min read (14506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~73 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3.
  • Islands are fundamental for studying patterns of biodiversity in time and space1,7.
  • Insects, the most diverse of all animal groups, remain underrepresented in global biogeographic studies and conservation assessments3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3. Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth’s land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends4. Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa5. The strength of island species–area relationships varies among biomes and is steepest in Mediterranean-type systems, which also support disproportionately high bee richness relative to flowering plant diversity. The number of endemic species is highest on large tropical islands, reflecting extensive in situ diversification. Major centres of bee endemism include Madagascar, Malesia (the Greater Sundas and Latest Guinea) and the Hawaiian islands, where a single large radiation of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) dominates6. Among islands that are capable of supporting endemic species, endemism scales strongly with total richness. These findings highlight the need to integrate island bee diversity into global conservation planning and position bees as a model for understanding insect evolution and conservation on islands.

Islands are fundamental for studying patterns of biodiversity in time and space1,7. The isolation and limited opportunities for colonization of remote islands have fostered evolutionarily distinct and highly endemic flora and fauna5,8,9. Consequently, islands have long been central to fundamental questions in macroecology, evolution, community ecology and species conservation10. Yet, despite their ecological and evolutionary importance, major gaps remain in our understanding of island colonization, evolution and diversification across animal taxa, especially arthropods.

Insects, the most diverse of all animal groups, remain underrepresented in global biogeographic studies and conservation assessments3. This gap largely reflects logistical and taxonomic challenges of assembling standardized, high-resolution data for insects across geographically and politically fragmented islands, which results in inadequate understanding of species’ distributions11. Consequently, tests of island biogeography theory have disproportionately focused on vertebrates (especially birds) and land vascular plants, and systematic studies across multiple archipelagos remain scarce both for insects and other invertebrates12,13,14 (but see Proios et al.15 for land snails).

Notable global efforts targeting other insect groups do exist, such as the Global Ant Biodiversity Informatics (GABI) database16, as well as efforts motivated by pest and pathogen spread, such as a global checklist of mosquito distributions17, and of patterns of island invasion by beetles18. Comparable progress has been made for Lepidoptera at regional scales, including recent large-scale analyses of butterfly biogeography across tropical Asian islands19. Nevertheless, comprehensive global syntheses—such as those available for plants20—of insect diversity and endemism across island systems are virtually absent.

Industry observers note that there are approximately 21,000 described species of bees worldwide21. They have an important role in global ecosystems, pollinating many wild flowering plants22 and crops23. On continents, bees exhibit a bimodal latitudinal diversity distribution, with peak richness in seasonally xeric mid-latitude regions that support ecosystems with a Mediterranean climate (hereafter referred to as Mediterranean-type ecosystems), as well as in adjacent desert and montane habitats2,4,24. This pattern deviates from the latitudinal diversity gradients of most other groups of plants and animals, which usually peak in the tropics25. Although the continental-scale biogeographical and ecological patterns of bees are becoming better understood, how they translate to island systems remains underexplored.

According to recent reports, generalizations about island bee biogeography have hitherto been rather qualitative in nature. For example, Michener2 noted that whereas very small bees might be carried over long distances by winds, wood-nesting bees may have dispersed across oceans via driftwood: a rafting hypothesis supported by quantitative evidence that wood-nesting bees are overrepresented in island faunas26, Michener also suggested Polynesian transport by seafarers for certain wood-nesting bee taxa that reached some of the most remote oceanic archipelagos, such as the Hawaiian islands. Consequently, bees detected by the even the first European voyages of discovery cannot be assumed to be native.

It has been revealed that recent phylogenetic evidence indicates that several bee lineages colonized upcoming biogeographic regions during the Neogene Period (around 23–2.6 million years ago) via island-hopping, showing how stepping-stone dispersal may have shaped bee composition. For example, the families Apidae, Megachilidae and Halictidae probably colonized Australia via movements from mainland Asia across the Indomalayan Archipelago27. Similar processes have been proposed to explain disjunct distributions in modern day Central America, where ancient archipelago chains acted as stepping stones between North and South America before the continents joined2.

Conversely, disjunct distribution patterns in other bee groups appear to reflect their more limited capacity to disperse and subsequently colonize islands. For example, following the breakup of Gondwana, stingless bees (Apidae, tribe Meliponini) appear to have been unable to cross the substantial marine barriers that appeared, and their present distribution in Indomalaya probably reflects episodes of sea level fluctuation and transient land-bridges, rather than long-distance overwater dispersal28.

Industry observers note that these examples indicate the importance of accurately documenting insular bee diversity to achieve a more complete and fine-grained understanding of global bee biogeography and conservation. Yet, despite this need, comprehensive data remain sparse. Only 542 bee species have been assessed for the global International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, including just 240 species recorded from islands and 68 island endemics. Of these assessed species, 26 are considered threatened, and for many of these, distributional data are not publicly accessible29. The limited representation of island taxa on global conservation lists does not reflect the well-established vulnerability of island biotas: for example, the majority of US federally listed endangered bee species are native Hawaiian endemics30.

Industry observers note that here we present a global assessment of native bee diversity on islands. Specifically, we investigate: (1) global patterns of native bee richness and endemism; (2) the influence of island characteristics (area and isolation), topography (elevation) and climate variables on both native bee richness and endemism; (3) how endemism scales with richness; and (4) the relationship between insular bee diversity and angiosperm richness. We expect the patterns of insular bee richness and endemism to be shaped by area and isolation, as predicted by island biogeography theory7, but also by biotic and climate constraints and associations, including mutualistic relationships with flowering plants22.

It has been revealed that by addressing these questions, our analyses fill knowledge gaps, providing a global baseline for investigating the evolutionary and biogeographic history, ecology and vulnerability of island bees, while highlighting priority regions for future research and conservation at both archipelago and single-island scales. More broadly, this baseline enables rigorous tests of major hypotheses in island biogeography and (meta)community assembly1 using this taxonomically diverse, and ecologically and economically important group.

In a recent development, our final dataset consists of 11,065 unique island-native bee species combinations, representing 4,128 native species across 305 islands (see Methods for details of this classification) (Fig. 1a). Consequently, of the approximately 21,000 bee species described worldwide, our data indicate that 20% occur on islands. Of these, 42% (1,742 species) are restricted exclusively to islands, accounting for around 8% of all described bee species. Although this proportion is lower than that reported for vascular plants, for which 21% of the global flora are island endemic, with 14.5% single-island endemic species (SIEs)9, as well as terrestrial mammals (about 12% single-island endemics31) and rodents specifically (about 17% endemics to islands32), it nevertheless represents a slightly higher contribution of islands to global bee diversity relative to the approximately 5–6% of global landmass represented by islands globally1. Although we focus here on native bee richness, we also recorded introduced species to distinguish genuine native diversity from non-native species accumulation. We identified at least 54 species as introduced on 143 islands, with the western honey bee (Apis mellifera) being by far the most widespread, introduced to 127 islands in our dataset (Extended Data Table 1). Invasion due to anthropogenic drivers is a major threat to insular diversity33, and evidence, at least for A. mellifera, suggests negative effects of invasive bees on native biodiversity on islands (see, for example, ref. 34).

It has been revealed that a, Map of global bee diversity on islands (n = 305 islands). Each circle represents an island for which there are recorded native bee species. The colour gradient is log-scaled and indicates the total number of native bee species recorded for each island; the size of the point or circle is proportional to the total number of endemic species found on each island. Endemism is measured as the total number of island (or island group; Methods) endemic species. Left, histogram showing the total number of endemic bee species by latitude. Right, histogram showing the total number of bees on islands by latitude (5° latitude steps; native richness maximum = 3,552 species (35° to 40° N), endemism maximum = 298 species (−10° to −5° N). Note that this pattern does not control for variation in the number and size distribution of islands across latitude (but see Fig. 2). Islands marked with an X have recorded bee species consisting exclusively of non-native species. b, Upset plot showing global distribution of bee species endemic to and shared between islands in different zoogeographical realms62 and the mainland. Of 4,128 native bee species found on islands, 1,742 are recorded only from islands, representing an 8.4% share of global bee diversity that is unique to islands. Each bar indicates the number of species unique to that geographic combination. Coloured bars and coloured realm names represent the number of species endemic to islands within that realm. Coloured circles indicate island-only comparisons. Grey bars indicate species that are shared across the island realms or mainland. Island base map in a adapted from ref. 63.

According to recent reports, bee species richness peaks in the Western Palaearctic Realm, whereas endemism (species only found on islands within these realms) is highest on Indomalayan (466 species) and Australasian (443 species) islands (Fig. 1b). Clear differences in island bee richness are also apparent among biomes (Fig. 2), however this pattern is influenced by variation in island area. Species richness was highest in Mediterranean-type biomes: Sicily (approximately 25,000 km2, 636 species), is the island with the highest species richness worldwide and Cyprus (approximately 9,300 km2, 384 species) has the highest species richness of the oceanic islands. The East Aegean islands (approximately 5,000 km2, 589 species) also support large bee faunas, dominated by widespread continental species, reflecting their limited degree of isolation. In contrast to the high richness, endemism on these islands is low, with only Crete (14 species) and Cyprus (23 species) showing comparatively high levels of island endemism. Despite its proximity to the Levant region and its complex origins in tectonic uplift, Cyprus is treated here as an oceanic island owing to its lack of historical land bridge connections to the mainland. The most species-rich Mediterranean-type oceanic island of strictly volcanic origin is Tenerife (2,000 km2, 57 species).

a, Biome-specific ISARs. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Slopes (β) are reported for each biome. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome; values in parentheses show total native bee richness. b, Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.13, 95% confidence interval [−0.21, −0.04], t(208.0) = −2.96, P = 0.003). The solid line represents the fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Point colour indicates the proportion of SIEs. c, Predicted bee species richness by island type (continental, fragment or oceanic) from the full mixed-effects model, holding other predictors constant (predictions represent an island of median area (around 445 km2), median isolation (approximately 605 km from mainland) and median sampling coverage (35% after sample-size adjustment, raw median 79%). Circles and lines indicate the model-predicted mean ± 95% confidence intervals, with the number of islands shown below each category.

Sources indicate that tropical islands, by contrast, account for moderate overall native species richness compared with Mediterranean-type islands but markedly higher levels of endemism. Latest Guinea supports 284 species, of which 210 (73%) are endemic, making it by far the richest island in the Australasian realm. The nearby Maluku Islands archipelago (34,000 km2) hosts 102 species, including 62 endemics (61%), and includes Seram (18,000 km2), the most species-rich tropical, oceanic island for bees (87 species).

It has been revealed that in the Neotropics, Hispaniola represents the most species-rich oceanic island, with 66 species. In the Nearctic, the predominantly oceanic California Channel Islands (approximately 910 km2) have a high overall richness (154 species) but low levels of endemism (5%). In the Afrotropics, Madagascar stands out with 226 species, of which 201 (89%) are endemic. Within Oceania, which consists only of oceanic islands, the Hawaiian islands (17,000 km2) are a major hotspot, with all 65 native species of wild bees belonging to a single lineage of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis), and endemic to the archipelago6. Among other oceanic systems, the Mediterranean-climate Canary Islands (approximately 5,400 km2) host a similarly high number of endemic species (57 out of 128 species), although at a lower proportional level of archipelago endemism (AE) (45%).

Industry observers note that globally, bee richness on islands peaks in the Northern Hemisphere at mid-latitudes (Fig. 1a), mirroring the mid-latitude peak of bee richness observed on mainlands4. This pattern contrasts with the latitudinal diversity gradient seen in other diverse insect groups, such as ants, whose global richness peaks predominantly in the tropics35. The lack of an island-specific bimodal diversity pattern comparable to that found for the mainlands2,4 is probably a consequence of the limited number of Mediterranean-type islands in the Southern Hemisphere. This asymmetry reflects the true distribution of islands globally36, and not simply sampling bias; our global dataset confirms data availability and sufficient coverage across these regions (Fig. 3). This pattern occurs both on continental and oceanic islands, although many of the larger islands within the Mediterranean-type biome were continental or complex in origin. Such environments favour diverse wild bee assemblages through a combination of evolutionary history and ecological conditions. Bees are thought to have originated in the arid environments of Western Gondwana2,27, with limited but predictable rainfall that generates short yet intense blooming periods and a high flowering plant diversity in open habitats2,4,37. These conditions promote temporal synchrony between bee flight periods and floral resources, fostering increased specialization and resource partitioning that reduces competition. This synchrony promotes local speciation and therefore increases richness, allowing these regions to defy the traditional latitudinal diversity gradient2. Our global results support these conclusions but trait-based research focusing on the biome-specific patterns of habitat and dietary specialization of bees on islands are needed to directly test these claims.

The index combines Chao–Jost sample coverage64 with a weighted-by-sampling effort, based on the total number of occurrence records. Coverage was calculated using a species/island abundance (count of all occurrences per species per island) matrix of all records to estimate the proportion of the total individuals per island that belong to the observed species, using a non-parametric estimator that accounts for the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons). Sources indicate that to test fundamental aspects of MacArthur and Wilson’s theory of island biogeography7 for bee diversity, we used a mixed-effects model with archipelago identity as the random effect. The final best model was selected based on Akaike information criterion corrected for sample sizes (AICc) and included log10-transformed island area in km2 and its interaction with biome, as well as isolation (log10-transformed distance to continental mainland in km) as fixed effects. This model explains 66% of the variance in species richness through fixed effects (area, isolation, island type and biome), and 75% variance when including archipelago identity (conditional R2). This moderate difference in R2 values indicates that native richness is strongly governed by broad biogeographic variables, with some unexplained regional structure.

Island area indicates a consistent positive effect on native bee richness but the island species–area relationship (ISAR) slopes differ significantly among biomes (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 1). Mediterranean-type biomes showed the strongest species–area response (β = 0.50), which is significantly steeper than that of all other biomes (Supplementary Table 2). Tropical islands exhibit an intermediate effect, (β = 0.28), which is indistinguishable from temperate islands (β = 0.18). By contrast, desert (β = 0.02) and boreal (β = 0.02) islands display flatter slopes, indicating that island size is not a major constraint on bee diversity in these biomes. The impact of biome on species area slopes is observed more clearly on oceanic islands (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 3), specifically, the ISAR slope for Mediterranean-type islands is significantly greater than for the others. This is not the case for continental islands, where these ISAR slope differences are far less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 3).

Richness decreases with island isolation (β = −0.13, P < 0.003) (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 1), corresponding to a reduction of roughly 15% in species richness for each tenfold increase in distance from the mainland. This isolation effect is uniform across all biomes, supporting the fundamental principle that remote islands receive fewer colonists and consequently maintain lower richness as a function of their area7. We also observe a clear influence of island type on richness. Oceanic islands support substantially fewer species than continental (β = −0.19, P = 0.01) and fragment islands (β = −0.27, P = 0.01; Supplementary Table 2), consistent with their lack of past land connections to the mainland, more limited historical species pools and generally younger geological ages, whereas a high proportion of continental shelf islands were connected to the mainland only a few thousand years ago, leading to more ‘harmonic’ biotas1. Alternative models (ΔAICc < 2) additionally include positive relationships with temperature seasonality and annual precipitation. Neither climate variable has a statistically significant effect (Supplementary Table 4).

It has been revealed that our results support the conclusion that ISARs can vary considerably as a function of island geo-environmental properties12,38. Specifically, bees may benefit from biome-specific increases in ecological complexity in Mediterranean-type biomes owing to temporal differences in habitat availability, which can permit increased richness even at small scales, resulting in area having a stronger effect on richness than in tropical or temperate biomes2,4. The finding that Mediterranean-type islands in our models have the steepest ISAR slopes and highest richness values align with the high seasonality of the climate and flowering plant diversity characteristic of Mediterranean climates39, providing diverse nesting sites and floral resources throughout the year.

Although biomes explain considerable variation in richness on islands, they represent broad proxies for climate and habitat diversity. The steep ISAR slope for Mediterranean-type systems suggests that explicitly measuring finer-scale variables, such as resource availability and microhabitat diversity, may provide deeper insights into the mechanisms underlying island bee biogeography. Habitat diversity and environmental heterogeneity, and the potentially associated diversity of mutualist partners, can constitute important predictors of species richness40. In our global models, these factors are likely to be implicitly incorporated when comparing between islands by combining area and biome. However, a single biome classification masks within-island variation as for many large islands with a high elevational range, such as Madagascar, Tenerife, New Guinea or Hawai’i (Major Island), representing the island as a single biome inevitably underestimates its pronounced environmental heterogeneity, which is recognized as a driver of high species diversity and endemism40. Additionally, regional geographic context is an important consideration, as shown by the islands of Lesvos and Cyprus, which show comparatively high species richness values for their area (positive residuals from the Mediterranean-type ISAR; top 5% among Mediterranean-type islands). These islands sit at the border between the European bee fauna and the exceptionally rich western Asian fauna, and the resulting high comparative species richness for their area may be due to this dual species pool from which bees can colonize41.

Industry observers note that sampling effort is uneven across regions, as expected for a global dataset (Fig. 3), with parts of Oceania, Indomalaya and Australasia being comparatively under-sampled. To account for this heterogeneity, we included sampling completeness, measured as the proportion of individuals belonging to observed species and weighted by sample size, as a fixed effect in the native richness model (Supplementary Table 1). Completeness has a positive effect on native bee richness (β = 0.21, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 3). Islands with a greater sampling completeness tend to have higher estimated richness. However, controlling for sampling completeness does not weaken the central results above. The island–biome–area effects remained strong after adjusting for sampling completeness confirming that these patterns were not a result of uneven sampling effort. This indicates that the relationships between area, isolation and richness, and in particular the contrast between mid-latitude richness and high tropical endemism, reflects true ecological differences (Fig. 3). Future efforts to digitize and provide open access to museum collections42,43, conduct targeted expeditions to historically difficult-to-sample islands2,44 and harness citizen science platforms such as iNaturalist45 will be critical to resolving knowledge gaps in island bee diversity, an important task given the projected gaps in global bee diversity46.

According to recent reports, to identify the biogeographic and climatic predictors of endemism and assess whether richness can explain endemism patterns, we tested the same linear mixed-effects models as for native richness (Fig. 4a,b). Across islands capable of supporting SIEs (SIE ≥ 1, n = 113), area is associated with increased SIE richness (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 5) and this relationship varies significantly with biome, as observed for richness. However, unlike richness, biome-specific area slopes for SIE differs significantly between tropical and temperate islands, with a steeper relationship in tropical islands (Δ = 0.27, P = 0.01), whereas the difference between tropical and Mediterranean-type islands was marginal (Δ = 0.28, P = 0.06; Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6). Isolation (log10-transformed distance to nearest landmass larger than 1,000 km2) has only a weak, non-significant positive influence (β = 0.09, P = 0.11; Fig. 4a,b). Temperature seasonality had a significant positive effect on SIE (β = 0.28, P = 0.018), and sampling completeness and elevation range each appeared as significant positive predictors in alternative models within ΔAICc < 2 (Supplementary Table 7). We note that sampling completeness could bias endemism estimates in both directions, overestimating endemism on well-studied islands where the same species have not yet been recorded elsewhere, and underestimating it where undiscovered endemics remain.

Industry observers note that the observed patterns are consistent across data subsets but without the interaction of area and biome. On oceanic islands with endemics (n = 69), area remains the strongest predictor (β = 0.32, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.38; Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). Among islands rich in SIE (>5% of native richness; n = 96), SIE richness increases with area (β = 0.36, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.66) and increases marginally with sampling completeness (β = 0.16, P = 0.02) (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). These results parallel global patterns of vascular plant endemism on islands47. The mid-latitudinal peak in bee species richness2, seen on islands predominantly in the Northern Hemisphere, does not translate into increased bee endemism. Rather, bee endemism is greatest in the tropics (Extended Data Fig. 5). Patterns for AE are broadly similar. Across islands hosting AEs (n = 217) area was again the main predictor and interacted with biome (Supplementary Table 5). However, AE–area slopes were consistent across tropical, temperate, and Mediterranean-type biomes, with only desert islands showing a significantly lower rate than tropical islands (Δ = 0.35, P = 0.01; Supplementary Table 6). Isolation (distance from mainland) is non-significant (β = −0.04, P = 0.48) and sampling completeness is also included as a significant effect, suggesting that islands with high numbers of AEs are also the best studied (β = 0.14, P = 0.01). Additionally, there is a significant positive effect of elevation (β = 0.18, P = 0.01) suggesting that topographically complex islands support a greater diversity of endemics at the archipelago scale (Extended Data Fig. 6).

A model predicting SIE from overall native richness alone shows a clear correlation (R2 = 0.44) and improved significantly with the inclusion of biome (ΔR2 = 0.15, χ2 = 33.1, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table 8). Although adding the interaction term yields a significant model improvement (ΔR2 = 0.02, χ2 = 8.15, P = 0.04), post hoc pairwise comparisons reveal no significant differences in slopes between biomes after correcting for multiple testing (Supplementary Table 8). This indicates a practically uniform global rate of increasing SIE with richness but with distinct baseline shifts; specifically, Mediterranean-type islands support significantly fewer baseline SIEs than all other biomes (Extended Data Fig. 7). Conversely, for AEs (R2 = 0.55), the full interaction model results in the best fit (ΔR2 = 0.14, χ2 = 72.54, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 8), demonstrating that the rate endemic species accumulate with increasing richness is biome-dependent. Pairwise comparisons indicate that the slope for Mediterranean-type biomes (0.42 ± 0.10) is significantly flatter than in desert (0.83 ± 0.12, P = 0.02), tropical (0.96 ± 0.03, P < 0.001) and temperate (0.75 ± 0.06, P = 0.01) biomes, indicating a partial decoupling between richness and AE (Supplementary Table 9). Although Mediterranean-type islands generally support fewer AEs than expected across the richness gradient, the Canary Islands stand out as an exception, showing high AE richness consistent with their high overall richness, although probably enhanced by their relative isolation from the primary Mediterranean source pool (Extended Data Fig. 6). This divergence also highlights that the AE model probably captures more ancient diversification compared with the SIE model48,49. This partial decoupling contrasts with vascular plants, for which the richest islands also tend to host the highest numbers of endemic species, particularly in the case of large tropical islands9. Our results are consistent with previous macroecological studies50, suggesting that the relationship between richness and endemism is not simple and varies among taxa.

In a recent development, together, these findings reveal that bee endemism is concentrated on large tropical islands and certain oceanic archipelagos rather than in areas of peak species richness globally. Latest Guinea and Madagascar stand out for supporting both high numbers and high proportions of endemic species. By contrast, certain other island systems, including the Caribbean, the Philippines and the Hawaiian islands, are characterized by only a high proportion of endemics. This apparent divergence between patterns of richness and endemism suggests a distinction between the factors structuring island assembly attributable to colonization and evolutionary diversification in bees. Wet, humid tropical conditions, combined with greater isolation of many oceanic tropical islands, present environmental barriers to bee colonization2. Therefore, successful colonizers are presented with greater ecological opportunity, and this can lead to high in situ diversification1. These patterns suggest distinct evolutionary histories: high endemism in Madagascar probably reflects multiple independent radiations51, whereas in other systems single radiations account for high proportions of endemism, such as Palaeorhiza in New Guinea52, Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) in the Hawaiian archipelago6 and Lasioglossum (Homalictus) across Pacific islands such as Samoa and Fiji53,54. Conversely, the factors that support high richness in Mediterranean-type islands are likely to include: (1) the adaptation to arid environments; but also (2) frequent arrivals from nearby continental source pools, providing sufficient gene flow to inhibit in situ diversification and thus result in lower endemism55. Globally, bees provide evidence that endemism, and by extension extinction risk, is not inextricably linked to overall species richness, often diverging into regions of high endemism but low richness or high richness with low endemism56.

Building on these findings, we additionally examine how plant diversity, as a potential biotic driver, covaries with bee richness, given that bees depend strongly on flowering plants for food and nesting resources22,24. Across the 175 islands for which we have both angiosperm richness data and native bee richness, we observe a positive correlation: angiosperm richness alone explains 49% of variation in bee richness across islands (R2 = 0.49), a relationship that persists after accounting for island area and isolation (β = 0.64, P < 0.001; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 10). The slope of the relationship between angiosperm and bee richness is largely consistent across biomes (likelihood ratio test: χ2 = 7.02, P = 0.06). However, temperate islands show a slightly steeper relationship compared with the tropical baseline (β = 0.55, P = 0.015; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 10). Additionally, we observe differences from the baseline in total supported bee richness in Mediterranean-type islands: they support 5.6 times more bee species than tropical islands at equivalent plant richness, area and isolation (P < 0.001; Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 11).

Native angiosperm richness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation for degrees of freedom (β = 0.60, 95% confidence interval [0.36, 0.84], t(126) = 5.00, P = 1.89 × 10−6). b, Bee species richness for each island (n = 175 islands) adjusted to the global mean angiosperm richness, area and isolation.
